46325.q: What did the FARC become after the peace agreement of 2016?
a: A new guerrilla group in Venezuela
46325.e: The FARC laid down its weapons and became a political party. The agreement guaranteed it seats in Congress for some years.
46325.m: After the peace agreement the FARC turned into a party.

46326.q: In which city did the Indochina Conference take place in 1954?
46326.e: The conference met in Geneva from 26 April to 21 July 1954. Once again Switzerland provided a neutral place for negotiations.
46326.m: The Indochina Conference took place in Geneva in 1954.

46327.q: Which military defeat of France came immediately before the Indochina Conference?
a: The Battle of Điện Biên Phủ
46327.e: The French fortress of Điện Biên Phủ fell on 7 May 1954, while the conference was already under way. This greatly weakened France's negotiating position.
46327.m: The fall of Điện Biên Phủ shaped the Indochina Conference.

46328.q: Along which line of latitude was Vietnam provisionally divided in 1954?
46328.e: The demarcation line ran along the 17th parallel. It was only meant to be temporary but became the border between North and South Vietnam until 1975.
46328.m: Vietnam was divided at the 17th parallel in 1954.

46329.q: What did the Geneva Accords of 1954 provide for the reunification of Vietnam?
a: Elections across all of Vietnam in 1956
46329.e: Nationwide elections were planned for 1956. They never took place because South Vietnam and the USA rejected them.
46329.m: The planned elections of 1956 never took place in Vietnam.

46330.q: Which French prime minister promised in 1954 to achieve a ceasefire in Indochina within 30 days?
46330.e: Pierre Mendès France became prime minister in June 1954 and set himself a deadline. He only just met it.
46330.m: Pierre Mendès France ended the French Indochina War in 1954.

46331.q: Which two countries jointly chaired the Indochina Conference in 1954?
46331.e: The British foreign secretary Anthony Eden and the Soviet foreign minister Vyacheslav Molotov chaired the conference together. The People's Republic of China also took part with Zhou Enlai.
46331.m: Britain and the Soviet Union chaired the Geneva Indochina Conference.

46332.q: What was the USA's attitude to the final declaration of the Indochina Conference?
a: It was the first to sign it
46332.e: The USA took part but did not sign the final declaration. It only stated that it would not use force against the agreements.
46332.m: The USA did not sign the Geneva final declaration of 1954.

46333.q: Which two other states of Indochina had their independence confirmed by the Geneva Conference in 1954?
46333.e: Besides the arrangements for Vietnam, the accords confirmed the independence of Laos and Cambodia. Foreign troops were to withdraw.
46333.m: In 1954 the independence of Laos and Cambodia was confirmed in Geneva.

46334.q: Which French president pushed through the Évian negotiations?
46334.e: Charles de Gaulle came to power in 1958 and recognised Algeria's right to self-determination in 1959. In 1961 generals in Algiers staged a coup against his policy.
46334.m: Charles de Gaulle led France to the Évian Accords.

46335.q: On which lake is Évian-les-Bains, after which the treaties of 1962 are named?
46335.e: Évian-les-Bains lies on the French southern shore of Lake Geneva, opposite Lausanne. Being close to Switzerland was important for the negotiations.
46335.m: Évian lies on the southern shore of Lake Geneva.

46336.q: What role did Switzerland play in the Évian negotiations?
a: It was a party to the war
46336.e: Switzerland made contacts, organised secret meetings and hosted the Algerian delegation. The diplomat Olivier Long was a key figure.
46336.m: Switzerland provided good offices in the Évian negotiations.

46337.q: Where did the Algerian delegation stay during the Évian negotiations?
46337.e: For security reasons, the delegation of the Algerian government in exile was housed in the canton of Vaud. A Swiss Army helicopter flew them to the negotiations in Évian and back.
46337.m: The Algerian delegation stayed in Switzerland during the negotiations.

46338.q: Which Algerian independence movement fought against France from 1954?
46338.e: The FLN began the armed struggle on 1 November 1954. Its government in exile later negotiated with France at Évian, while the OAS fought against independence.
46338.m: The FLN led Algeria's fight for independence.

46339.q: Roughly how long did the Algerian War, which the Évian Accords ended, last?
46339.e: The war began in November 1954 and ended with the ceasefire in March 1962. Hundreds of thousands of people died.
46339.m: The Algerian War lasted from 1954 to 1962.

46340.q: How were the Évian Accords confirmed in France?
a: By a ruling of the Constitutional Council
By a decree of the army
46340.e: On 8 April 1962 about 90 per cent of voters in France approved. In Algeria itself the vote was only allowed later.
46340.m: The French approved the Évian Accords in 1962.

46341.q: On which day did Algeria become independent after the Évian Accords?
46341.e: After a referendum in Algeria on 1 July 1962, independence was proclaimed on 5 July. The date recalls the French conquest of Algiers on 5 July 1830.

a: A mediator travels back and forth between the parties
The parties meet in each other's capitals in turn
Diplomats change their posts every year
46342.e: In shuttle diplomacy the parties to a conflict do not meet directly. A mediator carries proposals and answers from one side to the other.
46342.m: In shuttle diplomacy a mediator travels between the parties to a conflict.

46343.q: Which US Secretary of State is the term shuttle diplomacy especially associated with?
46343.e: The term “shuttle diplomacy” became known for Henry Kissinger's journeys after the Yom Kippur War of 1973. He repeatedly flew back and forth between Cairo, Jerusalem and Damascus.
46343.m: Henry Kissinger made shuttle diplomacy famous.

46344.q: After which war did Henry Kissinger carry out his well-known shuttle diplomacy in the Middle East?
a: After the Yom Kippur War of 1973
46344.e: After the war of October 1973, Israeli, Egyptian and Syrian troops faced each other at close quarters. Kissinger mediated the separation of forces.
46344.m: Kissinger's shuttle diplomacy followed the Yom Kippur War of 1973.

46345.q: Which agreements did Kissinger's shuttle diplomacy achieve in 1974?
46345.e: In 1974 disengagement agreements were reached between Israel and Egypt in Sinai and between Israel and Syria on the Golan Heights. They separated the armies with buffer zones.
46345.m: In 1974 Kissinger's shuttle diplomacy led to disengagement agreements.

46346.q: What are talks called in which the parties are in the same place but the mediator moves between separate rooms?
46346.e: In proximity talks the delegations sit in different rooms. They are a form of shuttle diplomacy over a short distance.
46346.m: Proximity talks are shuttle diplomacy between separate rooms.

46347.q: Why do mediators often choose shuttle diplomacy instead of direct meetings?
46347.e: Parties to a conflict often do not recognise each other or do not want to be seen together. The mediator can also soften or rephrase proposals before they reach the other side.
46347.m: Shuttle diplomacy helps when parties to a conflict do not want to talk directly.

46348.q: Which means of transport made Kissinger's shuttle diplomacy possible in such a short time?
46348.e: Kissinger often flew between the capitals several times a day. The English term “shuttle” recalls a shuttle service.
46348.m: Shuttle diplomacy in the Middle East was possible thanks to aeroplanes.

46349.q: What is meant by Track II diplomacy?
46349.e: In Track II diplomacy, experts, former officials or representatives of civil society, for example, meet informally. Track I, by contrast, means the official diplomacy of governments.
46349.m: Track II diplomacy is unofficial diplomacy outside governments.

46350.q: Why is official government diplomacy called “Track I”?
a: It is the first, official track of diplomacy
It only takes place once a year
It is only carried out by one state
It is the oldest diplomacy in Europe
46350.e: In 1981 the US diplomat Joseph Montville distinguished two tracks: the official diplomacy of governments (Track I) and unofficial contacts (Track II).
46350.m: Track I is official diplomacy, Track II unofficial diplomacy.

a: Talks with officials acting in a private capacity together with experts
Negotiations between half as many states
46351.e: In Track 1.5, government representatives also take part, but unofficially and together with non-state experts. The form lies between official and unofficial diplomacy.
46351.m: Track 1.5 diplomacy mixes officials and non-state experts.

46352.q: Which agreement began with secret unofficial talks arranged by a Norwegian research institute?
46352.e: From 1993 the research institute Fafo made secret meetings possible between Israeli academics and representatives of the PLO. This led to official negotiations and the agreement of 1993.
46352.m: The Oslo Accords are a classic example of Track II diplomacy.

46353.q: Which unofficial Israeli-Palestinian peace initiative presented in 2003 did Switzerland support?
46353.e: The Geneva Initiative was drawn up by Yossi Beilin and Yasser Abed Rabbo, who did not act on behalf of their governments. Switzerland supported the project financially and logistically.
46353.m: In 2003 Switzerland supported the unofficial Geneva Initiative.

46354.q: Which advantage is often attributed to Track II diplomacy?
a: Ideas can be tested without commitment
Results are immediately binding under international law
46354.e: Because no one is speaking officially, proposals can be tried out without a government losing face. Governments can distance themselves from them if necessary.
46354.m: Track II diplomacy allows ideas to be tested without official commitment.

46355.q: What is the concept called that divides diplomacy into nine tracks such as business, religion and the media?
46355.e: Louise Diamond and John McDonald developed the concept of multi-track diplomacy. It extends the distinction between Track I and Track II to nine tracks.
46355.m: Multi-track diplomacy distinguishes nine tracks of peace work.

46356.q: Who typically takes part in Track II dialogues?
a: Serving chiefs of the general staff
46356.e: Typical participants are experts from universities, think tanks and civil society, as well as former diplomats. They often have good contacts with the government but do not speak for it.
46356.m: Track II dialogues are attended mainly by experts and former officials.

46357.q: What do you call an autocracy in which a group of senior officers rules together?
46357.e: The Spanish word ‘junta’ means assembly or committee. Examples are the military governments in Argentina from 1976 to 1983 and in Greece from 1967 to 1974.
46357.m: A military junta is a government made up of several senior officers.

46358.q: What do you call a regime in which elections are held regularly but are neither free nor fair?
46358.e: In an electoral autocracy there are elections, but the opposition and media are suppressed. Research projects such as V-Dem distinguish it from closed autocracies without elections.
46358.m: Electoral autocracies hold elections that are neither free nor fair.

46359.q: Which title of the Russian tsars expressed the claim to unlimited sole rule?
46359.e: The Russian title ‘Samoderzhets’ means autocrat, literally ‘self-ruler’. It stressed that the tsar's power did not come from a constitution or a parliament.
46359.m: The Russian tsars called themselves autocrats, claiming unlimited power.

46360.q: Which feature fundamentally distinguishes an autocracy from a democracy?
a: The lack of checks on power by the people
46360.e: Autocracies also have armies, taxes and capitals. What matters is that the government cannot be checked and removed through free elections, separation of powers and independent courts.
46360.m: Autocracies above all lack effective control of power by the people.

46361.q: In research, what do you call a dictatorship in which power is centred entirely on one individual?
46361.e: The political scientist Barbara Geddes distinguished military regimes, one-party regimes and personalist regimes. In personalist regimes everything depends on the ruler and their inner circle.
46361.m: In personalist regimes power is concentrated in one person.

46362.q: What does political science mean by ‘autocratisation’?
a: The introduction of a planned economy
46362.e: Autocratisation means a process in which free elections, media freedom or the separation of powers are gradually weakened. It can happen in democracies as well as in states that are already authoritarian.
46362.m: Autocratisation is the gradual erosion of a state's democratic features.

46363.q: In research, what do you call states that mix features of democracy and autocracy?
46363.e: Hybrid regimes combine, for example, regular elections with restricted press freedom and a dependent judiciary. They lie in a grey zone between democracy and closed autocracy.
46363.m: Hybrid regimes lie in a grey zone between democracy and autocracy.

46364.q: Which feature did Juan Linz name for authoritarian regimes as opposed to totalitarian ones?
46364.e: According to Linz, authoritarian regimes allow a limited, unaccountable pluralism, for example the Church, the army or business associations. Totalitarian regimes, by contrast, tolerate no independent centres of power.
46364.m: Authoritarian regimes tolerate limited pluralism, totalitarian ones do not.

46365.q: Which values do authoritarian regimes often invoke instead of spreading a closed ideology?
a: Human rights and separation of powers
46365.e: The political scientist Juan Linz called such basic attitudes ‘mentalities’. They are more flexible than an ideology such as communism and do not demand total conviction from the population.
46365.m: Authoritarian regimes appeal to values such as order and nation rather than to a closed ideology.

46366.q: Using which regime as an example did Juan Linz develop his concept of the authoritarian regime in 1964?
46366.e: In 1964 Linz published the study ‘An Authoritarian Regime: Spain’. For him the Franco regime was neither a democracy nor a totalitarian system.
46366.m: Franco's Spain served Juan Linz as the model case of an authoritarian regime.

46367.q: Which authoritarian regime ended on 25 April 1974 with the Carnation Revolution?
46367.e: The Estado Novo built up by António de Oliveira Salazar was overthrown in 1974 by a largely bloodless military coup. Soldiers put carnations in the barrels of their rifles.
46367.m: The Carnation Revolution of 1974 ended Portugal's Estado Novo.

46368.q: Which research group led by Theodor W. Adorno developed the F-scale in 1950 to measure authoritarian attitudes?
46368.e: The study ‘The Authoritarian Personality’ investigated why people are receptive to anti-democratic ideas. The F stands for fascism.
46368.m: The F-scale from ‘The Authoritarian Personality’ was meant to measure authoritarian attitudes.

46369.q: How did Augusto Pinochet's military rule in Chile end?
46369.e: In 1988 a majority voted against another term for Pinochet. Free elections followed in 1989 and the return to democracy in 1990.
46369.m: Pinochet's rule ended after a lost referendum in 1988.

46370.q: According to Juan Linz, which form of politics do authoritarian regimes usually do without?
46370.e: Authoritarian regimes tend to rely on depoliticisation and a passive population. Totalitarian systems, on the other hand, constantly mobilise the masses for their aims.
46370.m: Authoritarian regimes prefer passive citizens to constantly mobilised ones.

46371.q: Which attitude do researchers measure when they study authoritarian attitudes in individual people?
a: Submission to authority and rejection of nonconformists
46371.e: Scales such as Bob Altemeyer's measure how strongly someone obeys authority, wants to punish nonconformists and clings to conventions.
46371.m: Authoritarian attitudes show in obedience to authority and harshness towards nonconformists.

46372.q: According to the model of Friedrich and Brzeziński, when is a dictatorship totalitarian?
a: When all the features of the model work together
When there is a secret police
When the country is at war
46372.e: The 1956 model is also called the ‘six-point syndrome’. According to the authors, only the combination of all six features marks a totalitarian dictatorship.
46372.m: Friedrich and Brzeziński described totalitarianism with six features.

46373.q: Which of the following is one of the features according to Friedrich and Brzeziński?
46373.e: A system of physical and psychological terror carried out by a secret police is part of the six-point syndrome. It is aimed at real and supposed opponents.
46373.m: A terroristic secret police is one of the hallmarks of totalitarian rule.

46374.q: Which feature in the model of Friedrich and Brzeziński concerns the economy?
46374.e: The authors named central control and direction of the entire economy. Added to this are ideology, a single party, terror, a monopoly on communication and a monopoly on weapons.
46374.m: Totalitarian states direct the economy centrally.

46375.q: Which monopoly belongs to the model of Friedrich and Brzeziński alongside the monopoly on weapons?
46375.e: The party controls press, radio and film almost completely. In this way the population is only meant to receive the information the regime wants.
46375.m: A totalitarian state claims a monopoly over the mass media.

46376.q: Which two dictatorships are seen as classic examples of totalitarian rule?
a: Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union under Stalin
Spain under Franco and Portugal under Salazar
Chile under Pinochet and Argentina under Videla
Greece under the colonels and Turkey
46376.e: Researchers such as Hannah Arendt or Friedrich and Brzeziński studied these two regimes above all. Spain under Franco, by contrast, is usually seen as an authoritarian dictatorship.
46376.m: Nazi Germany and Stalin's Soviet Union are the classic totalitarian dictatorships.

46377.q: Which thinker published the work ‘The Origins of Totalitarianism’ in 1951?
46377.e: In it Hannah Arendt examined antisemitism, imperialism and total domination. She saw ideology and terror as the essence of totalitarian systems.
46377.m: Hannah Arendt saw ideology and terror as the core of total domination.

46378.q: In which country was the term ‘totalitarian’ first used in the 1920s?
46378.e: The liberal Giovanni Amendola used ‘totalitario’ critically in 1923 for the methods of the Fascists. Mussolini then adopted the term positively for his ‘Stato totalitario’.
46378.m: The term totalitarian arose in Italy in the early Fascist period.

46379.q: What do you call the alignment of all clubs, associations and German states with the line of the Nazi party from 1933?
46379.e: Through Gleichschaltung, states, trade unions, parties and clubs were dissolved or put under Nazi control. Independent forces in society were meant to disappear.
46379.m: From 1933 Gleichschaltung removed the independence of associations and states.

46380.q: Which country is often named as an example of competitive authoritarianism?
46380.e: Under Putin in the 2000s, elections with opposition parties took place, but the media and the courts favoured the government. The political scientists Levitsky and Way coined the term in 2002.
46380.m: Competitive authoritarianism combines real elections with unfair conditions.

46381.q: Which image do Levitsky and Way use for the position of the opposition under competitive authoritarianism?
46381.e: Elections take place and the opposition can take part, but the state systematically favours the government. Media, money and the courts create an ‘uneven playing field’.
46381.m: Under competitive authoritarianism the opposition fights on an uneven playing field.

46382.q: What distinguishes competitive authoritarianism from a fully closed authoritarian regime?
a: The opposition can in principle win elections
There are no elections at all
46382.e: Under competitive authoritarianism, elections are real, if unfair, contests. The rulers have to reckon with defeat, which can make these regimes unstable.
46382.m: Under competitive authoritarianism an opposition election victory remains possible in principle.

46383.q: Which Peruvian president dissolved Congress in a ‘self-coup’ in 1992 and is seen as an example of competitive authoritarianism?
46383.e: On 5 April 1992 Fujimori had Congress dissolved and the judiciary restructured. After that he governed with elections that were distorted by bribery and media control.
46383.m: Fujimori's self-coup of 1992 is a well-known example of securing power in an authoritarian way.

46384.q: Under competitive authoritarianism, what is typical of the courts?
a: They are formally independent but influenced by the government
There are no courts at all
They are controlled by the opposition
They only rule on foreign nationals
46384.e: Courts continue to exist, but governments fill judges' posts with loyal people or put judges under pressure. Alongside elections, parliament and the media, the judiciary is an arena in which the opposition can challenge the government.
46384.m: Under competitive authoritarianism there are courts, but the government influences them.

46385.q: Which book did Steven Levitsky publish in 2018 together with Daniel Ziblatt?
46385.e: In ‘How Democracies Die’ the authors describe how elected politicians can gradually hollow out democratic institutions.
46385.m: ‘How Democracies Die’ shows how democracies can be hollowed out from within.

46386.q: Which tool do competitive authoritarian governments typically use against critical media?
46386.e: Instead of open violence, such regimes often rely on seemingly legal means such as tax audits, defamation lawsuits or withdrawing licences. In this way they keep up the appearance of the rule of law.
46386.m: Competitive authoritarian regimes often suppress criticism by seemingly legal means.

46387.q: What is meant by an electoral autocracy?
a: A regime that holds elections but controls them so that it cannot lose
A democracy with an especially large number of elections
A monarchy with no elections at all
A state in which only party members may vote
46387.e: The political scientist Andreas Schedler described a ‘menu of manipulation’, such as controlling the media, excluding candidates or putting pressure on voters. The elections take place, but they are not fair.
46387.m: Electoral autocracies hold elections they cannot lose.

46388.q: In the GDR, what was the practice called of simply folding the ballot paper without marking it and putting it in the box?
46388.e: Voters approved the single list of the National Front by simply folding the paper. Anyone who used the voting booth stood out and made themselves look suspicious.
46388.m: Paper folding shows that GDR elections were not secret ballots.

46389.q: In which GDR election in 1989 did civil rights activists prove electoral fraud by observing the vote counting themselves?
46389.e: In the local elections of 7 May 1989, the leadership announced almost 99 per cent approval. Opposition members had observed public counts and counted far more votes against.
46389.m: The rigged local elections in May 1989 fuelled protest against the GDR leadership.

46390.q: Which body of the OSCE observes elections in its member states?
a: The Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights
The Council of Europe's Venice Commission
46390.e: The ODIHR, based in Warsaw, sends out election observation missions. Their reports show whether elections were free and fair.
46390.m: The OSCE's ODIHR uses election observation to judge whether elections are free and fair.

46391.q: According to the official result, how high was approval in Austria in the referendum on the ‘Anschluss’ in April 1938?
46391.e: The vote only took place after the German army had marched in, under massive propaganda and without a truly secret ballot. The official result was 99.73 per cent yes.
46391.m: Almost unanimous results are a typical sign of sham votes.

46392.q: What is a typical feature of elections to the Supreme People's Assembly in North Korea?
a: There is only one candidate per constituency
Many parties compete against each other
Only members of the military may vote
The election takes place only online
46392.e: Voters can only approve the candidate put forward. The official approval rates are close to 100 per cent.
46392.m: Elections with only one candidate per constituency offer no real choice.

46393.q: What is the deliberate redrawing of constituency boundaries to your own advantage called?
46393.e: The term goes back to Elbridge Gerry, who as governor of Massachusetts signed a redistricting plan with a salamander-shaped district in 1812. Electoral autocracies also use this technique.
46393.m: Gerrymandering distorts elections through cleverly drawn constituency boundaries.

46394.q: Which institution described Hungary in 2022 as a ‘hybrid regime of electoral autocracy’?
a: The Council of Europe in Strasbourg
46394.e: The European Parliament adopted a report with this assessment in September 2022. Among other things it criticised media concentration and restrictions on the judiciary.
46394.m: In 2022 the European Parliament classed Hungary as an electoral autocracy.

46395.q: What does the word ‘theocracy’ literally mean?
46395.e: The word is made up of the Greek ‘theos’ (god) and ‘kratein’ (to rule). It was coined by the ancient historian Flavius Josephus.

46396.q: What is the principle founded by Khomeini on which the Islamic Republic of Iran is based?
46396.e: The principle of ‘Velayat-e faqih’ gives a supreme Islamic jurist the highest authority in the state. It was written into the constitution in 1979.
46396.m: In Iran a supreme jurist stands above the elected bodies.

46397.q: Which Iranian body checks laws for compatibility with Islam and decides whether candidates may stand in elections?
46397.e: The Guardian Council has twelve members, six clerics and six jurists. By vetting candidates it can strongly steer elections in advance.
46397.m: Iran's Guardian Council helps decide who may be elected at all.

46398.q: Which reformer shaped a strictly church-regulated city order in Geneva from 1541, often described as theocratic?
46398.e: With the ‘Ordonnances ecclésiastiques’, Calvin set up a consistory that supervised the lives of the citizens. Formally, however, the city council remained the secular authority.
46398.m: Calvin's Geneva is seen as an example of a city order strongly shaped by the church.

46399.q: What does the term ‘hierocracy’ (from Greek ‘hieros’, holy) refer to?
46399.e: While theocracy means rule in the name of God, hierocracy stresses that priests actually govern. Rule by the rich is called plutocracy, rule by experts technocracy.
46399.m: In a hierocracy a priesthood rules.

46400.q: Which Spaniard was burned as a heretic in Geneva in 1553 because of his teachings?
46400.e: The physician and theologian Michael Servetus denied the Trinity. The Geneva council sentenced him to death with Calvin's approval.
46400.m: The burning of Servetus shows the religious strictness of Geneva in the Reformation era.

46401.q: Who was at the head of the traditional religious and secular government in Tibet until 1959?
46401.e: The Ganden Phodrang government united religious and political leadership under the Dalai Lama. In 1959 the 14th Dalai Lama fled to India.
46401.m: In old Tibet the Dalai Lama was both religious and secular leader.

46402.q: Which Iranian body elects the Supreme Leader and can in theory remove him?
46402.e: The Assembly of Experts is made up of elected Islamic clerics. In 1989 it chose Khomeini's successor.
46402.m: In Iran the Assembly of Experts elects the Supreme Leader.

46403.q: What does the term ‘kleptocracy’ literally mean?
46403.e: The word is made up of the Greek ‘kleptes’ (thief) and ‘kratos’ (rule). It refers to regimes whose leaders enrich themselves from state assets.
46403.m: In a kleptocracy the rulers enrich themselves at the state's expense.

a: Assets that rulers have unlawfully moved abroad
Taxes a state spends on weapons
UN aid money for poor countries
46404.e: Rulers such as Suharto, Mobutu or Abacha enriched themselves at the state's expense and hid large sums in foreign accounts, including in Switzerland. Such assets are called potentate funds.
46404.m: Potentate funds are assets embezzled by rulers and hidden abroad.

46405.q: What did Mobutu Sese Seko call the Congo from 1971?
46405.e: Mobutu renamed both the state and the river Zaire. His regime is seen as a textbook example of a kleptocracy and ended in 1997.
46405.m: Under Mobutu the Congo was called Zaire from 1971 to 1997.

46406.q: Which Swiss law has governed the freezing and return of potentate funds since 2016?
a: The Federal Act on Illicitly Acquired Assets
46406.e: The law (FIAA) allows assets of foreign politically exposed persons to be frozen and returned to their countries of origin. It replaced the so-called ‘Lex Duvalier’.
46406.m: Switzerland can freeze potentate funds and return them to the states concerned.

46407.q: Whose money did Switzerland return to Nigeria in several instalments?
46407.e: The Nigerian military dictator Sani Abacha had embezzled huge sums in the 1990s. After court proceedings Switzerland returned hundreds of millions of dollars.
46407.m: The return of the Abacha funds is a well-known case of Swiss restitution practice.

46408.q: Which ruler was overthrown in the Philippines in 1986 by the ‘People Power’ movement?
46408.e: After massive protests on EDSA avenue in Manila, Marcos fled into exile in 1986. He was accused of plundering billions.
46408.m: The People Power movement ended Marcos's rule in 1986.

46409.q: Which organisation publishes the Corruption Perceptions Index every year?
46409.e: Transparency International was founded in Berlin in 1993. Its index rates how corrupt a country's public sector is perceived to be.
46409.m: Transparency International measures perceived corruption worldwide.

46410.q: What did Aristotle call the degenerate form of aristocracy, in which a few rule for their own benefit?
46410.e: In Aristotle's theory of forms of government, oligarchy is the counterpart of aristocracy. For Aristotle, it is mainly the rich who rule in an oligarchy.
46410.m: For Aristotle, oligarchy is the self-serving rule of a few rich people.

46411.q: What does the sociologist Robert Michels' ‘iron law of oligarchy’ of 1911 state?
a: Large organisations inevitably produce a small leadership group
Dictatorships never last longer than 30 years
Every revolution ends in a monarchy
46411.e: Robert Michels studied the German SPD. He concluded that even democratic parties are steered by a few leaders.
46411.m: Michels believed every large organisation tends towards rule by a few.

46412.q: What is the rule of the thirty men who governed Athens in 404 BC after the Peloponnesian War called?
46412.e: Installed under Sparta, the Thirty ruled by terror under Critias. Democracy was restored as early as 403 BC.
46412.m: The Thirty Tyrants set up a short, violent oligarchy in Athens.

46413.q: Who was allowed to sit in the Great Council of the Republic of Venice from 1297?
a: Only men from long-established noble families
Only clergy appointed by the Pope
46413.e: With the ‘Serrata’, the closing of the Great Council, membership was limited to certain noble families. Venice thus became an aristocratic oligarchy.
46413.m: From 1297 Venice was an aristocratic oligarchy.

46414.q: What do you call the rule of a few families in cities such as Bern before 1798?
46414.e: In Bern, Lucerne, Fribourg and Solothurn, a small number of families eligible for office decided politics. The French invasion of 1798 ended this order.
46414.m: Under the Ancien Régime a few patrician families ruled in some Swiss cities.

46415.q: Which group gained great political influence in Russia in the 1990s after the end of the Soviet Union?
a: The descendants of the tsar's family
46415.e: These so-called oligarchs became rich through the privatisation of state companies. In 1996 they supported the re-election of President Boris Yeltsin.
46415.m: In the 1990s Russian oligarchs gained great political influence.

46416.q: How did a few Russian bankers get hold of large state companies in the mid-1990s?
a: Through privatisations far below their value
Through the expropriation of Western firms
46416.e: In the so-called loans-for-shares auctions of 1995, banks received shares as security for loans to the state. As the state did not repay, the companies went cheaply to the lenders.
46416.m: In the 1990s a few bankers acquired Russia's state companies cheaply.

46417.q: What happened several times to democracy in Athens during the Peloponnesian War?
a: It was briefly abolished by coups
It was replaced by a hereditary monarchy
It was banned by the Persians
It was extended to women and slaves
46417.e: In 411 BC the ‘Council of Four Hundred’ seized power, in 404 BC the ‘Thirty Tyrants’. Both times Athens soon returned to democracy.
46417.m: Athens' democracy was overthrown several times by oligarchs during the war.

46418.q: Which state in southern Africa is an absolute monarchy today?
46418.e: In Eswatini, called Swaziland until 2018, King Mswati III has ruled with far-reaching power since 1986. Lesotho, by contrast, is a constitutional monarchy.
46418.m: Eswatini is Africa's last absolute monarchy.

46419.q: According to the Basic Law of 1992, which text serves as the constitution in Saudi Arabia?
a: The Charter of the United Nations
46419.e: The Basic Law names the Quran and the Sunnah as the constitution of the kingdom. The king combines law-making and government; there is no elected parliament.
46419.m: In Saudi Arabia the Quran and the Sunnah count as the constitution.

46420.q: How are the members of the Shura Council in Saudi Arabia chosen?
a: Its members are appointed by the king
It is elected directly by the people
Its members are sent by parties
46420.e: The Consultative Council advises the king but has no law-making power of its own. Its members are appointed, not elected.
46420.m: The Saudi Shura Council gives advice but is appointed by the king.

46421.q: Which ruler has governed Brunei since 1967 and is also prime minister?
46421.e: Hassanal Bolkiah is head of state and head of government and also runs other ministries. He is one of the longest-reigning monarchs in the world.
46421.m: In Brunei the sultan combines leadership of state and government in one person.

46422.q: Which European state is considered an absolute elective monarchy?
46422.e: The Pope is elected by the conclave and combines legislative, executive and judicial power. Monaco and Liechtenstein are constitutional monarchies.
46422.m: The Pope is head of an absolute elective monarchy.

46423.q: With which doctrine did absolute monarchs traditionally justify their rule?
46423.e: According to the divine right of kings, the king receives his power directly from God and is answerable only to him. This idea shaped the absolutism of the 17th and 18th centuries.
46423.m: Absolute monarchs appealed to the divine right of kings.

46424.q: Which sultan ruled Oman from 1970 until his death in January 2020?
46424.e: Qaboos came to power in 1970 by deposing his father and modernised the country. After his death he was succeeded by his cousin Haitham bin Tariq.
46424.m: Sultan Qaboos shaped Oman for half a century.

46425.q: How can candidates stand in parliamentary elections in Eswatini?
a: Only as individuals without a party
Only with the approval of neighbouring states
46425.e: In the Tinkhundla system, candidates stand individually in constituencies. Parties may not take part in elections, and the king keeps the decisive power.
46425.m: In Eswatini parties may not take part in elections.

46426.q: Which sociologist described ‘sultanism’ as an extreme form of patrimonial rule?
46426.e: In ‘Economy and Society’, Weber called rule based entirely on the ruler's free whim sultanistic. Later researchers applied the term to modern dictatorships.
46426.m: Max Weber understood sultanism as rule by personal whim.

46427.q: Which feature is especially typical of a sultanistic regime?
46427.e: Under sultanism the ruler treats the state as his property. Loyalty is based on fear and reward, not on an ideology.
46427.m: Under sultanism the ruler treats the state as his private property.

46428.q: Which dictator had the capital of the Dominican Republic renamed after himself?
46428.e: Santo Domingo was called Ciudad Trujillo from 1936 to 1961. Trujillo is seen as a textbook example of a sultanistic ruler and was assassinated in 1961.
46428.m: Trujillo even named the capital after himself.

46429.q: What was the feared militia of the Duvalier dictatorship in Haiti called?
46429.e: François ‘Papa Doc’ Duvalier relied on this militia, which was personally loyal to him. His son Jean-Claude took power in 1971 and was overthrown in 1986.
46429.m: The Tontons Macoutes secured the Duvaliers' rule through terror.

46430.q: Which family dominated Nicaragua until the Sandinista revolution of 1979?
46430.e: Anastasio Somoza García and his sons ruled Nicaragua for decades like a family possession. Dynastic succession is typical of sultanistic regimes.
46430.m: The Somozas ruled Nicaragua as a family dynasty until 1979.

46431.q: Which president of Turkmenistan renamed months after himself and his mother?
46431.e: Niyazov had himself called ‘Turkmenbashi’ and made his book ‘Ruhnama’ compulsory reading. He ruled until his death in 2006.
46431.m: Niyazov's personality cult in Turkmenistan had sultanistic features.

46432.q: Which ruling couple was executed in Romania on 25 December 1989?
46432.e: Nicolae and Elena Ceaușescu were shot after a short military trial on 25 December 1989. Researchers described their regime as a mix of totalitarianism and sultanism, because family members held many key posts.
46432.m: The Ceaușescu regime combined totalitarian and sultanistic features.

46433.q: In which work did Karl Marx analyse Louis Bonaparte's coup in 1852?
a: The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte
46433.e: Marx interpreted Bonapartism as rule by the executive that seemingly rises above the classes. The title alludes to an earlier coup by the Bonaparte family.
46433.m: In ‘The Eighteenth Brumaire’ Marx interpreted Bonapartism.

46434.q: Why did Louis Napoléon Bonaparte carry out a coup in December 1851?
a: He had lost the presidential election
The king had returned to Paris
46434.e: As president he was not allowed to be re-elected. So on 2 December 1851 he dissolved the National Assembly and a year later had himself proclaimed Emperor Napoleon III.
46434.m: The coup of 1851 paved the way to the Second Empire.

46435.q: How did Bonapartist rulers typically legitimise their power?
46435.e: Napoleon I and Napoleon III had constitutional changes confirmed by plebiscites. In this way they appealed directly to the people and bypassed parliament.
46435.m: Bonapartism relies on plebiscites rather than parliaments.

46436.q: What title did Napoleon Bonaparte hold at first after his coup of 1799?
46436.e: After the overthrow of the Directory in November 1799 he became First Consul. In 1802 he had himself made Consul for life by plebiscite, and in 1804 he became emperor.
46436.m: Napoleon first ruled as First Consul before he became emperor.

46437.q: In which Swiss canton did Louis Napoléon spend part of his youth and receive honorary citizenship?
46437.e: He lived with his mother Hortense at Arenenberg Castle on the Untersee. Today it houses the Napoleon Museum Thurgau.
46437.m: Arenenberg Castle in Thurgau was the youthful home of Napoleon III.

46438.q: How did Louis Napoléon Bonaparte become President of France in December 1848?
a: Through a popular vote of all men
46438.e: He won France's first direct presidential election by a large majority. Only afterwards did he extend his power through the coup.
46438.m: Napoleon III first came to power through a popular vote.

46439.q: According to Karl Marx, which section of the population did Napoleon III rely on in particular?
46439.e: In ‘The Eighteenth Brumaire’, Marx wrote that France's many small farmers carried Napoleon III. Because no class was strong enough, the ruler could seemingly place himself above all of them.
46439.m: Marx saw the small farmers as Napoleon III's most important support.

46440.q: Which event ended Napoleon III's Second Empire in 1870?
46440.e: Napoleon III was taken prisoner by the Prussians at Sedan on 2 September 1870. Two days later the republic was proclaimed in Paris.
46440.m: The Second Empire ended with the defeat at Sedan.

46441.q: Which tyrant ruled Athens in the 6th century BC and promoted festivals such as the Panathenaea?
46441.e: Peisistratos seized power several times and finally ruled until his death in 527 BC. He promoted buildings, cults and festivals.
46441.m: Peisistratos was the best-known tyrant of Athens.

46442.q: What were the names of the two Athenians who murdered Hipparchus in 514 BC and were honoured as ‘tyrant slayers’?
46442.e: They killed the brother of the tyrant Hippias. Although the tyranny only ended in 510 BC, they were honoured with statues in Athens.
46442.m: Harmodius and Aristogeiton were regarded as tyrant slayers in Athens.

46443.q: Which procedure was meant to prevent the return of a tyranny in the Athens of Cleisthenes?
46443.e: With ostracism, citizens could banish a politician who had become too powerful for ten years. The names were scratched onto pieces of pottery.
46443.m: Ostracism was meant to protect Athens from new tyrants.

46444.q: Which tyrant of Samos is known from a ballad by Schiller about a ring?
46444.e: According to Herodotus, Polycrates threw a valuable ring into the sea to reduce his good fortune, but he found it again in the belly of a fish. Schiller turned the story into a ballad in 1797.
46444.m: Schiller's ‘The Ring of Polycrates’ tells of a tyrant's uncanny luck.

46445.q: At the court of which tyrant of Syracuse does the story of the Sword of Damocles take place?
46445.e: Dionysius had a sword hung over Damocles by a single horsehair. In this way he showed how threatened a ruler's life is despite all the splendour.
46445.m: The Sword of Damocles stands for a constantly looming danger.

46446.q: What did ‘tyranny’ originally mean in ancient Greece?
46446.e: A tyrant usually came to power through force or popular favour, not through inheritance. Only later did the word take on the meaning of cruel despotic rule.
46446.m: Originally tyranny meant sole rule that was not inherited.

46447.q: Why did tyrants in ancient Greece often find support among the people?
a: They stood up against the powerful noble families
They abolished all taxes for ever
They were considered chosen by the gods
46447.e: In Corinth, for example, Cypselus overthrew the noble Bacchiad family. Many tyrants made use of the people's dissatisfaction with rule by a few nobles.
46447.m: Many Greek tyrants rose in the struggle against the nobility.

46448.q: Which Athenian lawgiver explicitly refused to become a tyrant?
46448.e: Solon carried out reforms around 594 BC and could have taken sole power. He declined and went travelling after his reforms.

46449.q: According to the Federal Constitution, what may the Swiss Federal Council do in the event of a serious threat to internal or external security?
a: Change the constitution without a popular vote
46449.e: Under Article 185 of the Federal Constitution, the Federal Council can issue ordinances in the event of serious disturbances. These must be limited in time.
46449.m: The Federal Council may only issue emergency ordinances for a limited time.

46450.q: Which Roman general had himself appointed dictator in 82 BC without the usual time limit?
46450.e: After a civil war, Lucius Cornelius Sulla used the emergency office to reorganise the state and persecute his opponents. After a few years he voluntarily withdrew from politics.
46450.m: Sulla turned the time-limited emergency office into a tool of personal power.

46451.q: What did Gaius Julius Caesar have himself appointed at the beginning of 44 BC?
46451.e: With the dictatorship for life, the originally time-limited emergency office lost its exceptional character. A few weeks later, on the Ides of March, Caesar was murdered.
46451.m: Caesar's dictatorship for life turned the emergency into permanent rule.

46452.q: What was the longest a dictator was allowed to stay in office in the Roman Republic?
46452.e: The dictator was appointed in emergencies and had sweeping powers. The six-month limit was meant to prevent him from ruling permanently.
46452.m: The Roman dictatorship was intended as a time-limited emergency office.

46453.q: How long did the state of emergency imposed in Egypt after Sadat's assassination in 1981 last without interruption?
46453.e: The state of emergency lasted throughout Hosni Mubarak's time in office. It was only lifted after his overthrow, in May 2012.
46453.m: In Egypt the state of emergency became a tool of rule for over three decades.

46454.q: What did the Swiss Federal Council receive from the Federal Assembly on 30 August 1939?
a: The power to amend the constitution
The right to elect the general
46454.e: With the full powers decree, the Federal Council could act during the Second World War without the usual legislative procedure. On the same day the Federal Assembly elected Henri Guisan as general.
46454.m: During the Second World War the Federal Council governed with extraordinary full powers.

46455.q: What do critics warn about when a state of emergency is extended again and again?
a: That the emergency becomes a normal tool of government
That parliament gains too much power
46455.e: In a state of emergency the government often rules by decree and restricts fundamental rights. The philosopher Giorgio Agamben warned that this state can become the rule in modern states.
46455.m: A permanent state of emergency can hollow out democracy.

46456.q: How long did the state of emergency imposed in Turkey after the attempted coup of July 2016 last?
46456.e: The state of emergency was extended several times and lifted in July 2018. During this time tens of thousands of public employees were dismissed by decree.
46456.m: A long-extended state of emergency can become a government's instrument of power.

46457.q: Which philosopher designed the ‘Panopticon’ at the end of the 18th century, a prison in which one guard can watch all the prisoners unnoticed?
46457.e: The English philosopher Jeremy Bentham designed the Panopticon around 1791. Because the prisoners never know whether they are being watched, they behave obediently all the time.
46457.m: Jeremy Bentham's Panopticon is seen as a symbol of surveillance.

46458.q: Which French thinker described in ‘Discipline and Punish’ in 1975 how the principle of the Panopticon shapes modern societies?
46458.e: Michel Foucault interpreted the Panopticon as a model of a power that works through constant possible observation. People then discipline themselves.
46458.m: Michel Foucault showed that the mere possibility of being watched controls behaviour.

46459.q: What is the all-present leader figure in George Orwell's 1949 novel ‘1984’ who watches over all of life called?
46459.e: In ‘1984’ there are posters everywhere with the words ‘Big Brother is watching you’. Today the term generally stands for a state that watches everything.
46459.m: Big Brother from Orwell's ‘1984’ has become the symbol of the surveillance state.

46460.q: What did the Stasi call its method of psychologically wearing down opponents of the regime through targeted rumours, character assassination and failures at work?
46460.e: ‘Zersetzung’ was set out in the Stasi's Directive 1/76. Instead of arrests, opponents were to be unsettled, isolated and made incapable of acting.
46460.m: Through Zersetzung the Stasi quietly destroyed people without arresting them.

46461.q: What did the Stasi collect in sealed preserving jars so that suspects could later be tracked down with sniffer dogs?
46461.e: The Stasi took scent samples with cloths, for example from chair seats during interrogations, and kept them in jars. Dogs were meant to use them to identify people.
46461.m: The Stasi even kept preserved scents of suspects.

46462.q: According to an investigation in 1989, roughly how many files on people and organisations had the federal police in Switzerland created?
46462.e: In 1989 a parliamentary commission of inquiry revealed that state security had kept around 900,000 files. The scandal led to a large demonstration in Bern in 1990.
46462.m: The Secret Files Scandal showed that excessive surveillance can happen even in a democracy.

46463.q: What is the spyware of the Israeli company NSO Group called, which according to investigations in 2021 was also used to spy on journalists and opposition figures?
46463.e: Pegasus can take over mobile phones unnoticed and read messages and access the camera and microphone. In 2021 an international network of journalists revealed its misuse by several governments in the ‘Pegasus Project’.
46463.m: The Pegasus spyware shows how states can use smartphones for surveillance.

46464.q: What is China expanding right down to the villages with the ‘Xueliang’ (Sharp Eyes) programme?
46464.e: With the ‘Xueliang’ (Sharp Eyes) programme, camera surveillance has been extended into villages since the mid-2010s. The name picks up a slogan from the Mao era saying that the masses have sharp eyes.
46464.m: With the ‘Sharp Eyes’ programme China is extending video surveillance into the countryside.

46465.q: According to the State Council's plan of 2014, what is the Chinese social credit system meant to rate?
a: The ‘trustworthiness’ of citizens, companies and authorities
Only the school marks of children and teenagers
Only the health of the population
Only the creditworthiness of foreign companies
46465.e: In 2014 the State Council presented a plan for the years 2014 to 2020. It announced the rating of the ‘trustworthiness’ of citizens, companies and authorities.
46465.m: The social credit system is meant to rate the ‘trustworthiness’ of people and companies.

46466.q: What penalty applies in China to people on a blacklist as ‘dishonest debtors’?
a: They may not buy plane or high-speed train tickets
They automatically lose their right to vote
They may not have any more children
46466.e: Anyone who does not comply with a court ruling, for example to pay debts, can end up on a blacklist. Among other things, those affected may then not book flights or high-speed trains.
46466.m: In China blacklists restrict travel for defaulting debtors.

46467.q: How did the well-known social credit pilot project in the Chinese city of Rongcheng work?
a: Everyone started with 1,000 points and could gain or lose points
Only companies received points, residents did not
Ratings were made only by neighbours in an app
All residents had to pass an exam about the party
46467.e: The coastal city of Rongcheng in Shandong province gave all adults a starting balance of 1,000 points. Good behaviour earns points, offences cost points.
46467.m: With its points system Rongcheng became the best-known test case of social credit.

46468.q: Which private rating system of a large Chinese online group is often confused with the state social credit system?
46468.e: Sesame Credit (Zhima Credit) was introduced in 2015 by the Alibaba affiliate Ant Financial and rates customers' creditworthiness. It is a company product and not part of the state system.
46468.m: Sesame Credit is a private credit rating and not the state social credit system.

46469.q: Which statement best describes the Chinese social credit system according to current knowledge?
a: It consists of many regional and sector-specific systems
It is a single nationwide score for every person
It is used only for foreign tourists
It was completely abolished again in 2015
46469.e: Experts stress that there is no single score for all 1.4 billion people. Many blacklists, local pilot projects and company ratings exist side by side.
46469.m: The social credit system is a patchwork of many lists and subsystems.

46470.q: What has every company in China received since 2015 as part of the social credit system?
a: A seat in the National People's Congress
46470.e: Since 2015 every company and organisation in China has been given an 18-digit unified social credit code. Offences and ratings are also stored under this number.
46470.m: Chinese companies carry a unified social credit code.

46471.q: Apart from private individuals, who is rated especially extensively in the Chinese social credit system?
a: International organisations such as the UN
46471.e: A large part of the system concerns firms, for example on taxes, environmental rules or product safety. Bad ratings can lead to more inspections or exclusion from contracts.
46471.m: The social credit system also rates companies on a large scale.

46472.q: What is the Chinese government's stated aim with the social credit system?
a: More ‘trustworthiness’ in society and the economy
46472.e: Officially, the system is meant to fight fraud, breach of contract and counterfeiting. Critics also see it as a means of steering behaviour and punishing deviation.
46472.m: China justifies the social credit system with the fight against fraud and breaches of trust.

46473.q: What does the name ‘Great Firewall’ for Chinese internet censorship allude to?
46473.e: The Great Wall of China is known as the ‘Great Wall’ in English. A firewall is a protective system that filters data traffic; the name combines the two.
46473.m: The name Great Firewall alludes to the Great Wall of China.

46474.q: Which tool do many people in China use to get round the Great Firewall?
46474.e: A VPN routes data traffic in encrypted form through a server abroad. The authorities try to detect and block such connections; unapproved VPN services are banned.
46474.m: Many people get round Chinese internet censorship with VPN connections.

46475.q: Which technique does the Great Firewall use to examine the content of data packets in order to detect banned keywords or VPN connections?
46475.e: With deep packet inspection, not only the sender and destination but also the contents of data packets are checked. This makes it possible to track down keywords and disguised connections.
46475.m: Deep packet inspection examines the contents of data packets.

46476.q: What is the method called in which requests for internet addresses are deliberately given false answers so that a site cannot be reached?
46476.e: With DNS spoofing or DNS poisoning, the name service returns false IP addresses. Blocked sites such as Google or Facebook then lead nowhere.
46476.m: In China blocked sites are made unreachable through DNS manipulation.

46477.q: Where did Google redirect its Chinese search page in 2010, after the company no longer wanted to go along with censoring search results?
46477.e: After hacker attacks and a dispute about censorship, Google redirected google.cn to its uncensored site in Hong Kong in March 2010. However, this is blocked in mainland China.
46477.m: In 2010 Google moved its search from mainland China to Hong Kong.

46478.q: Why does China block platforms such as Wikipedia, Google and YouTube?
a: They cannot be fully controlled by the state
They charge fees that are too high
They are only available in English
46478.e: Foreign platforms would have to censor content according to Chinese rules and hand over data. Wikipedia has been blocked in all language versions since 2019; instead there are state-controlled Chinese services.
46478.m: China blocks platforms that escape state control.

46479.q: Why were pictures of the cartoon character Winnie the Pooh censored at times on Chinese social networks?
a: Because users compared him with Xi Jinping
Because the bear is a symbol of Taiwan
Because honey is banned in China
Because the character comes from Russia
46479.e: Users put photos of Xi Jinping next to pictures of Winnie the Pooh to make fun of him. The censors removed such comparisons because they damaged the leader's image.
46479.m: In China censorship also hits mockery of the country's leaders.

46480.q: What does Russia call the 2019 law that is meant to allow the state to cut the Russian internet off from the global network in an emergency?
46480.e: The so-called ‘sovereign internet’ requires providers to route data traffic through state-controlled nodes. This allows the regulator Roskomnadzor to block content centrally.
46480.m: With the sovereign internet Russia wants to control its networks on the Chinese model.

46481.q: Which presenter made disparaging comments on clips from Western television in the GDR programme ‘Der schwarze Kanal’ (The Black Channel)?
46481.e: Karl-Eduard von Schnitzler presented the programme from 1960 to 1989. He showed Western reports and reinterpreted them in the spirit of SED propaganda.
46481.m: ‘The Black Channel’ was meant to present Western television as lies.

46482.q: What did the number ‘301’ stand for in the name of the Nazis' cheap radio, the ‘Volksempfänger VE 301’ (people's receiver)?
46482.e: The number recalls 30 January 1933, the day Hitler became Reich Chancellor. The cheap set was meant to bring propaganda into as many homes as possible.
46482.m: The Volksempfänger was a tool of Nazi propaganda.

46483.q: What was the Nazi party's newspaper called?
46483.e: From 1920 the ‘Völkischer Beobachter’ was the central organ of the Nazi party. After 1933 it was the most important newspaper in the press that had been brought into line.
46483.m: The ‘Völkischer Beobachter’ was the mouthpiece of the Nazi party.

46484.q: Which editor held up a poster against the war in front of the camera during the main news of Russian state television in March 2022?
46484.e: Marina Ovsyannikova protested against the attack on Ukraine on Channel One on 14 March 2022. Among other things, her poster said that viewers were being lied to here.
46484.m: Ovsyannikova's protest broke through the propaganda of Russian state television live on air.

46485.q: What must many regional television channels in China broadcast simultaneously every evening at 7 pm?
a: The main news of state broadcaster CCTV
The weather forecast for all of China
46485.e: The programme ‘Xinwen Lianbo’ has been broadcast every evening at 7 pm since 1978. It reports at length on the party leadership and is seen as the leading propaganda medium.
46485.m: Every evening ‘Xinwen Lianbo’ sets out the official view in China.

46486.q: What was the maximum penalty in Russia from March 2022 for spreading alleged ‘false information’ about the army?
46486.e: Shortly after the attack on Ukraine, Russia passed a law against ‘fake news’ about the armed forces. Many independent media then stopped operating or went into exile.
46486.m: In Russia harsh penalties are meant to prevent any deviation from the official account of the war.

46487.q: What is the well-known Russian troll factory in St Petersburg called?
46487.e: The Internet Research Agency employed hundreds of staff who spread comments and posts using fake accounts. It became known from about 2013.
46487.m: The Internet Research Agency is the best-known example of a troll factory.

46488.q: Which businessman, later head of the Wagner mercenary group, admitted in 2023 that he had founded the Internet Research Agency?
46488.e: Yevgeny Prigozhin financed the troll factory and admitted this in February 2023. He was killed in a plane crash in August 2023.
46488.m: Yevgeny Prigozhin was behind the Russian troll factory.

46489.q: According to US special counsel Robert Mueller's indictment of 2018, which election did the Internet Research Agency try to influence?
46489.e: In February 2018 Mueller charged 13 Russian individuals and three organisations. They were accused of stirring up opinion and conflict on social media with fake accounts.
46489.m: Troll factories try to influence elections in other countries.

46490.q: What are the internet commentators in China who write pro-government posts on behalf of the state mockingly called?
46490.e: The name refers to the rumour that the writers received 50 fen (0.5 yuan) per post. In Chinese they are called ‘wumao’.
46490.m: The 50 Cent Party spreads controlled comments in China.

46491.q: What did a 2017 study led by Harvard political scientist Gary King find about the strategy of state-paid commentators in China?
a: They mostly distract rather than argue with critics
They write almost only in English
They work exclusively with computer programs
46491.e: The researchers estimated around 448 million fake posts a year. These are mainly meant to crowd out sensitive discussions through cheerleading and distraction.
46491.m: Controlled comments in China rely mainly on distraction rather than argument.

46492.q: What do you call faking a broad citizens' movement that is in reality controlled by an organisation?
46492.e: The term comes from the artificial turf brand ‘AstroTurf’, because an artificial rather than a real ‘grassroots movement’ is created. Troll factories use this technique deliberately.
46492.m: In astroturfing a popular movement is only faked.

46493.q: How did the work of the Russian troll factory in St Petersburg become known from the inside in 2015?
a: A journalist got herself hired undercover
The company published a report itself
The Russian police searched the offices
A computer virus exposed all the data
46493.e: The journalist Lyudmila Savchuk got herself hired and reported on shift work, daily quotas and fake profiles. She later also took the company to court.
46493.m: Lyudmila Savchuk exposed the troll factory's work from the inside.

46494.q: What is meant by the human rights crime of ‘enforced disappearance’?
a: State bodies abduct people and conceal their fate
The state strips critics of their citizenship
Authorities delete data from the population register
46494.e: In an enforced disappearance, state bodies arrest people and then deny any knowledge of where they are. Since 2006 there has been a separate UN convention against it.
46494.m: Since 2006 there has been a separate UN convention against enforced disappearance.

46495.q: What was Hitler's decree of 1941 called, under which resistance fighters from occupied territories were secretly taken to Germany without their relatives learning anything?
46495.e: The Night and Fog Decree of December 1941 was meant to deter people through complete uncertainty. It is seen as an early example of enforced disappearance by the state.
46495.m: With the Night and Fog Decree the Nazis made people vanish without a trace.

46496.q: Under the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court, what crime is systematic enforced disappearance?
46496.e: Article 7 of the Rome Statute explicitly lists enforced disappearance among crimes against humanity. The condition is a widespread or systematic attack on the civilian population.
46496.m: Systematic enforced disappearance is a crime against humanity.

46497.q: How were many prisoners killed during the Argentine military dictatorship, whose bodies were never meant to be found?
a: They were thrown from planes into the sea
They were walled up in mines
46497.e: In the so-called death flights, drugged prisoners were dropped over the Río de la Plata or the Atlantic. An officer involved, Adolfo Scilingo, made this public in 1995.
46497.m: In Argentina the death flights were meant to remove every trace of the victims.

46498.q: Under which code name did a Syrian military photographer smuggle tens of thousands of photos of bodies out of the Assad regime's prisons?
46498.e: The photographer ‘Caesar’ fled abroad with the pictures in 2013. The photos document the torture and death of many disappeared people, and the USA later named a sanctions law after him.
46498.m: The Caesar photos document the fate of disappeared prisoners in Syria.

46499.q: What is the measure permitted in China under which suspects can be held at a secret location for up to six months?
a: Residential surveillance at a designated location
Provisional custody in the home village
Re-education through labour in the border area
House arrest in your own home
46499.e: The measure is known as ‘Residential Surveillance at a Designated Location’. Human rights organisations see it as a legalised form of enforced disappearance.
46499.m: In China secret detention outside normal prisons can be ordered by law.

46500.q: From which region did China transfer surveillance methods to Xinjiang from 2016?
46500.e: Chen Quanguo became party chief of Xinjiang in 2016 after previously working in Tibet, and transferred the surveillance methods used there. Under him numerous internment camps were built.
46500.m: Under Chen Quanguo repression in Xinjiang was greatly intensified.

46501.q: What are the internal documents on the running of the camps in Xinjiang, published in 2019 by an international network of journalists, called?
46501.e: The ‘China Cables’ contained instructions on how camps were to be secured, escapes prevented and inmates re-educated. They contradicted the claim that these were voluntary schools.
46501.m: The China Cables proved that the camps in Xinjiang were coercive.

46502.q: What did the ‘Xinjiang Police Files’ published in 2022 show in large numbers for the first time?
a: Photos of detainees and shoot-to-kill orders
46502.e: The hacked police data contained thousands of portrait photos of prisoners, including teenagers and elderly people. They also included rules to shoot at people fleeing.
46502.m: The Xinjiang Police Files gave the detainees a face.

46503.q: To what sentence was the Uyghur economics professor Ilham Tohti sentenced in 2014?
46503.e: Ilham Tohti had criticised discrimination against the Uyghurs and was sentenced to life imprisonment for ‘separatism’. He later received several international human rights prizes.
46503.m: Ilham Tohti is serving a life sentence for his peaceful criticism.

46504.q: Which government was the first to officially classify China's treatment of the Uyghurs as genocide, in January 2021?
46504.e: US Secretary of State Mike Pompeo declared on 19 January 2021 that China was committing genocide against the Uyghurs. The following administration confirmed this assessment.
46504.m: The USA calls the persecution of the Uyghurs genocide.

46505.q: Which German researcher was one of the first to analyse public building tenders and documents to prove the scale of the camps in Xinjiang?
46505.e: Adrian Zenz analysed tenders for camps, job adverts for guards and statistics. China imposed sanctions on him for this in 2021.
46505.m: Adrian Zenz made the scale of the camps visible using Chinese documents.

46506.q: What does the 2021 US law to prevent Uyghur forced labour presume as a rule about goods from Xinjiang?
a: That they were made with forced labour
That they may be imported duty-free
That they are especially environmentally friendly
46506.e: The law reverses the burden of proof: importers must show that no forced labour was involved. Otherwise the goods may not be imported into the USA.
46506.m: For goods from Xinjiang, importers in the USA must prove that no forced labour is behind them.

46507.q: Which day of remembrance marks the entry into force of the UN Convention against Torture on 26 June 1987?
a: The International Day in Support of Victims of Torture
46507.e: The convention came into force on 26 June 1987. That is why this day is now the International Day in Support of Victims of Torture.
46507.m: On 26 June the victims of torture are remembered worldwide.

46508.q: According to the definition in Article 1 of the UN Convention against Torture, who must be involved in an act for it to count as torture?
a: A group of at least three people
46508.e: Torture in the sense of the convention is the deliberate infliction of severe pain by or with the consent of an official. The convention is therefore aimed at violence by the state.
46508.m: Torture in the sense of the UN convention always comes from the state or is approved by it.

46509.q: What does Article 3 of the UN Convention against Torture forbid?
a: Deportation to a state where torture is a risk
Detention without a lawyer for more than 24 hours
46509.e: Article 3 contains the principle of non-refoulement. No one may be handed over to a country where they face a real risk of torture.
46509.m: No one may be deported to a country where they face torture.

46510.q: What does the UN Convention against Torture say about torture in war or during a public emergency?
a: It is never allowed, even then
It is allowed with a court's consent
46510.e: Article 2 states that no exceptional circumstances can justify torture. An order from a superior is no justification either.
46510.m: The ban on torture is absolute and has no exceptions.

46511.q: How does the UN Committee against Torture monitor whether states comply with the Convention against Torture?
a: States must regularly submit reports to it
It sends its own soldiers to the states
It imposes prison sentences on ministers
46511.e: The Committee against Torture (CAT) consists of ten independent experts and meets in Geneva. It examines the reports of the states parties and makes recommendations.
46511.m: The UN Committee against Torture in Geneva regularly examines states' reports.

46512.q: What does the 2002 Optional Protocol to the UN Convention against Torture make possible?
a: Unannounced visits to places of detention
A financial penalty for states that torture
A separate world criminal court for torture
46512.e: The protocol (OPCAT) creates a UN subcommittee and obliges states to set up national visiting bodies. These may visit prisons, police stations and psychiatric institutions.
46512.m: Regular visits to places of detention are meant to prevent torture.

46513.q: Which former dictator was arrested in London in 1998, with the House of Lords later ruling that extradition for torture was permissible?
46513.e: Spain requested Pinochet's extradition for torture crimes. The Law Lords relied on the Convention against Torture, which obliges states to prosecute torturers.
46513.m: The Pinochet case showed that even former heads of state can be held to account for torture.

46514.q: What does the abbreviation KGB stand for in English?
a: Command of the Secret Federal Police
46514.e: KGB is the abbreviation of the Russian ‘Komitet gosudarstvennoy bezopasnosti’. It was both the intelligence service and the secret police of the Soviet Union.
46514.m: The KGB was the Soviet Union's Committee for State Security.

46515.e: The KGB was created in March 1954, a year after Stalin's death. Its predecessors included the Cheka and the NKVD.
46515.m: The KGB was founded in 1954 after Stalin's death.

46516.q: Who founded the Cheka, the first secret police of Soviet power, in 1917?
46516.e: Felix Dzerzhinsky led the Cheka from December 1917. During the civil war it persecuted opponents of the Bolsheviks with mass terror.
46516.m: Felix Dzerzhinsky's Cheka was the ancestor of the KGB.

46517.q: Which long-serving KGB chief became General Secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union in 1982?
46517.e: Yuri Andropov led the KGB from 1967 to 1982 and harshly persecuted dissidents. After Brezhnev's death he became party leader, but died as early as 1984.
46517.m: Yuri Andropov rose from KGB chief to party leader.

46518.q: In which GDR city was Vladimir Putin stationed as a KGB officer in the 1980s?
46518.e: Putin worked for the KGB in Dresden from 1985 to 1990. After the end of the Soviet Union he headed the domestic intelligence service FSB in 1998 and 1999.
46518.m: Vladimir Putin worked as a KGB officer in Dresden.

46519.q: Which diagnosis did Soviet psychiatrists often use to commit dissidents to psychiatric hospitals without a trial?
46519.e: The supposed ‘sluggish schizophrenia’ had hardly any symptoms and could be diagnosed in dissenters at will. This punitive psychiatry worked closely with the KGB.
46519.m: The Soviet Union misused psychiatry to lock up dissenters.

46520.q: Which Russian intelligence service took over most of the KGB's domestic tasks after the end of the Soviet Union?
46520.e: The KGB was dissolved in 1991 and split into several services. From 1995 the FSB took over at home, while the SVR is responsible for abroad.
46520.m: The FSB is the most important successor of the KGB in Russia.

46521.q: Who founded the Gestapo in Prussia in April 1933?
46521.e: Hermann Göring was then Prussian interior minister and created the Secret State Police Office on 26 April 1933. Its first head was Rudolf Diels.
46521.m: Hermann Göring founded the Gestapo in Prussia in 1933.

46522.q: Which memorial stands in Berlin today on the site of the former Gestapo headquarters?
a: Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe
46522.e: The Gestapo headquarters was at Prinz-Albrecht-Strasse 8, with its own prison for interrogation and torture. Today the Topography of Terror documentation centre provides information there.
46522.m: Where the Gestapo headquarters once stood, the Topography of Terror now recalls its crimes.

46523.q: What did the Prussian Gestapo law of February 1936 lay down?
a: Gestapo measures were not subject to any judicial review
The Gestapo was placed under the army
The Gestapo could only persecute foreigners
46523.e: Under the law of 10 February 1936, those affected could no longer challenge Gestapo measures in administrative courts. The Gestapo thus stood above the law in practice.
46523.m: From 1936 the Gestapo acted without any judicial control.

46524.q: What was the name of the head of the Gestapo from 1939, who vanished without trace after the end of the war?
46524.e: Heinrich Müller, known as ‘Gestapo Müller’, headed Office IV of the Reich Security Main Office. His fate after 1945 has still not been clearly established.

46525.q: In which authority was the Gestapo combined with the Criminal Police and the SD in 1939?
a: The High Command of the Wehrmacht
46525.e: The Reich Security Main Office was formed in September 1939 under Reinhard Heydrich. It played a central part in planning the Holocaust.
46525.m: From 1939 the Reich Security Main Office bundled together the police terror of the Nazi state.

46526.q: Which harmless-sounding term did the Gestapo use for torture during interrogations?
46526.e: By ‘intensified interrogation’ the Gestapo meant beatings, sleep deprivation and other abuse. Such cover terms were meant to conceal crimes.
46526.m: Cover words such as ‘intensified interrogation’ concealed torture.

46527.q: How did the International Military Tribunal in Nuremberg judge the Gestapo in 1946?
46527.e: The court declared the Gestapo and SD, the SS and the Corps of Political Leaders of the Nazi party to be criminal organisations. This made it easier to prosecute their members.
46527.m: At Nuremberg the Gestapo was condemned as a criminal organisation.

46528.q: In which country was the Securitate the secret police?
46528.e: The Securitate was the state security service of the Socialist Republic of Romania. Under Nicolae Ceaușescu it became one of the harshest secret services of the Eastern Bloc.
46528.m: The Securitate was Romania's feared secret police.

46529.q: In which year was the Securitate founded?
46529.e: The Securitate was set up in August 1948 with Soviet help. It was meant to secure communist rule in Romania.

46530.q: What did people in Romania have to register with the police from 1983 so that leaflets could be traced?
46530.e: Every typewriter had to be registered and a typing sample handed in. In this way the Securitate could match texts critical of the regime to a particular machine.

46531.q: Which Nobel Prize winner for Literature from Romania was spied on by the Securitate for years and wrote about her file?
46531.e: Herta Müller belonged to the German-speaking minority in the Banat and refused to cooperate with the Securitate. She received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2009.
46531.m: Herta Müller dealt with her persecution by the Securitate in her books.

46532.q: With which cruel method did the communist regime try to ‘re-educate’ prisoners in Pitești prison (1949 to 1951)?
a: Prisoners had to torture each other
Prisoners were released to the West for money
Prisoners were taught by party teachers
Prisoners were taken to camps in Siberia
46532.e: In Pitești prison, mainly students were forced to give up their beliefs and abuse fellow prisoners. It is seen as one of the cruellest re-education programmes in the Eastern Bloc.
46532.m: The Pitești experiment was meant to break prisoners inwardly through torture.

46533.q: Why was the defection of senior Securitate general Ion Mihai Pacepa to the USA in 1978 so dangerous for the Ceaușescu regime?
a: He knew the regime's secrets and revealed them
He took Romania's state treasure with him
It started a war with the USA
46533.e: Ion Mihai Pacepa was deputy head of the foreign intelligence service. He passed his knowledge to the USA and later described the inner workings of the dictatorship in the book ‘Red Horizons’.
46533.m: With Pacepa one of the highest-ranking intelligence officers of the Eastern Bloc defected.

46534.q: Which pastor was to be evicted from his home in Timișoara in December 1989 under pressure from the authorities, which sparked the popular uprising in Romania?
46534.e: Churchgoers and other citizens formed a human chain to protect the Hungarian Reformed pastor László Tőkés. This grew into the revolution that overthrew Ceaușescu.
46534.m: The protest for Pastor Tőkés became the spark of the Romanian revolution.

46535.q: What was special about the order of the Soviet secret police NKVD of July 1937 against ‘anti-Soviet elements’?
a: It set quotas for how many people were to be shot
It allowed free elections in the regions
46535.e: Order No. 00447 laid down quotas for shootings and camp imprisonment for each region. These quotas were often raised further.
46535.m: In the Great Terror people were arrested and killed according to set victim quotas.

46536.q: After which NKVD chief is the peak of Stalin's terror in 1937 and 1938 also named in Russia?
46536.e: In Russian the period is called the ‘Yezhovshchina’ after Nikolai Yezhov. He himself was removed in 1938 and shot in 1940.
46536.m: The perpetrators of the purges often became victims themselves.

46537.q: Which marshal of the Red Army was sentenced to death in a secret trial in 1937, which began a purge of the army leadership?
46537.e: Tukhachevsky was shot for an alleged conspiracy. After that thousands of officers were arrested, which greatly weakened the Red Army before the Second World War.
46537.m: Stalin's purge weakened his own army.

46538.q: Which leading figure of the SA did Hitler have murdered in the purge at the end of June 1934?
46538.e: In the killings the Nazis called the ‘Röhm Putsch’, Ernst Röhm and many other rivals were killed. Afterwards Hitler strengthened his power and the SS rose.
46538.m: In 1934 Hitler eliminated rivals within the party by murder.

46539.q: What was the name of Khrushchev's 1956 speech in which he denounced Stalin's crimes before the Congress of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union?
46539.e: In the ‘Secret Speech’ at the 20th Party Congress, Khrushchev criticised the personality cult and the mass persecutions. Many victims were then rehabilitated.
