46540.q: Which exiled revolutionary and opponent of Stalin was murdered by a Soviet agent in exile in Mexico in 1940?
46540.e: Ramón Mercader killed Leon Trotsky with an ice axe in Mexico City in August 1940. The murder shows that Stalin's purges also reached abroad.
46540.m: Stalin even had Leon Trotsky murdered in exile.

46541.q: Which relative did North Korea's ruler Kim Jong-un have executed in December 2013?
46541.e: Jang Song-thaek was regarded as the second most powerful man in the country. He was convicted as a ‘traitor’ and executed, which strengthened Kim Jong-un's power.
46541.m: Kim Jong-un also secured his power by executing close relatives.

a: Reporting people to the authorities for base motives
46542.e: In a denunciation, someone is informed on to the authorities, often out of envy, revenge or a desire for advantage. In dictatorships this can mean prison or death.
46542.m: In dictatorships denunciation turns neighbours into dangers.

46543.q: Which Soviet boy was celebrated as a hero after 1932 because he had supposedly reported his own father?
46543.e: Propaganda presented Pavlik Morozov as a role model who put the party above his family. Today the story is considered to have been heavily falsified.
46543.m: Pavlik Morozov was made into a role model for reporting your own family.

46544.q: Which Nazi law of 1934 made critical remarks about the state and the party a punishable offence and led to many denunciations?
46544.e: The Treachery Act punished even jokes and disparaging remarks about the Nazi leadership. Many cases began with reports from people around those affected.
46544.m: The Treachery Act made even a critical joke dangerous.

46545.q: What was the lowest Nazi party official called who watched the residents of a few buildings and reported anything unusual?
46545.e: The block leader, colloquially block warden, was responsible for about 40 to 60 households. He was seen as the party's eyes and ears in the neighbourhood.
46545.m: In the Nazi state the block warden kept watch on the neighbourhood.

46546.q: What were the informers called who secretly reported colleagues, friends or family members to the Stasi in the GDR?
46546.e: The unofficial collaborators (IM) were not employees of the Stasi. In 1989 there were an estimated 189,000 of them.
46546.m: In the GDR unofficial collaborators spied on the people around them.

46547.q: In Switzerland, what is the offence called when someone knowingly falsely accuses a person of a crime to an authority in order to trigger criminal proceedings against them?
46547.e: Article 303 of the Swiss Criminal Code punishes false accusation with a prison sentence of up to five years or a fine. In this way the rule of law protects people from malicious reports.
46547.m: In Switzerland anyone who knowingly reports someone falsely commits an offence.

46548.q: What did research, for example by Robert Gellately, on the Gestapo files in Würzburg show?
a: Many cases began with reports from the public
The Gestapo had an officer in every building
The public almost never reported anything
Almost all cases came from bugging devices
46548.e: The Gestapo had relatively few staff and depended on tip-offs from the public. Gellately showed that people's cooperation is what made its system possible.
46548.m: Without voluntary informers the Gestapo could hardly have been so effective.

46549.q: When was the songwriter Wolf Biermann stripped of his GDR citizenship?
46549.e: On 16 November 1976, while he was on a concert tour in the West, the GDR took away Biermann's citizenship. He was not allowed to return.
46549.m: Wolf Biermann was stripped of his GDR citizenship in November 1976.

46550.q: What did the GDR use in November 1976 as the occasion for stripping Wolf Biermann of his citizenship?
a: A concert he gave in the West
An attempt to escape over the Wall
46550.e: On 13 November 1976 Biermann performed at the sports hall in Cologne at the invitation of the IG Metall union. The concert was broadcast on television and also seen in the GDR.
46550.m: The Cologne concert of 1976 gave the SED its pretext for stripping his citizenship.

46551.q: How did well-known GDR writers such as Christa Wolf and Stefan Heym react to Biermann being stripped of his citizenship?
a: In an open letter they asked for it to be reconsidered
They welcomed it in a newspaper
They immediately left the GDR together
46551.e: On 17 November 1976 artists such as Christa Wolf, Stefan Heym and Heiner Müller asked in an open letter for the measure to be reconsidered. More than a hundred others then joined them, and many were punished for it.
46551.m: The protest against Biermann's expulsion split the GDR's cultural scene.

46552.q: What happened to many GDR artists who protested against Biermann being stripped of his citizenship?
a: They hardly got any more work, and some left the GDR
They were allowed to travel freely to the West
They were appointed to the government
46552.e: Those who protested were punished, watched or hardly got any more roles and commissions. Well-known artists such as the actor Manfred Krug then moved to the West.
46552.m: After Biermann's expulsion the GDR lost many well-known artists.

46553.q: What did the SED impose on Wolf Biermann in December 1965?
a: A ban on performing and publishing
46553.e: After the 11th Plenum of the SED Central Committee in December 1965, Biermann was banned from performing and publishing. After that his songs only appeared in the West; he was not stripped of his citizenship until 1976.
46553.m: Wolf Biermann was banned from performing in the GDR from 1965.

46554.q: How did Wolf Biermann release his album ‘Chausseestrasse 131’ in 1968 despite the performing ban?
a: He recorded it in his flat, and it was released in the West
He secretly recorded it in a GDR radio studio
He sang it live on GDR television
He handed it out as sheet music to schools
46554.e: Because he was not allowed to perform, Biermann recorded his songs in his East Berlin flat at Chausseestrasse 131. The record came out in the West, where it made him even better known.
46554.m: Despite the ban Biermann simply recorded his songs in his own flat.

46555.q: What punishment did the chemist and regime critic Robert Havemann receive after protesting against Biermann's expulsion?
46555.e: Robert Havemann publicly protested against his friend being stripped of his citizenship. After that he was under house arrest in Grünheide from 1976 to 1979.
46555.m: Robert Havemann was put under house arrest for his solidarity with Biermann.

46556.q: In which city was Wolf Biermann born in 1936, before he voluntarily moved to the GDR in 1953?
46556.e: Biermann grew up in Hamburg in a communist family. His father was murdered in Auschwitz in 1943, and as a teenager Biermann deliberately moved to the GDR.
46556.m: Wolf Biermann went from Hamburg to the GDR as a convinced communist.

46557.q: How did King Victor Emmanuel III react to the March on Rome in 1922?
a: He had the army fire on the Fascists
46557.e: Prime Minister Luigi Facta wanted to declare a state of siege, but the king refused to sign. Instead, at the end of October 1922, he asked Mussolini to form a government.
46557.m: In 1922 the king made Mussolini head of government instead of stopping the Fascists.

46558.q: How strong were the Fascists in the Italian parliament when Mussolini became head of government in 1922?
a: They had no seats in parliament at all
46558.e: In the election of May 1921 the Fascists stood as part of Giolitti's centre-right electoral bloc and entered parliament with about 35 deputies. So they were a small minority when Mussolini became head of government a year later.
46558.m: Mussolini came to power in 1922 even though his movement was only a small minority in parliament.

46559.q: Which party did Mussolini found in November 1921 from his loosely organised fighting leagues?
46559.e: In November 1921 Mussolini brought the fighting leagues and gangs of thugs together into the Partito Nazionale Fascista (PNF). A year later this party organised the March on Rome.
46559.m: The Partito Nazionale Fascista was founded in November 1921.

46560.q: What did the Italian Acerbo Law of 1923 lay down?
a: The strongest list receives two thirds of the seats
All parties except the PNF are banned
Parliament is replaced by a corporate chamber
The king may no longer appoint a government
46560.e: Under the Acerbo Law, the strongest list, provided it reached at least 25 per cent, received two thirds of the seats. In this way the Fascists secured a large majority in the 1924 election.
46560.m: The Acerbo Law gave the strongest list a two-thirds majority in parliament.

46561.q: How did Mussolini begin the open transition to a one-party dictatorship on 3 January 1925?
46561.e: In his speech to the Chamber of Deputies, Mussolini took political responsibility for Fascist violence. After that the opposition and the free press were eliminated step by step.
46561.m: With his speech of 3 January 1925 Mussolini openly made Italy a dictatorship.

46562.q: What is the walkout of the opposition from the Italian parliament after the murder of Matteotti in 1924 called?
46562.e: The opposition deputies left parliament in protest. The name recalls the withdrawal of the plebeians to the Aventine Hill in ancient Rome; the protest, however, had no effect.
46562.m: With the Aventine Secession the opposition boycotted parliament in 1924 without success.

46563.q: According to historians' current estimates, roughly how many people took part in the March on Rome?
46563.e: Contemporary reports spoke of 50,000 to over 70,000 participants. Historians today tend to assume 40,000 to 50,000 poorly armed Fascists, whom the army could easily have stopped.
46563.m: The March on Rome was militarily weak and worked mainly as a threatening show.

46564.q: Which later aviation minister was one of the four leaders of the March on Rome?
46564.e: Italo Balbo was one of the four quadrumvirs of the March on Rome, together with De Bono, De Vecchi and Bianchi. He later became aviation minister and was famous for long-distance flights.
46564.m: Italo Balbo helped lead the March on Rome and later became aviation minister.

46565.q: What did Fascist corporatism mean in Italy?
a: Workers and employers were grouped by sector under state supervision
Large firms could freely form cartels
Trade unions took over the running of factories
46565.e: The basic text was the Carta del Lavoro of 1927. Officially, labour and capital were meant to cooperate; in reality the system served mainly to control the workforce.
46565.m: Under corporatism the state controlled workers and employers together.

46566.q: According to its own doctrine, what was Fascist corporatism meant to overcome?
a: The class struggle between workers and employers
The monarchy in favour of a republic
The market economy on the Soviet model
46566.e: Workers and employers were to be grouped into corporations by branch of the economy and cooperate under state direction. In reality the system served mainly to control the workforce.
46566.m: Corporatism aimed to replace class struggle with state-directed cooperation.

46567.q: Which institution replaced the elected Chamber of Deputies in Italy in 1939?
a: The Chamber of Fasces and Corporations
46567.e: In 1939 the Chamber of Deputies was abolished and replaced by the Camera dei Fasci e delle Corporazioni. Its members were no longer elected but held their seats by virtue of their offices in the party and the corporations.
46567.m: From 1939 the Chamber of Fasces and Corporations sat in Italy instead of elected deputies.

46568.q: On what basis was the Italian economy divided into corporations in 1934?
46568.e: In 1934, 22 corporations were created, one for each area such as agriculture, industry or services. Each included representatives of the workers, the employers and the party.
46568.m: Fascist Italy divided its economy into corporations by sector.

46569.q: Which employee organisations were the only ones allowed to represent workers in Fascist Italy from 1926?
46569.e: The 1926 law on collective labour relations recognised only the Fascist syndicates. Free trade unions thus lost any legal basis.
46569.m: In Fascist Italy there were no free trade unions from 1926.

46570.q: What was forbidden to workers and employers alike in Fascist Italy from 1926?
46570.e: Conflicts between labour and capital were no longer to be fought out openly but decided by state labour courts. That is why both strikes and lockouts were banned.
46570.m: The Fascist state banned strikes and lockouts and decided labour disputes itself.

46571.q: Which ministry did Mussolini set up in 1926 to steer the corporate system?
46571.e: The Ministero delle Corporazioni was created in 1926 and supervised the syndicates and later the corporations. At times Mussolini ran it himself.
46571.m: From 1926 a ministry of its own steered Italy's corporate system.

46572.q: Why do many historians prefer to speak of the ‘transfer of power’ rather than the ‘seizure of power’?
a: Because conservative elites handed power to Hitler
Because Hitler won the election with an absolute majority
Because the victorious powers installed Hitler
Because Hitler ruled through a military coup
46572.e: ‘Seizure of power’ is a term from Nazi propaganda that suggests a heroic victory. In fact Hitler was brought into government by conservative circles around the Reich President.
46572.m: Hitler did not conquer power alone; it was handed to him by conservative elites.

46573.q: How many Nazi party members apart from Hitler sat in Hitler's first cabinet of 30 January 1933?
46573.e: Apart from Hitler, only Wilhelm Frick as interior minister and Hermann Göring as minister without portfolio belonged to the Nazi party. Most of the ministers were conservatives.
46573.m: In Hitler's first cabinet the Nazis were outnumbered.

46574.q: Which vice-chancellor believed in 1933 that he could ‘box in’ and tame Hitler within the government?
46574.e: Franz von Papen became vice-chancellor and thought the conservative ministers could control Hitler. This ‘taming’ plan failed within a few months.
46574.m: Papen's taming plan badly underestimated Hitler.

46575.q: What percentage of the vote did the Nazi party receive in the Reichstag election of 5 March 1933?
46575.e: Despite terror against the opposition, the Nazi party only reached 43.9 per cent. For a majority it needed the votes of its German National partner.
46575.m: Even in the unfree election of March 1933 the Nazi party missed an absolute majority.

46576.q: What majority did the Enabling Act need in the Reichstag, because it changed the constitution?
46576.e: In the Weimar Republic, laws changing the constitution needed a two-thirds majority. This was achieved on 23 March 1933 with the votes of the centre-right parties, including the Centre Party.
46576.m: In 1933 the Enabling Act reached the necessary two-thirds majority with the help of centre-right parties.

46577.q: What is the staged event of 21 March 1933 called, at which Hitler appeared next to Hindenburg in the Garrison Church?
46577.e: For the opening of the new Reichstag, Hitler appeared respectfully in Potsdam next to the aged Reich President. The ceremony was meant to show the link between old Prussia and the new regime.
46577.m: The Day of Potsdam symbolically linked the Nazi regime with Prussian tradition.

46578.q: Whose leadership did Hitler have murdered in the so-called ‘Röhm Putsch’ in the summer of 1934?
46578.e: At the end of June and the beginning of July 1934, Hitler had Ernst Röhm and other SA leaders as well as other opponents killed without trial. In this way he removed a rival to the Reichswehr and secured its support.
46578.m: In the so-called Röhm Putsch of 1934 Hitler had the SA leadership murdered without trial.

46579.q: To whom did soldiers of the Reichswehr have to swear their oath from August 1934?
46579.e: After Hindenburg's death, the Reichswehr swore its oath to Hitler as a person, no longer to the constitution. This personal bond later made resistance harder for many officers.
46579.m: From 1934 German soldiers swore their oath personally to Hitler.

46580.q: What was a well-known short formula of the Nazi leader principle?
46580.e: Every leader could give orders downwards and was answerable only to the next leader up. At the top stood Hitler, who was accountable to no one.
46580.m: Under the leader principle you gave orders downwards and were answerable only upwards.

46581.q: What did the leader principle replace in the party, the state and associations?
46581.e: Leaders were no longer elected but appointed from above. Votes and majority decisions were regarded as ‘un-German’ and abolished.
46581.m: The leader principle replaced democratic elections with appointment from above.

46582.q: Since which year had Hitler held a dictatorial position as chairman of the Nazi party?
46582.e: In July 1921 Hitler pushed through that he became party chairman with dictatorial powers. So the leader principle applied in the party long before 1933.
46582.m: The leader principle applied in the Nazi party from as early as 1921.

46583.q: Under the ‘Law for the Organisation of National Labour’ of 1934, what were the employer and the workforce called?
46583.e: The law applied the leader principle to businesses. The employer became the ‘Betriebsführer’ (works leader), the employees the ‘Gefolgschaft’ (followers), who owed him loyalty.
46583.m: With works leader and followers the leader principle was carried into the factories.

46584.q: What were the regional Nazi party leaders who ran a party district called?
46584.e: Within the party the Reich was divided into Gaue, each headed by a Gauleiter. The Gauleiter were directly subordinate to Hitler and had great power in their region.
46584.m: Gauleiter were the Nazi party's regional rulers and answered directly to Hitler.

46585.q: Which historian made the phrase famous that in the Nazi state people had to ‘work towards the Führer’?
46585.e: Ian Kershaw took the phrase from a 1934 speech by a Nazi official. It explains how officials without exact orders tried to anticipate Hitler's supposed wishes and thereby drove radicalisation.
46585.m: Many officials worked towards the Führer and so radicalised the regime.

46586.q: What do historians call the coexistence of competing centres of power in the Nazi state despite the leader principle?
46586.e: Party, state, SS and special commissioners often had overlapping responsibilities and competed with each other. Only Hitler stood above this confusion as the final decision-maker.
46586.m: Despite the leader principle the Nazi state was a polycracy of rival power centres.

46587.q: Which slogan expressed unconditional submission to Hitler?
46587.e: The slogan was spread at rallies and on posters. It shows the core of the leader principle: orders from above were to be carried out without objection.
46587.m: The leader principle demanded unconditional obedience to Hitler.

46588.q: Whom did the Nazi ‘national community’ explicitly exclude?
a: Groups persecuted as ‘alien to the community’
46588.e: The national community promised solidarity among all ‘national comrades’, but excluded Jews, political opponents and other groups as ‘alien to the community’. Inclusion and exclusion were inseparable.
46588.m: The national community was always also based on excluding those said to be alien to it.

46589.q: Which earlier experience did the Nazis like to refer to with the term ‘national community’?
a: The ‘spirit of 1914’ at the start of the war
46589.e: At the start of the First World War, many Germans invoked a unity across all classes and parties. Nazi propaganda built on this mood.
46589.m: The Nazi national community built on the mood of unity of 1914.

46590.q: What was the Nazi organisation called that offered holidays, theatre visits and sport for workers?
46590.e: ‘Strength Through Joy’ was part of the German Labour Front and organised cheap leisure activities, even cruises. In this way the workforce was to be won over to the regime.
46590.m: With ‘Strength Through Joy’ the regime courted workers with cheap leisure.

46591.q: Which cheap radio set was meant to bring propaganda into as many German homes as possible from 1933?
46591.e: The People's Receiver (Volksempfänger) was presented in 1933 and cost much less than other radios. Listening together to the Führer's speeches was meant to make the national community something people could experience.
46591.m: With the People's Receiver Nazi propaganda came into people's living rooms.

46592.q: Where was the money saved on ‘Stew Sunday’ meant to go?
46592.e: Households were supposed to eat only a simple one-pot stew once a month and donate what they saved. The collections made sacrifice for the national community visible and at the same time put social pressure on people.
46592.m: Stew Sunday was meant to show willingness to make sacrifices for the national community.

46593.q: Which slogan put the individual entirely beneath the community?
a: ‘You are nothing, your nation is everything’
‘Everyone is the architect of their own fortune’
46593.e: The slogan expresses that the individual only counted as part of the nation. Personal rights and freedoms had to take second place.
46593.m: In the national community the individual counted for nothing compared with the nation.

46594.q: Which service became compulsory by law for young men in 1935?
46594.e: From 1935 young men had to do six months of labour service, for example building roads or in farming. The service was meant to blur class differences and educate people for the national community.
46594.m: The Reich Labour Service was meant to educate young men for the national community.

46595.q: Which car did the regime praise as a symbol of the national community, although savers had not received it by the end of the war?
46595.e: Hundreds of thousands paid into a savings scheme for the KdF car. But during the war the factory produced military vehicles, and not a single saver received their car.
46595.m: For the savers the KdF car remained an unkept promise.

46596.q: What did it mean that the Hitler Youth became the ‘state youth’ by law from 1936?
a: Alongside home and school it was an official body for raising children
It was led directly by the Wehrmacht
It only accepted children of civil servants
46596.e: The Hitler Youth Law of 1 December 1936 made the Hitler Youth an official educating body alongside family and school. Other youth organisations were banned or absorbed.
46596.m: From 1936 the Hitler Youth brought up children on behalf of the state alongside family and school.

46597.q: What did the ‘youth service duty’ that applied from 1939 mean?
a: Service in the Hitler Youth became compulsory
All young people had to work in arms factories
All young people had to join the Wehrmacht immediately
Young people had to serve abroad for a year
46597.e: From 1939 service in the Hitler Youth was compulsory for all young people aged 10 to 18. Anyone who avoided it could be punished, and so could their parents.
46597.m: From 1939 service in the Hitler Youth was compulsory.

46598.q: Which principle was supposed to apply in the Hitler Youth?
46598.e: Older teenagers led younger groups, and adults stayed in the background. As a result many young people escaped the influence of their parents and teachers.
46598.m: In the Hitler Youth young people led other young people.

46599.q: What were the youngest members of the German Young People (Deutsches Jungvolk) colloquially called?
46599.e: The ten- to fourteen-year-olds in the Deutsches Jungvolk were called ‘Pimpfe’. To be accepted they had to pass a ‘Pimpf test’ with sport and knowledge of Nazi ideology.
46599.m: The Pimpfe were the youngest boys in the Hitler Youth.

46600.q: What was the organisation for girls aged 14 to 18 within the Hitler Youth called?
46600.e: The League of German Girls (BDM) took in girls aged 14 to 18; younger ones were in the Young Girls' League. The aim was to bring them up as wives and mothers in line with Nazi ideology.
46600.m: In the Hitler Youth girls were taken into the League of German Girls.

46601.q: Which young people in Hamburg stood out for their love of American jazz and were persecuted?
46601.e: The Swing Youth listened to banned jazz music, dressed casually and rejected the drill of the Hitler Youth. The regime persecuted them, and some were even sent to youth concentration camps.
46601.m: The Swing Youth set jazz and a relaxed style against the drill of the Hitler Youth.

46602.q: What were the Nazi elite schools run by the Hitler Youth called?
46602.e: From 1937 the Adolf Hitler Schools were run by the Reich Youth Leadership and the German Labour Front. They were meant to train the party's next generation of leaders.
46602.m: The Adolf Hitler Schools were meant to raise future party leaders.

46603.q: What happened to the remaining Jewish civil servants as a result of the First Regulation to the Reich Citizenship Law?
a: They had to join the Nazi party
They were drafted into the Wehrmacht
46603.e: In 1933, Jewish front-line veterans of the First World War, among others, had still been exempt from exclusion from the civil service. With the regulation to the Reich Citizenship Law they too had to leave office.
46603.m: With the regulation to the Reich Citizenship Law all Jewish civil servants lost their posts, including former front-line soldiers.

46604.q: What did the Blood Protection Law of 1935 forbid?
46604.e: The law was one of the Nuremberg Laws. It banned marriages between Jews and non-Jews and, with further bans, reached right into private households.
46604.m: The Blood Protection Law intruded into private life with racist bans.

46605.q: What was the provision called that already excluded civil servants of Jewish origin from state service in 1933?
46605.e: The Law for the Restoration of the Professional Civil Service of April 1933 contained the so-called Aryan paragraph. It was an early step in depriving Jews of their rights, which the Nuremberg Laws later made harsher.
46605.m: The Aryan paragraph of 1933 was a forerunner of the Nuremberg Laws.

46606.q: Under the First Regulation to the Reich Citizenship Law, how many Jewish grandparents were enough for someone to count as a ‘full Jew’?
46606.e: The First Regulation to the Reich Citizenship Law classed people with at least three Jewish grandparents as ‘full Jews’. What counted was the religion of the grandparents, which shows the absurdity of the racial theory.
46606.m: The Nazi definition of Jews absurdly rested on the grandparents' religion.

46607.q: What did the Nazi courts call relationships that were forbidden under the Blood Protection Law?
46607.e: Love relationships between Jews and non-Jews were prosecuted as ‘racial defilement’ and punished with prison or penal servitude. Many people were denounced for this.
46607.m: Nazi courts prosecuted relationships between Jews and non-Jews as ‘racial defilement’.

46608.q: To which further group did a circular from the Reich Interior Ministry explicitly extend the Blood Protection Law?
46608.e: In the same year the law was announced, a circular from the Interior Ministry also applied the Blood Protection Law to ‘Gypsies’ and Black people. In this way the racial laws were extended to further groups.
46608.m: Besides the Jews, the racial laws also hit the Sinti and Roma.

46609.q: Why did the Nazi regime have antisemitic signs temporarily removed in 1936?
a: Because of a state visit from Rome
Because of the World Exhibition in Paris
46609.e: During the Olympic Games in Garmisch-Partenkirchen and Berlin, Germany wanted to appear open to the world. After the Games the persecution continued undiminished.
46609.m: For the 1936 Olympic Games the regime hid its antisemitism only briefly.

46610.q: What was the name of the German diplomat whose death in Paris served the Nazis as a pretext in November 1938?
46610.e: The diplomat was a legation secretary at the German embassy in Paris. He was shot on 7 November and died on 9 November 1938.
46610.m: The diplomat's death in Paris served as the pretext for the November pogroms.

46611.q: Which deportation in October 1938 also affected the parents of the assassin Herschel Grynszpan?
46611.e: At the end of October 1938, up to 18,000 Jews of Polish origin were forcibly taken to the Polish border. The news of his family's misery drove Grynszpan to his act.
46611.m: The Polish Action in October 1938 came immediately before the November pogroms.

46612.q: Why were the Nazi leaders gathered in Munich on the evening of 9 November 1938?
46612.e: Every year on 9 November the Nazi party commemorated the failed putsch of 1923 in Munich. At this gathering in the Old Town Hall, the news of the diplomat's death was announced.
46612.m: The pogroms began on the anniversary of Hitler's putsch in Munich.

46613.q: The Nazi party officially gave 91 Jewish deaths in the November pogroms. How do historians judge this figure today?
a: The real number was much higher
There were no deaths at all
46613.e: If the deaths in the camps and the suicides are included, historians arrive at several hundred victims. The official figure played down the scale.
46613.m: The official death toll of the pogroms played down their real scale.

46614.q: Who received the insurance payments for the damage to Jewish property?
46614.e: The insurance companies had to pay, but the money was confiscated for the Reich. The victims had to repair the damage themselves.
46614.m: After the pogroms the state even took the insurance money away from the victims.

46615.q: What did a regulation of 12 November 1938 order?
a: The exclusion of Jews from economic life
The obligation to wear a yellow star
The removal of citizenship from all Jews abroad
The deportation of all Jews to Poland
46615.e: From 1939 Jews were no longer allowed to run shops or craft businesses. Their businesses were ‘Aryanised’, meaning forcibly transferred to non-Jews.
46615.m: After the pogroms Jews were completely pushed out of economic life.

46616.q: Roughly how many Jewish children did Great Britain take in through the Kindertransport after the pogroms?
46616.e: Between December 1938 and the start of the war in 1939, about 10,000 Jewish children came to Great Britain without their parents. Most never saw their parents again.
46616.m: The Kindertransport saved about 10,000 Jewish children by bringing them to Great Britain.

46617.e: Reinhard Heydrich, head of the Reich Security Main Office, invited the state secretaries and SS leaders and chaired the meeting. He wanted to assert his leading role in organising the mass murder.
46617.m: Reinhard Heydrich chaired the Wannsee Conference.

46618.q: Who wrote the minutes of the Wannsee Conference?
46618.e: Adolf Eichmann was responsible for ‘Jewish affairs’ in the Reich Security Main Office and wrote the minutes. He was convicted and executed in Israel in 1962.
46618.m: Adolf Eichmann wrote the minutes of the Wannsee Conference.

46619.q: Which Jews did the minutes of the Wannsee Conference include in their list?
a: Even the Jews of neutral countries such as Switzerland
Only the Jews in the occupied territories in the East
46619.e: The minutes listed all the countries of Europe, including Switzerland with 18,000 Jews, Sweden and Spain. So the plans were aimed at all the Jews of Europe, not only those under German control.
46619.m: Even the Jews of neutral Switzerland were on the Wannsee Conference list.

46620.q: According to the minutes, how many European Jews were to be affected by the so-called ‘Final Solution’?
46620.e: The minutes named a total of about eleven million people across Europe. The figure shows how comprehensively the planned genocide was conceived.
46620.m: The planners of the Wannsee Conference counted on about eleven million Jews in Europe.

46621.q: Why are the minutes of the Wannsee Conference such an important document?
a: They prove in writing how authorities coordinated the genocide of the Jews
They bear Hitler's signature on a murder order
They were published in all German newspapers in 1942
They are the only source on the Holocaust
46621.e: Of 30 copies, only one survived, the Foreign Office copy. In dry official language it shows how ministries and the SS coordinated the deportation and murder of the Jews of Europe.
46621.m: Only one of the 30 copies of the minutes has survived.

46622.q: Where were the Wannsee minutes found in 1947?
a: In the files of the Foreign Office
In the Führer bunker in Berlin
In the camp administration of Auschwitz
46622.e: In March 1947 the US prosecutor Robert Kempner learned of the find in the Foreign Office files. The document became a key piece of evidence in the subsequent Nuremberg trials.
46622.m: The Wannsee minutes were discovered in Foreign Office files in 1947.

46623.q: Who had instructed Heydrich in writing on 31 July 1941 to prepare an ‘overall solution of the Jewish question’?
46623.e: Hermann Göring gave Heydrich this order in writing. At the conference Heydrich explicitly referred to it to prove his authority.
46623.m: Göring's order of July 1941 was the basis for Heydrich's conference.

46624.q: Why is the Wannsee Conference not seen as the place where the genocide was decided?
a: Because the mass murder was already under way and the meeting was about organisation
Because Hitler banned the conference at short notice
Because most participants rejected the plan
Because only Wehrmacht officers took part
46624.e: Shootings in the East and the first gassings had already begun. The conference was about involving the ministries and coordinating the deportations.
46624.m: The Wannsee Conference coordinated the organisation of a genocide that was already under way.

46625.q: Where does the word ‘Holocaust’ come from?
46625.e: Holocaust comes from the Greek ‘holokaustos’, a burnt offering that was completely burnt. Because the word recalls a sacrifice, many prefer the Hebrew term Shoah.
46625.m: The word Holocaust originally means a completely burnt offering.

46626.q: Which units murdered hundreds of thousands of Jews in mass shootings behind the Eastern Front from 1941?
46626.e: The Einsatzgruppen of the Security Police and SD followed the Wehrmacht into the Soviet Union. Supported by police battalions and helpers, they shot Jews in huge numbers.
46626.m: In 1941 the Einsatzgruppen began the mass murder by shooting in the East.

46627.q: In which ravine near Kyiv were over 33,000 Jews shot in two days in September 1941?
46627.e: At Babyn Yar, a special commando and police units murdered over 33,000 Jewish people on 29 and 30 September 1941. It is one of the largest single massacres of the Holocaust.
46627.m: Babyn Yar near Kyiv stands for mass murder by shooting.

46628.q: Which three extermination camps belonged to the so-called ‘Operation Reinhard’?
46628.e: In these three camps in occupied Poland, well over a million people, almost all of them Jews, were murdered in 1942 and 1943. The camps served only for murder, not for forced labour.
46628.m: Belzec, Sobibor and Treblinka were pure extermination camps of Operation Reinhard.

46629.q: Which poison gas did the SS use in the gas chambers of Auschwitz-Birkenau?
46629.e: Zyklon B was originally a pesticide based on hydrogen cyanide. From 1941 the SS used it in Auschwitz to murder people.
46629.m: In Auschwitz the SS murdered people with the cyanide poison Zyklon B.

46630.q: Which marking in the passports of German Jews was introduced in 1938 at the urging of the Swiss authorities?
46630.e: Switzerland wanted to be able to recognise and turn away Jewish refugees at the border. So from autumn 1938 Germany stamped a red ‘J’ in the passports of Jews.
46630.m: The J stamp of 1938 was also due to pressure from the Swiss authorities.

46631.q: Which expert commission investigated Switzerland's role in the Second World War from 1996?
46631.e: The Independent Commission of Experts under the historian Jean-François Bergier investigated refugee policy and economic relations, among other things. It presented its final report in 2002.
46631.m: The Bergier Commission examined Switzerland's role in the Second World War.

46632.q: What did the Swiss authorities decide regarding Jewish refugees in August 1942?
a: To close the border to them
To take them in without limit
To pay for their onward journey to America
To give them immediate work permits
46632.e: Refugees ‘only on racial grounds’ were not considered political refugees and were turned back at the border. Many of those turned away were later murdered.
46632.m: In 1942 Switzerland closed its border to Jewish refugees.

46633.q: Who coined the image of a Berlin-Rome ‘axis’ in a speech in Milan in 1936?
46633.e: In November 1936 Mussolini spoke of a Berlin-Rome axis around which other European states could revolve. This gave rise to the term ‘Axis powers’.
46633.m: The term Axis goes back to a speech by Mussolini in 1936.

46634.q: Which 1936 treaty between Germany and Japan was directed against the Communist International?
46634.e: The Anti-Comintern Pact of November 1936 was directed against the Communist International, which was controlled from Moscow. Italy joined it in 1937.
46634.m: In 1936 the Anti-Comintern Pact united Germany and Japan against communism.

46635.q: What was the military alliance between Germany and Italy of May 1939 called?
46635.e: In the Pact of Steel, Germany and Italy committed themselves to mutual military support, even in a war of aggression. However, Italy only entered the war in June 1940.
46635.m: With the Pact of Steel of 1939 Germany and Italy became military allies.

46636.q: Which treaty of September 1940 linked Germany, Italy and Japan?
46636.e: The Tripartite Pact was signed in Berlin on 27 September 1940. The three states divided spheres of influence in Europe and East Asia between them and promised each other support.
46636.m: The Tripartite Pact of 1940 turned the Berlin-Rome-Tokyo axis into an alliance.

46637.q: Which war drove Italy closer to Germany in 1935 and 1936 because of the League of Nations' sanctions?
46637.e: Because of the invasion of Ethiopia, the League of Nations imposed sanctions on Italy. Germany supported Italy, which brought the two dictatorships closer together.
46637.m: The Abyssinian War isolated Italy and brought it to Germany's side.

46638.q: In which month did Italy sign an armistice with the Allies and thus leave the Axis?
46638.e: The Armistice of Cassibile was announced on 8 September 1943. German troops then occupied large parts of Italy.
46638.m: Italy left the Axis alliance with an armistice in September 1943.

46639.q: Which of these countries fought in the Second World War as an ally on the side of the Axis powers?
46639.e: Hungary joined the Tripartite Pact in November 1940 and fought on Germany's side from 1941. Sweden, Portugal and Turkey remained neutral for a long time during the war.
46639.m: Hungary joined the Tripartite Pact in 1940 and became Germany's ally.

46640.q: On which day did Germany declare war on the USA, a few days after the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor?
46640.e: Japan attacked Pearl Harbor on 7 December 1941. Four days later Germany and Italy declared war on the USA, although the Tripartite Pact did not oblige them to do so.
46640.m: With the declaration of war on the USA in 1941 the war finally became a world war.

46641.q: What do you call the strong rise of far-right groups in Switzerland in 1933?
46641.e: After Hitler was appointed Reich Chancellor, numerous ‘Fronts’ sprang up in Switzerland or gained supporters. This wave is called the Front Spring (Frontenfrühling).
46641.m: In the Front Spring of 1933 far-right groups in Switzerland gained ground.

46642.q: How successful was the Front movement in elections in Switzerland?
a: It won only a few seats and remained a minority
From 1934 it had a member of the Federal Council
It became the largest party in the National Council
46642.e: The Frontists had their greatest success in Zurich in 1933 with 10 of 125 seats on the city council. After that they remained insignificant in elections.
46642.m: The Frontists remained a small minority in Swiss elections.

46643.q: Which greeting did the Swiss Frontists use?
46643.e: The Frontists used the cry ‘Harus!’ as a leader's salute. In this way they imitated the greetings of their German and Italian models with a word of their own.
46643.m: The greeting of the Swiss Frontists was ‘Harus!’.

46644.q: What did the popular initiative supported by the Fronts, which was voted on in 1935, demand?
a: A total revision of the Federal Constitution
46644.e: The Fronts and conservative groups wanted to rebuild the Federal Constitution fundamentally, partly in an authoritarian direction. They failed clearly at the ballot box.
46644.m: In 1935 the Fronts wanted to rebuild the Federal Constitution with a total revision.

46645.q: What was the result of the September 1935 popular vote on a total revision of the Federal Constitution?
a: The Federal Council cancelled the vote
46645.e: The initiative failed with about 72 per cent voting no. The result is seen as a clear commitment to the existing democratic order.
46645.m: In 1935 Swiss voters clearly rejected a total revision of the Federal Constitution.

46646.q: Which Nazi party regional group leader was shot in Davos in 1936?
46646.e: The Jewish student David Frankfurter shot Wilhelm Gustloff in February 1936. After that the Federal Council banned the Nazi party's national leadership in Switzerland.
46646.m: After the assassination of Wilhelm Gustloff the Federal Council banned the Nazi party's national leadership.

46647.q: Which text was judged to be a forgery in the Bern trial of 1935?
a: ‘The Protocols of the Elders of Zion’
46647.e: Jewish organisations sued Frontists who had spread the antisemitic hate pamphlet. In 1935 the court in Bern found that it was a forgery.
46647.m: In the Bern trial the Protocols of the Elders of Zion were exposed as a forgery.

46648.q: Which Frontist organisation did the Federal Council ban in November 1940?
46648.e: After Germany's victory over France, the National Movement of Switzerland sought to adapt to the Nazi regime. The Federal Council banned it on 19 November 1940.
46648.m: In 1940 the Federal Council banned the pro-Nazi National Movement of Switzerland.

46649.q: What did the Federal Council want to strengthen with its culture message of 1938?
a: The introduction of a single national language
46649.e: With the message of December 1938, the Federal Council officially backed spiritual national defence against Nazism and Fascism. It described Switzerland as a nation built on will, with several cultures.
46649.m: The culture message of 1938 made spiritual national defence official policy.

46650.q: Which member of the Federal Council is seen as the most important promoter of spiritual national defence?
46650.e: Philipp Etter headed the Department of Home Affairs and was responsible for the culture message. He stressed Switzerland's diversity and Christian conservative values.
46650.m: Federal Councillor Philipp Etter played a key role in shaping spiritual national defence.

46651.q: Which cultural foundation came out of the culture message?
46651.e: The culture message proposed a foundation supported by the Confederation to promote culture. This led to Pro Helvetia, which still promotes Swiss culture at home and abroad today.
46651.m: Pro Helvetia is a legacy of spiritual national defence.

46652.q: Which 1939 exhibition in Zurich is seen as the most effective expression of spiritual national defence?
46652.e: The 1939 national exhibition presented Switzerland as a diverse, independent nation. Shortly before the war began, the ‘Landi spirit’ strengthened national unity.
46652.m: The Landi of 1939 strengthened Switzerland's will to remain independent.

46653.q: Which language became Switzerland's fourth national language by popular vote in 1938?
46653.e: Recognising Romansh was also a response to Italian Fascist claims that presented Romansh as an Italian dialect. The proposal was accepted by a very large majority.
46653.m: Since 1938 Romansh has been Switzerland's fourth national language.

46654.q: Which Swiss film of 1938 about a soldier at the time of the First World War shaped spiritual national defence?
46654.e: Leopold Lindtberg made ‘Füsilier Wipf’, which showed the bond between the people and the army. The film was a big box-office success.
46654.m: In 1938 the film ‘Füsilier Wipf’ strengthened Swiss national feeling.

46655.q: Which circles originally called for a ‘spiritual’ defence of democracy against Fascism?
46655.e: At first, left-wing politicians and intellectuals called for democracy to be defended against Fascist propaganda with radio, film and culture too. From 1938 the Federal Council also supported the movement.
46655.m: Spiritual national defence also had its roots on the left.

46656.q: After 1945, which danger was spiritual national defence mainly directed against?
46656.e: During the Cold War the movement turned against communist infiltration. After strong criticism from artists and writers, official support ended from 1962.
46656.m: In the Cold War spiritual national defence was directed against communism.

46657.q: Who shaped the Portuguese Estado Novo for decades as head of government?
46657.e: Salazar was finance minister from 1928 and ruled Portugal from 1932 to 1968. The constitution of 1933 founded the Estado Novo (‘New State’).
46657.m: Salazar ruled Portugal as head of government from 1932.

46658.q: Where was the notorious Tarrafal prison camp, in which the Estado Novo held political prisoners?
46658.e: The Tarrafal camp, opened in 1936 on the island of Santiago (Cape Verde), was called the ‘camp of slow death’ because of its deadly climate.
46658.m: Tarrafal on Cape Verde was the most feared camp of the Estado Novo.

46659.q: Which alliance did Portugal join as a founding member in 1949 despite its dictatorship?
46659.e: Because of its strategic position, above all the Azores, Portugal became a founding member of NATO in 1949. In the Cold War anti-communism counted for more than democracy.
46659.m: Despite its dictatorship Portugal was a founding member of NATO.

46660.q: Which economic organisation did Portugal join as a founding member together with Switzerland in 1960?
a: The European Coal and Steel Community
46660.e: The European Free Trade Association EFTA was founded in 1960 by seven states, including Switzerland, Portugal, Austria and Great Britain.
46660.m: Portugal and Switzerland founded EFTA together in 1960.

46661.q: Which opposition candidate in the 1958 presidential election was murdered by the secret police in 1965?
46661.e: In 1958 General Humberto Delgado challenged the regime and announced that he would remove Salazar. After the rigged election he went into exile and was murdered in Spain by PIDE agents in 1965.
46661.m: Humberto Delgado paid for his opposition to Salazar with his life.

46662.q: In the 1933 plebiscite on the Estado Novo constitution, how were abstentions counted?
46662.e: Anyone who did not vote was counted in the yes camp. In this way the constitution achieved seemingly overwhelming approval.
46662.m: In the 1933 constitutional plebiscite abstentions counted as approval.

46663.q: What was the only permitted political organisation in the Estado Novo called?
46663.e: The União Nacional was founded in 1930 and provided all the deputies at elections. Opposition parties were banned.
46663.m: The União Nacional was Salazar's single party.

46664.q: Which object became the symbol of censorship in the Estado Novo?
46664.e: The censors crossed out unwanted passages in newspapers and books with a blue pencil. In Portugal the ‘lápis azul’ still stands for censorship today.
46664.m: The censors' blue pencil stood for the lack of press freedom under Salazar.

46665.q: What concession did neutral Portugal make to the Allies in 1943?
a: It let Great Britain use bases on the Azores
It sent troops to North Africa
It rejoined the League of Nations
46665.e: Portugal invoked its old alliance with England and allowed airfields on the Azores to be used. These were important for the Battle of the Atlantic.
46665.m: In 1943 Salazar opened the Azores to the Allies.

46666.q: Who carried out the overthrow of the dictatorship in Portugal on 25 April 1974?
46666.e: The ‘Armed Forces Movement’ of young officers toppled the dictatorship almost without bloodshed. In Lisbon, Captain Salgueiro Maia forced the government to surrender.
46666.m: In 1974 young officers overthrew the dictatorship in Portugal.

46667.q: What was the large Tagus bridge in Lisbon, now called ‘Ponte 25 de Abril’, called before the revolution?
46667.e: The suspension bridge, opened in 1966, bore the dictator's name. After the revolution it was renamed after the date of the overthrow.
46667.m: The Lisbon bridge was renamed from the dictator to the date of freedom.

46668.q: How did the coup leaders in Portugal receive the signal to start on the night of 25 April 1974?
46668.e: First the Eurovision song ‘E Depois do Adeus’ was played on the radio, and after midnight came ‘Grândola, Vila Morena’. Then the officers knew the plan was starting.
46668.m: Songs on the radio gave the signal for the Carnation Revolution.

46669.q: What threatened Portugal in the ‘hot summer’ of 1975 after the Carnation Revolution?
a: A civil war between factions of the army
The return of the old dictatorship
46669.e: Moderate and radical left-wing officers faced each other. On 25 November 1975 the moderates prevailed and secured the path to parliamentary democracy.
46669.m: In 1975 Portugal was on the brink of civil war.

46670.q: What did Portugal become with the new constitution of 1976 after the Carnation Revolution?
a: A democracy with a freely elected parliament
46670.e: In 1976 free parliamentary and presidential elections took place. General António Ramalho Eanes became president and Mário Soares prime minister.
46670.m: Portugal has been a democracy since 1976.

46671.q: What happened to Portugal's colonies such as Angola and Mozambique after the Carnation Revolution?
a: They were handed over to Spain
They were placed under the UN
46671.e: The long colonial wars in Africa were a main reason for the overthrow. The new government quickly granted the colonies independence.
46671.m: After the Carnation Revolution Portugal's colonies became independent.

46672.q: Which alliance had won the Spanish parliamentary election in February 1936?
46672.e: The Popular Front of Republicans, Socialists and Communists won narrowly. The country's political division then escalated until the coup.
46672.m: The Popular Front's election victory in 1936 came before the civil war.

46673.q: Which organisation recruited the International Brigades for the Spanish Republic?
46673.e: From 1936 the Comintern organised the brigades with volunteers from over 50 countries. They fought on the side of the Republic.
46673.m: The Comintern set up the International Brigades.

46674.q: How did Switzerland deal with the roughly 800 Swiss who had fought on the side of the Republic?
a: Military courts convicted many for serving in a foreign army
The Federal Council honoured them as defenders of democracy
They went unpunished because Switzerland was neutral
46674.e: Serving in a foreign army was forbidden in Switzerland, so many volunteers in Spain were sentenced to prison on their return. Only in 2009 did a federal law rehabilitate them.
46674.m: The Swiss fighters in Spain were convicted and only rehabilitated in 2009.

46675.q: Which battle from July to November 1938 was the largest and costliest of the civil war?
46675.e: The Republican offensive across the Ebro failed after months of fighting. After that the Republic's army was decisively weakened.
46675.m: The Battle of the Ebro decided the civil war in Franco's favour.

46676.q: On which day did Franco declare the civil war over?
46676.e: After the fall of Madrid at the end of March 1939, Franco announced victory on 1 April. A period of harsh persecution of the defeated followed.
46676.m: The Spanish Civil War ended on 1 April 1939.

46677.q: What form of state did Spain have immediately before the civil war?
a: A military dictatorship under Primo de Rivera
46677.e: After King Alfonso XIII left, the Second Spanish Republic was proclaimed on 14 April 1931. The generals' coup was directed against it.
46677.m: The civil war began as an uprising against the Second Spanish Republic.

46678.q: Which fortress in Toledo did the rebels defend for weeks in 1936 until Franco's troops relieved them?
46678.e: The siege of the Alcázar became a heroic legend of the Nationalists. Franco used its relief at the end of September 1936 for his propaganda.
46678.m: The Alcázar of Toledo became a myth of Franco's side.

46679.q: How did most of Franco's troops from Africa reach the Spanish mainland in 1936?
a: By an airlift with German and Italian planes
On ships of the British navy
On ferries of the Spanish Republic
46679.e: As most of the fleet stayed loyal to the Republic, German Ju 52s and Italian planes flew soldiers across the Strait of Gibraltar. It was one of the first major airlifts.
46679.m: An airlift brought Franco's Army of Africa to Spain.

46680.q: What happened in Barcelona in May 1937?
a: Fighting within the Republican camp between anarchists and communists
An air raid by the Condor Legion
The proclamation of the Second Republic
46680.e: In the May Days, anarchists and the POUM fought on one side, communists and government troops on the other. After that the POUM was banned and persecuted.
46680.m: In May 1937 the Republican side fought itself in Barcelona.

46681.q: What policy did Great Britain and France officially follow towards the Spanish Civil War?
a: A naval blockade of both sides
46681.e: A committee in London was meant to prevent arms deliveries to both sides. The agreement was broken by several states and weakened above all the Republic.
46681.m: The Western powers' non-intervention ended up helping Franco.

46682.q: How did Spain manage the transition to democracy after Franco's death in 1975?
a: Through reforms within the existing system
Through a victory by foreign troops
46682.e: In 1976 the old parliament voted for its own abolition with the Political Reform Act, and the people confirmed it by referendum. This is called a negotiated transition.
46682.m: Spain's democracy came about through reforms rather than an overthrow.

46683.q: What role did King Juan Carlos play in Spain's transition to democracy?
a: He supported the path to democracy
He abdicated immediately after Franco's death
46683.e: Franco had chosen Juan Carlos as his successor. In 1976 the king appointed the reformer Adolfo Suárez, under whom the first free elections took place in June 1977.
46683.m: King Juan Carlos promoted Spain's path to democracy.

46684.q: How did King Juan Carlos react to the attempted coup of 23 February 1981, when armed men stormed the Spanish parliament?
a: He backed the constitution on television
He openly supported the coup leaders
He stayed silent until the coup was over
46684.e: Lieutenant Colonel Antonio Tejero and members of the Guardia Civil held the deputies for hours. During the night the king, in uniform, defended democracy on television, after which the coup failed.
46684.m: In 1981 a television address by the king helped to stop the attempted coup.

46685.q: Which 1977 law long prevented the prosecution of crimes from the Franco era?
46685.e: The Amnesty Law freed political prisoners but also protected perpetrators of the regime. People speak of a ‘pact of silence’.
46685.m: The Amnesty Law of 1977 also protected the perpetrators of the dictatorship.

46686.q: How did the Spanish constitution of 1978 organise the country's regions?
a: As autonomous communities with their own parliaments
As cantons with their own constitutions
As provinces without their own rights
46686.e: The constitution allowed regions such as Catalonia and the Basque Country extensive self-government. Today there are 17 autonomous communities.
46686.m: After Franco Spain gave its regions extensive autonomy.

46687.q: Which organisation killed Franco's head of government and intended successor with a bomb in Madrid in 1973?
46687.e: A bomb under the road threw Luis Carrero Blanco's car into the air. His death weakened the hardliners who wanted to continue the regime after Franco.
46687.m: The murder of Carrero Blanco deprived Francoism of its designated successor.

46688.q: What happened to Franco's remains in 2019?
a: They were moved from the Valley of the Fallen to a cemetery
They were buried in Madrid Cathedral
46688.e: The government had Franco exhumed from the state monument and buried in the Mingorrubio cemetery near Madrid. The step was part of coming to terms with the dictatorship.
46688.m: Since 2019 Franco no longer lies in the Valley of the Fallen.

46689.q: Which Spanish law of 2007 was the first to comprehensively recognise the victims of the civil war and the dictatorship?
46689.e: The law condemned the dictatorship and made it possible to search for mass graves and remove Francoist symbols. In 2022 it was followed by an extended Democratic Memory Law.
46689.m: Since 2007 Spain has faced its past by law.

46690.q: From when to when did the colonels rule Greece?
46690.e: In the night of 21 April 1967 troops occupied Athens and arrested leading politicians. The regime collapsed in 1974 after the Cyprus crisis.
46690.m: The colonels ruled Greece from 1967 to 1974.

46691.q: What did the coup leaders of 1967 mainly want to prevent?
a: An expected election victory by the Centre Union
46691.e: Elections had been called for May 1967, which Georgios Papandreou's Centre Union would probably have won. The colonels justified the coup with an alleged communist threat.
46691.m: The colonels pre-empted a democratic election with a coup.

46692.q: Which event led to the collapse of the Greek military junta in 1974?
a: A coup in Cyprus directed from Athens
A general strike by dock workers
46692.e: In July 1974 the junta had the Cypriot president Makarios overthrown in order to unite Cyprus with Greece. Turkey then occupied the north of the island, and the humiliated junta gave up power.
46692.m: The Cyprus adventure of 1974 brought down the junta.

46693.q: Which uprising in Athens was crushed by a tank in November 1973?
a: The dock workers' uprising in Piraeus
46693.e: Students occupied the Polytechnic and broadcast calls against the junta over a radio station. On 17 November a tank broke through the gate, and people were killed.
46693.m: The Polytechnic uprising of 1973 became a symbol of resistance to the junta.

46694.q: Who led the Greek military junta as its strongman until 1973?
46694.e: Colonel Georgios Papadopoulos was the main mind behind the 1967 coup and became head of government. In November 1973 hardliners within the junta overthrew him.
46694.m: Georgios Papadopoulos was the leader of the colonels.

46695.q: What happened to King Constantine II of Greece in December 1967?
a: After a failed counter-coup he fled to Rome
He was deposed and arrested by the junta
He took over leadership of the junta himself
He abdicated in favour of his son
46695.e: The king tried to overthrow the colonels with loyal troops but failed. He never returned as king.
46695.m: King Constantine II went into exile after his failed counter-coup.

46696.q: Who returned from exile in Paris in July 1974 and formed a civilian government?
46696.e: Karamanlis had already been prime minister before the junta. He began the ‘Metapolitefsi’, the transition to democracy, and founded New Democracy.
46696.m: Konstantinos Karamanlis led Greece back to democracy in 1974.

46697.q: How did the trials of the junta leaders end in 1975?
a: With death sentences that were commuted to life imprisonment
With acquittals because of the statute of limitations
With fines and a ban on leaving the country
46697.e: Papadopoulos, Pattakos and Makarezos were sentenced to death for high treason. The government commuted the sentences to life imprisonment.
46697.m: In 1975 the junta leaders had to answer in court.

46698.q: Where did the junta send many opposition figures into exile?
a: To prison islands such as Gyaros and Leros
46698.e: Thousands of opponents were deported to remote islands without a court ruling. Torture in custody was widespread.
46698.m: The junta sent its opponents to remote prison islands.

46699.q: Which office did Miklós Horthy hold in Hungary from 1920 to 1944?
46699.e: Hungary formally remained a kingdom, but a return of the Habsburgs was prevented. Horthy ruled as regent in place of a king.
46699.m: Horthy ruled Hungary as regent of a kingdom without a king.

46700.q: What military career did Horthy have before 1920?
46700.e: Horthy was last commander-in-chief of the Austro-Hungarian navy. Mockers called him an admiral without a fleet in a country without a sea.
46700.m: Horthy was an admiral before he ruled Hungary.

46701.q: How much of its territory did Hungary lose in the Treaty of Trianon in 1920?
46701.e: Hungary lost about 70 per cent of its territory, and millions of Hungarians then lived in neighbouring states. Revising Trianon became the main aim of Horthy's policy.
46701.m: The Treaty of Trianon took about two thirds of its territory from Hungary.

46702.q: Which Hungarian law of 1920 is seen as one of the first antisemitic laws in interwar Europe?
46702.e: The law limited the proportion of Jewish students at universities. In practice it was aimed at the Jewish minority.
46702.m: The numerus clausus law of 1920 discriminated against Jewish students in Hungary.

46703.q: How did Horthy react when the former King Charles IV tried twice to return to Hungary in 1921?
a: He prevented his return to the throne
He had him crowned in Budapest
46703.e: Horthy had Charles's troops stopped, partly under pressure from the neighbouring states. Parliament then deposed the Habsburgs.
46703.m: In 1921 Horthy prevented the return of the Habsburgs.

46704.q: How did Hungary regain territory in Slovakia and northern Transylvania in 1938 and 1940?
46704.e: Germany and Italy decided on the borders in Vienna in Hungary's favour. As a result Hungary bound itself closely to the Axis powers.
46704.m: With the Vienna Awards Hungary gained territory and bound itself to Hitler.

46705.q: After the German occupation in 1944, how many Hungarian Jews were deported, mostly to Auschwitz, before the transports were stopped in July?
46705.e: From mid-May 1944, Hungarian gendarmes and the SS deported about 437,000 people within a few weeks. Horthy only stopped the transports at the beginning of July 1944.
46705.m: Almost half a million Hungarian Jews were deported within a few weeks in 1944.

46706.q: Who took power in Hungary in October 1944 after Horthy had announced an armistice and been forced to resign?
a: Ferenc Szálasi of the Arrow Cross
Gyula Gömbös of the government party
Mátyás Rákosi of the Workers' Party
46706.e: The Germans kidnapped Horthy's son and removed the regent. The Fascist Arrow Cross under Szálasi then murdered thousands of Jews in Budapest.
46706.m: After Horthy's fall the Arrow Cross terrorised Hungary.

46707.q: What happened to Miklós Horthy after the Second World War?
a: He lived in exile in Portugal until his death
He was sentenced to death in Nuremberg
He went on ruling Hungary until 1956
46707.e: Horthy only appeared as a witness at Nuremberg and was never charged. He died in Estoril in Portugal in 1957; in 1993 he was reburied in his birthplace, Kenderes.
46707.m: Horthy died in exile in Portugal.

46708.q: What is the wave of violence against communists and Jews in 1919 and 1920 that accompanied Horthy's rise called?
46708.e: After the end of Béla Kun's Soviet Republic, officers' detachments from Horthy's National Army murdered thousands of supposed opponents. The term distinguishes it from the preceding Red Terror.
46708.m: Horthy's seizure of power was accompanied by the White Terror.

46709.q: What kind of regime did Ioannis Metaxas set up in Greece in 1936?
a: A dictatorship on the Fascist model
A monarchy with a strong parliament
46709.e: On 4 August 1936 Metaxas dissolved parliament, banned the parties and suspended parts of the constitution. His regime adopted symbols of Fascist states.
46709.m: In 1936 Metaxas set up a dictatorship on the Fascist model.

46710.q: What form of state did Greece have during the Metaxas dictatorship?
46710.e: King George II had returned in 1935 and signed the decrees with which Metaxas suspended the constitution. Monarchy and dictatorship supported each other.
46710.m: Metaxas ruled with the approval of the Greek king.

46711.q: What pretext did Metaxas use in August 1936 for suspending the constitution?
a: An assassination attempt on the king
46711.e: Metaxas claimed that a general strike announced by communists threatened the state. He declared a state of emergency and banned the parties.
46711.m: Metaxas used fear of communism for his seizure of power.

46712.q: Which ideological goal did the Metaxas regime proclaim?
46712.e: After ancient Greece and Byzantium, a third great era was to follow. For this the regime adopted symbols and forms of Fascist states.
46712.m: Metaxas dreamt of a Third Hellenic Civilisation.

46713.q: On which model did Metaxas build a state youth organisation?
46713.e: The National Youth Organisation EON was meant to bring up young people in the spirit of the regime. It was modelled on Fascist youth movements, and other youth associations were absorbed into it.
46713.m: Under Metaxas there was a state youth organisation on the Fascist model.

46714.q: Which Greek national holiday commemorates Metaxas's rejection of the Italian ultimatum in 1940?
46714.e: Mussolini demanded that Italian troops be allowed to occupy strategic points in Greece; Metaxas refused, and ‘ochi’ means ‘no’. The Greek army then pushed the Italians back into Albania.
46714.m: With his ‘Ochi’ Metaxas said no to Mussolini.

46715.q: Against which neighbouring country was the fortified Metaxas Line built?
46715.e: The line of bunkers protected the northern border in Macedonia and Thrace. In April 1941 the Wehrmacht partly bypassed it through Yugoslavia.
46715.m: The Metaxas Line secured the border with Bulgaria.

46716.q: What did arrested communists have to sign under Metaxas in order to be released?
a: A plea for mercy to the Pope
46716.e: Security minister Konstantinos Maniadakis forced prisoners to make public declarations renouncing communism. Many others were banished to islands.
46716.m: Under Metaxas opponents had to renounce their beliefs publicly.

46717.q: What happened a few months after Metaxas's death in January 1941?
46717.e: Metaxas died in Athens while the war against Italy was still going on. In April 1941 the Wehrmacht attacked Greece and occupied the country.
46717.m: A few months after Metaxas's death the Wehrmacht occupied Greece.

46718.q: In which year did Józef Piłsudski take power in Poland with the May Coup?
46718.e: In May 1926 troops loyal to him marched on Warsaw, and after fighting the government resigned. Piłsudski then dominated Poland until his death.
46718.m: Piłsudski seized power in 1926 with the May Coup.

46719.q: What was the authoritarian regime under Piłsudski called?
46719.e: Sanacja means ‘healing’: political life was to be ‘healed’ of corruption and party squabbling. The Endecja was the National Democratic opposition.
46719.m: Piłsudski's regime called itself Sanacja, meaning healing.

46720.q: Against whom did Poland under Piłsudski win the ‘Miracle on the Vistula’ in 1920?
46720.e: In the Battle of Warsaw in August 1920, Poland stopped the Soviet advance in the Polish-Soviet War.
46720.m: In 1920 Poland stopped the Red Army on the Vistula.

46721.q: Which office did Piłsudski hold from 1918 to 1922?
46721.e: After independence in November 1918, Piłsudski became provisional head of state. Later he turned down the weak office of president.
46721.m: Piłsudski was the first head of state of independent Poland.

46722.q: How did Piłsudski's regime deal with the opposition before the parliamentary elections in 1930?
a: It had leading opposition figures arrested and convicted
It took them into a unity government
It let them stand freely and win
46722.e: The regime had deputies of the centre-left opposition arrested and held in the fortress of Brest. In the Brest trial they were sentenced to prison.
46722.m: Piłsudski eliminated the opposition with arrests and trials.

46723.q: What does the Bereza Kartuska camp, set up in 1934, show about Poland under the Sanacja regime?
a: Opponents were held without a court ruling
Poland took in many refugees from Germany
Prisoners of war were exchanged there
Offenders were trained in farm work
46723.e: In the Bereza Kartuska camp, communists, Ukrainian nationalists and far-right radicals were held without a court ruling.
46723.m: In the Bereza Kartuska camp the Polish regime locked up opponents without trial.

46724.q: What did the Polish April Constitution of 1935 bring about?
a: It greatly strengthened the president at the expense of parliament
It made Poland a federal state
It abolished women's right to vote
46724.e: The president received far-reaching rights, including dissolving parliament. The constitution consolidated the authoritarian system of the Sanacja.
46724.m: The April Constitution of 1935 made the president the centre of power.

46725.q: With which state did Poland sign a non-aggression pact in January 1934?
46725.e: Piłsudski wanted to secure Poland between Germany and the Soviet Union; a similar treaty with the Soviet Union had existed since 1932. Hitler terminated the pact in 1939.
46725.m: In 1934 Poland signed a non-aggression pact with Hitler's Germany.

46726.q: Where is Józef Piłsudski's heart buried?
46726.e: His body lies in Wawel Cathedral in Kraków. At his own wish, his heart was buried in his mother's grave in Vilnius, near his birthplace.
46726.m: Piłsudski's heart rests in Vilnius with his mother.

46727.q: Why was Piłsudski arrested by the Germans in 1917?
a: He refused to let his legionnaires swear an oath to the Central Powers
He had planned an attack on the Kaiser
He had smuggled gold out of Warsaw
46727.e: Piłsudski refused to have his legionnaires sworn in to the Central Powers and was held in the fortress of Magdeburg. In November 1918 he was released and returned to Warsaw.
46727.m: His imprisonment in Magdeburg made Piłsudski a national hero.

46728.q: Which event of March 1933 did Engelbert Dollfuss use in order to govern without parliament?
a: The resignation of all three presidents of the National Council
The burning of the parliament building
A general strike by the Social Democrats
An attempted coup by the Heimwehr
46728.e: After a crisis over procedural rules, all three presidents resigned. Dollfuss spoke of parliament having ‘eliminated itself’ and prevented it from meeting again.
46728.m: In 1933 Dollfuss used a parliamentary crisis to govern in an authoritarian way.

46729.q: How did Engelbert Dollfuss govern from 1933, after he had sidelined parliament?
a: With a coalition of all parties
With resolutions of the state parliaments
46729.e: Dollfuss relied on an old wartime law from 1917 and used it to issue emergency decrees. In this way he governed by bypassing parliament.
46729.m: From 1933 Dollfuss governed with emergency decrees, without parliament.

46730.q: What was the single organisation that Dollfuss founded in 1933 in place of the parties called?
46730.e: The Fatherland Front was meant to gather all Austrians ‘loyal to the government’. Other parties were banned one after another.
46730.m: The Fatherland Front was the single party of the corporate state.

46731.q: Against whom did government troops and the Heimwehr fight in Vienna and Linz in February 1934?
a: Against the Social Democrats' Republican Defence League
46731.e: The uprising began in Linz and was crushed with artillery, including against council housing blocks in Vienna. After that social democracy was banned.
46731.m: In the February fighting of 1934 Austrian social democracy was smashed.

46732.q: How did Austria describe itself under the May Constitution of 1934?
46732.e: The constitution began with ‘In the name of God, the Almighty’ and replaced parties with occupational corporate bodies. No more elections were held.
46732.m: In 1934 the May Constitution made Austria a Christian corporate state.

a: He was shot during the Nazis' July Putsch in 1934
He was killed in the February fighting of 1934
He was executed after the Anschluss in 1938
He died in an assassination in Rome
46733.e: On 25 July 1934 Austrian Nazis broke into the Federal Chancellery and shot Dollfuss. The putsch itself failed.
46733.m: Dollfuss was murdered by Nazis in 1934.

46734.q: Who succeeded Dollfuss as federal chancellor in 1934?
46734.e: Schuschnigg continued the corporate state until the Anschluss with Germany in March 1938. Miklas was federal president, Starhemberg leader of the Heimwehr.
46734.m: Kurt Schuschnigg was the second and last chancellor of the corporate state.

46735.q: Which form of cross did the Austrian single organisation of the corporate state use as its badge?
46735.e: The crutch cross was meant to look Christian and Austrian and to stand clearly apart from the symbols of the Nazis.
46735.m: The crutch cross was the symbol of Austrofascism.

46736.q: Which foreign state did Dollfuss mainly rely on against Hitler's Germany?
46736.e: Mussolini guaranteed Austria's independence and pushed Dollfuss to take a hard line against the left. Once Italy moved closer to Germany from 1936, this protection was gone.
46736.m: The corporate state depended on Mussolini's protection.

46737.q: What was the most important detention camp of the corporate state for political opponents called?
46737.e: In the Wöllersdorf camp in Lower Austria, Social Democrats, communists and Nazis were held without a court ruling.
46737.m: In the Wöllersdorf camp the corporate state locked up its opponents without trial.

46738.q: Which armed organisation openly renounced democracy in 1930 and later became a pillar of the corporate state?
46738.e: In the Korneuburg Oath, the Heimwehr rejected parliamentarism and the party state. The Defence League, by contrast, belonged to the Social Democrats, the SA to the Nazis.
46738.m: The Heimwehr turned against democracy and supported the corporate state.

46739.q: On which day was the presidential election held after which the largest protests since independence began in Belarus?
46739.e: On election night itself, thousands took to the streets in Minsk and other cities. The police responded with violence and mass arrests.
46739.m: The election of 9 August 2020 sparked the mass protests in Belarus.

46740.q: What share of the vote did the electoral commission officially give the incumbent in 2020?
46740.e: According to the official result, Lukashenko received about 80 per cent and his challenger about 10 per cent. The EU and independent observers did not recognise the result.
46740.m: The official 2020 election result was widely regarded as rigged.

46741.q: What did the Belarusian opposition politician Maria Kalesnikava do in September 2020 when the authorities tried to deport her to Ukraine?
a: She tore up her passport and stayed in the country
She asked for asylum in Ukraine
She switched to the government side
46741.e: Kalesnikava had previously been abducted in Minsk. In 2021 she was sentenced to eleven years in prison, and in December 2025 she was released and deported.
46741.m: Maria Kalesnikava chose prison rather than exile.

46742.q: To what sentence was the Swiss-Belarusian dual national Natallia Hersche sentenced in December 2020?
a: Two and a half years in prison
Ten years in a prison camp
46742.e: Hersche had been arrested at a women's march in Minsk in September 2020. She was released early in February 2022.
46742.m: A Swiss woman was also imprisoned because of the protests in Belarus.

46743.q: According to estimates, how many people demonstrated in Minsk on 16 August 2020?
46743.e: At the ‘March for Freedom’ well over 100,000 people filled the centre of Minsk. It was the largest demonstration in the country's history.
46743.m: In August 2020 more people took to the streets in Minsk than ever before.

46744.q: How did women often appear at the protests in Belarus in 2020?
a: Dressed in white with flowers, in solidarity chains
46744.e: The peaceful women's marches were meant to show that the protest was non-violent. Even so, many women were arrested too.
46744.m: Women in white with flowers became the face of the protests in Belarus.

46745.q: Which body did the Belarusian opposition set up in August 2020 to negotiate a peaceful transfer of power?
46745.e: Its presidium also included the Nobel Prize winner for Literature Svetlana Alexievich. The authorities persecuted almost all its members, and many were arrested or forced into exile.
46745.m: The Coordination Council was meant to prepare a peaceful change of power in Belarus.

46746.q: Through which messaging service did channels such as NEXTA coordinate the protests despite internet blocks?
46746.e: The Telegram channel NEXTA was run from Poland and had millions of subscribers. It spread videos and calls to action when the state slowed down the internet.
46746.m: In 2020 Telegram channels became the main medium of the protests in Belarus.

46747.q: What did workers at a state vehicle plant in Minsk shout at Lukashenko during his visit on 17 August 2020?
46747.e: The fact that even workers at state enterprises, seen as pillars of the regime, turned against him showed how broad the protests were. There were strikes at several plants.
46747.m: In 2020 even workers at state enterprises turned against Lukashenko.

46748.q: What job did Lukashenko do before his political career?
46748.e: In Soviet times Lukashenko ran a sovkhoz in the Shklou district. To this day he cultivates the image of a down-to-earth farmer.
46748.m: Lukashenko entered politics as the head of a state farm.

46749.q: What was introduced in 1995 by a referendum called by Lukashenko?
a: Russian as an equal official language
The abolition of the death penalty
A ban on the Communist Party
Membership of the Council of Europe
46749.e: The referendum strengthened ties with Russia and also replaced the state symbols with versions in the Soviet style.
46749.m: Since 1995 Russian has been an equal official language in Belarus.

46750.q: What did the 2004 referendum in Belarus remove?
a: The limit on the president's terms of office
The ban on the death penalty
46750.e: Since then Lukashenko has been able to stand as often as he likes. The OSCE criticised the vote as neither free nor fair.
46750.m: Since 2004 there has been no term limit for the president in Belarus.

46751.q: With which state has Belarus formed a ‘Union State’ since the treaty of 1999?
46751.e: The Union State provides for close economic, political and military cooperation. Economically, Belarus depends heavily on Russian gas and loans.
46751.m: Belarus and Russia form a Union State.

46752.q: Among other things, what did the Belarusian constitutional referendum of February 2022 make possible?
a: Stationing nuclear weapons, as neutrality was removed from the constitution
46752.e: The constitution lost its provision on neutrality and being free of nuclear weapons. Russia then stationed tactical nuclear weapons in Belarus.
