46752.m: Since 2022 Belarus's constitution allows nuclear weapons on its territory.

46753.q: For which term of office did Lukashenko have himself elected in January 2025?
46753.e: According to the electoral commission he received about 87 per cent of the vote, with no real opponents. The EU did not recognise the election.
46753.m: In 2025 Lukashenko began his seventh term.

46754.q: What role did Lukashenko play in the Wagner Group's mutiny in Russia in June 2023?
a: He mediated between Putin and Prigozhin
He closed the border with Russia
46754.e: After talks with Lukashenko, Yevgeny Prigozhin called off the march on Moscow. Wagner fighters were offered the chance to stay in Belarus.
46754.m: In 2023 Lukashenko acted as a mediator in the Wagner mutiny.

46755.q: Which nickname is often used for Alexander Lukashenko in Western media?
46755.e: The nickname refers to the fact that he has ruled for decades without free elections and suppresses the opposition and the media.
46755.m: Lukashenko is regarded as Europe's last dictator.

46756.q: What role did Belarus play in Russia's attack on Ukraine in February 2022?
a: It let Russian troops attack from its territory
It sent its own troops to Kyiv
It closed its border to Russian troops
46756.e: Russian troops were in Belarus for an exercise and advanced from there towards Kyiv. Belarus is therefore regarded as complicit in the attack.
46756.m: In 2022 Lukashenko made his country available as a staging area against Ukraine.

46757.q: In which city did the founding meeting of Operation Condor take place at the end of November 1975?
46757.e: The intelligence chiefs of several South American military regimes met in Santiago de Chile at the end of November 1975. The host was the Chilean military government under Pinochet.
46757.m: Operation Condor was founded in Santiago de Chile in 1975.

46758.q: What was the intelligence service of the Pinochet dictatorship, which played a leading role in organising Operation Condor, called?
46758.e: The DINA under Manuel Contreras persecuted opponents of the regime in Chile and abroad. Contreras was later given numerous long prison sentences.
46758.m: The DINA was Pinochet's feared intelligence service.

46759.q: What was discovered in a police station in Paraguay in 1992?
a: Secret files on the persecution of regime opponents
A hidden gold store of the dictatorship
The grave of the dictator Stroessner
46759.e: The human rights activist Martín Almada came across the ‘Archives of Terror’. They prove the cooperation of the dictatorships in Operation Condor and are now part of UNESCO's Memory of the World.
46759.m: The ‘Archives of Terror’ prove the existence of Operation Condor.

46760.q: What characterised the so-called ‘Phase III’ of Operation Condor?
a: Attacks on regime opponents even outside Latin America
Joint training of soldiers in Panama
46760.e: In Phase III the intelligence services involved planned assassinations of opposition figures in Europe and the USA. One example is the 1976 assassination in Washington.
46760.m: Operation Condor hunted opposition figures worldwide.

46761.q: What does the murder of the Chilean general Carlos Prats in Buenos Aires in 1974 show?
a: Pinochet's intelligence service pursued opponents even in exile
Prats was a supporter of Pinochet
46761.e: Carlos Prats was Allende's army chief, loyal to the constitution, and lived in Argentina after the coup. He and his wife were killed by a DINA car bomb.
46761.m: The constitution-loyal general Carlos Prats was murdered in exile by the DINA.

46762.q: What happened in 1976 to the former Bolivian president Juan José Torres in exile in Argentina?
a: He became a minister in Argentina
He returned to Bolivia as president
He was granted asylum in Switzerland
46762.e: The left-leaning general was president of Bolivia from 1970 to 1971. In June 1976 he was abducted and murdered in Buenos Aires, which is attributed to Operation Condor.
46762.m: Not even former heads of state were safe from Operation Condor in exile.

46763.q: In which country did a court find in a major trial in 2016 that Operation Condor was a criminal organisation?
46763.e: In May 2016 a court in Buenos Aires convicted, among others, the former junta leader Reynaldo Bignone. For the first time Operation Condor was classified by a court as a cross-border criminal conspiracy.
46763.m: In 2016 an Argentine court convicted those responsible for Operation Condor.

46764.q: What consequence did Operation Condor have for political refugees within South America?
a: They were no longer safe even in a neighbouring country
They automatically received asylum in Europe
They were allowed to return freely to their home countries
They were placed under UN protection
46764.e: Because the intelligence services exchanged information and handed prisoners over across borders, fleeing to a neighbouring country no longer offered protection. Many exiles were abducted in Argentina and handed over to their home countries.
46764.m: For the persecuted, Operation Condor removed the protection that borders had offered.

46765.q: Which four institutions formed the Chilean military junta after the 1973 coup?
a: Army, navy, air force and Carabineros
Army, navy, police and intelligence service
Army, air force, Church and judiciary
Navy, air force, Senate and army
46765.e: The junta consisted of the heads of the army (Pinochet), the navy (Merino), the air force (Leigh) and the militarised police, the Carabineros (Mendoza). Pinochet quickly established himself as the leading figure.
46765.m: The Chilean junta united the heads of the three armed services and the Carabineros.

46766.q: Who appointed Augusto Pinochet commander-in-chief of the army in August 1973?
46766.e: After Carlos Prats resigned, Allende appointed Pinochet army chief on 23 August 1973 because he thought he was loyal to the constitution. Less than three weeks later Pinochet led the coup.
46766.m: Allende himself made Pinochet army chief shortly before the coup.

46767.q: What happened in Santiago de Chile in June 1973, just under three months before the coup?
a: A tank regiment tried unsuccessfully to stage a coup
46767.e: In the so-called ‘Tanquetazo’, a tank regiment attacked the seat of government but was stopped by troops loyal to the constitution. The incident is seen as a forerunner of the September coup.
46767.m: The failed coup attempt of June 1973 was a dress rehearsal for the coup.

46768.q: How did Salvador Allende address the people for the last time on 11 September 1973?
a: In a radio address from the besieged presidential palace
In a television debate with Pinochet
46768.e: Allende spoke on Radio Magallanes, one of the last pro-government stations still broadcasting. The speech is seen as an important historical document.
46768.m: Allende's farewell speech was broadcast on the radio.

46769.q: What was the so-called ‘Caravan of Death’ in October 1973?
a: A military commando that murdered prisoners in several cities
A column of refugees from Chile to Argentina
A protest convoy by lorry drivers
A prisoner transport to Easter Island
46769.e: A commando under General Sergio Arellano Stark flew by helicopter through southern and northern Chile and had political prisoners killed there without trial. Around a hundred people died.
46769.m: The Caravan of Death shows the targeted violence shortly after the coup.

46770.q: Which occupational group largely paralysed Chile's supplies with long strikes in 1972 and 1973?
46770.e: The lorry owners' strikes against the Allende government greatly worsened the supply crisis. They were partly financed by the US intelligence service, the CIA.
46770.m: The lorry strikes contributed to the crisis before the coup.

46771.q: What were the US-trained economists who implemented a radically free-market economic policy after the coup called?
46771.e: Many of these economists had studied under Milton Friedman at the University of Chicago. Under Pinochet they pushed through privatisation and deregulation.
46771.m: The Chicago Boys shaped the economic policy of the Pinochet dictatorship.

46772.q: Which Spanish investigating judge obtained Augusto Pinochet's arrest in London in 1998?
46772.e: Baltasar Garzón issued an international arrest warrant for crimes against Spanish nationals. Pinochet was held in Great Britain for about 17 months but was then sent back to Chile on health grounds.
46772.m: The Pinochet case made the principle of universal jurisdiction well known.

46773.q: In which year did Alfredo Stroessner take power in Paraguay after a coup?
46773.e: Stroessner staged a coup in May 1954 and became president in August 1954. He ruled until his overthrow in February 1989.

46774.q: Who overthrew Alfredo Stroessner in February 1989?
a: A general from his own power apparatus
46774.e: General Andrés Rodríguez, a close companion of Stroessner who was related to his family by marriage, led the coup. He then became president himself.
46774.m: A confidant from his own camp overthrew Stroessner.

46775.q: Which legal tool did Stroessner keep in force for almost his entire rule?
46775.e: The state of siege was renewed every 90 days and suspended fundamental rights. This allowed opponents to be held without trial.
46775.m: Stroessner ruled permanently under a state of siege.

46776.q: What is the period of Alfredo Stroessner's rule in Paraguay called?
46776.e: The term ‘Stronato’ comes from the dictator's name. In a similar way, the rule of Porfirio Díaz in Mexico is called the ‘Porfiriato’.
46776.m: Stroessner's dictatorship is called the Stronato in Paraguay.

46777.q: Which indigenous people of Paraguay was so persecuted under Stroessner that international organisations spoke of genocide?
46777.e: In the 1970s the Aché were hunted, abducted and forced into reservations, and many died. Human rights organisations and researchers therefore accused the regime of genocide.
46777.m: The Aché were among the main victims of the Stronato.

46778.q: Which office did Alfredo Stroessner hold before he took power?
46778.e: From 1951 Stroessner was commander-in-chief of the Paraguayan armed forces. He used this position for the coup in 1954.
46778.m: Stroessner used his position as army chief to take power.

46779.q: How did Alfredo Stroessner have himself confirmed in office during his rule?
46779.e: Stroessner had himself elected eight times, with electoral fraud and intimidation preventing real competition. The elections were meant to give the regime a democratic appearance.
46779.m: Sham elections gave Stroessner's dictatorship a veneer of legality.

46780.q: In which city did Alfredo Stroessner die in 2006?
46780.e: After his overthrow, Stroessner lived in exile in Brazil until his death. He died in Brasília in 2006 without ever having been brought to trial.
46780.m: Stroessner was never convicted for his crimes.

46781.q: By which short nickname was Rafael Trujillo often known in the Dominican Republic?
46781.e: Trujillo had himself called ‘El Jefe’ (the boss) and officially also ‘Benefactor of the Fatherland’. The personality cult around him was everywhere.
46781.m: Trujillo cultivated a pronounced personality cult as ‘El Jefe’.

46782.q: Which occupying power trained Rafael Trujillo as a young officer?
46782.e: The USA occupied the Dominican Republic from 1916 to 1924 and built up a National Guard. Trujillo was trained there by US Marines and rose quickly.
46782.m: Trujillo's rise began in the National Guard built up by the USA.

46783.q: What does the attack that Trujillo had carried out on the Venezuelan president Rómulo Betancourt in 1960 show?
a: Venezuela was an ally of Trujillo
46783.e: Trujillo's agents tried to kill Betancourt with a car bomb; he survived with injuries. Betancourt was a fierce critic of the dictators in the Caribbean.
46783.m: Trujillo's attack on Betancourt isolated him internationally.

46784.q: How did the Organization of American States (OAS) react to Trujillo's assassination attempt in Venezuela in 1960?
46784.e: The OAS members broke off diplomatic relations and imposed economic sanctions. This weakened the regime shortly before Trujillo's assassination.
46784.m: In 1960 the OAS punished Trujillo with sanctions.

46785.q: What happened in 1956 to the Basque exile politician Jesús de Galíndez, who had written a critical study of Trujillo?
a: He was abducted in New York and disappeared
He became a minister under Trujillo
He received the Nobel Peace Prize
46785.e: Galíndez was abducted in New York in 1956 and probably murdered in the Dominican Republic. The case showed how far Trujillo's reach extended.
46785.m: Trujillo's reach extended all the way to New York.

46786.q: What role did the official presidents of the Dominican Republic often have during the Trujillo dictatorship?
a: They were puppets without power of their own
They kept strict control over Trujillo
They were freely elected by the people
They were installed by the USA
46786.e: At times Trujillo installed relatives or confidants as president. At the time of the 1961 assassination, for example, Joaquín Balaguer was formally president, but power lay with Trujillo.
46786.m: Under Trujillo the presidents were only puppets.

46787.q: What did the Dominican Republic offer at the Évian refugee conference in 1938?
46787.e: The Dominican Republic was one of the few countries that offered to take people in. From 1940 several hundred Jewish refugees settled in Sosúa on the north coast.
46787.m: The Dominican Republic took in Jewish refugees from Europe.

46788.q: What happened to the Trujillo family at the end of 1961, a few months after the dictator was assassinated?
a: They had to leave the country
They were executed after a trial
They allowed free elections and stayed in power
46788.e: After the assassination, his son Ramfis Trujillo had several conspirators killed. Under pressure from the USA, the family left the country at the end of 1961.
46788.m: The Trujillo era ended when the family fled in 1961.

46789.q: Which force did Anastasio Somoza García lead before he took power in Nicaragua?
46789.e: The National Guard was built up under US occupation, and Somoza García became its head in 1933. Until 1979 it remained the family's most important instrument of power.
46789.m: The National Guard was the Somozas' power base.

46790.q: Who had Augusto César Sandino murdered in 1934?
46790.e: After peace talks, Sandino was shot by members of the National Guard on Somoza García's orders. Two years later Somoza García took power himself.
46790.m: The murder of Sandino paved Somoza García's way to power.

46791.q: To whom did power in Nicaragua pass after the death of Anastasio Somoza García in 1956?
a: To a military council of the neighbouring countries
46791.e: After the assassination of Somoza García, his son Luis Somoza Debayle became president. The younger son Anastasio led the National Guard and later became president himself.
46791.m: The Somozas passed power on within the family.

46792.q: How did the rule of Anastasio Somoza García, founder of the Somoza dynasty, end in 1956?
a: He was shot in an assassination
He was overthrown by the Sandinistas
He resigned after losing an election
He fled into exile in Miami
46792.e: The young poet Rigoberto López Pérez shot Somoza García in León. Somoza died a few days later, and his sons took power.
46792.m: The founder of the Somoza dynasty died in 1956 from the effects of an assassination.

46793.q: At which military academy was Anastasio Somoza Debayle trained?
46793.e: Anastasio Somoza Debayle graduated from the US Military Academy at West Point in 1946. He was seen as a close ally of the USA in the Cold War.
46793.m: The last Somoza was a West Point graduate.

46794.q: Why did the Somoza regime also lose support among the American public in 1979?
a: Television pictures showed a National Guardsman shooting a US reporter
Somoza had declared war on the USA
Nicaragua had joined the Warsaw Pact
Somoza had stopped oil deliveries to the USA
46794.e: In June 1979 a National Guardsman shot the ABC reporter Bill Stewart while his camera crew was filming. The pictures were shown on US television and weakened support for Somoza.
46794.m: The pictures of Bill Stewart's death helped to end support for Somoza.

46795.q: Where did Anastasio Somoza Debayle flee to first in July 1979?
46795.e: Somoza flew to Miami on 17 July 1979 but was not allowed to stay in the USA permanently. He then moved on to Paraguay.
46795.m: In 1979 Somoza found no permanent refuge in the USA.

46796.q: Roughly how long did the Somoza family dominate Nicaragua?
46796.e: Anastasio Somoza García came to power through a coup in 1936, and his son was overthrown in 1979. That makes about 43 years (1979 minus 1936 is 43).
46796.m: The Somozas ruled Nicaragua for over four decades.

46797.q: Through which revolt did Fulgencio Batista become one of the most powerful men in Cuba in 1933?
a: The attack on the Moncada Barracks
46797.e: Batista was then a sergeant and led a revolt of non-commissioned officers in September 1933. After that, as army chief, he effectively controlled Cuban politics.
46797.m: In 1933 Batista rose from sergeant to a power in Cuba.

46798.q: How did Fulgencio Batista first become president of Cuba in 1940?
46798.e: Batista won the 1940 election and governed until 1944 under a new, progressive constitution. Only in 1952 did he return as a dictator through a coup.
46798.m: Batista was first an elected president and later a dictator.

46799.q: How did Fulgencio Batista return to power in March 1952?
46799.e: On 10 March 1952 Batista staged a coup shortly before the planned elections, in which he had little chance. He partly suspended the constitution of 1940.
46799.m: With the 1952 coup Batista became a dictator.

46800.q: Which barracks did Fidel Castro and his followers attack on 26 July 1953?
46800.e: The attack on the Moncada Barracks in Santiago de Cuba failed, but it became the founding myth of the 26th of July Movement. Afterwards Castro gave his speech ‘History will absolve me’ in court.
46800.m: The attack on Moncada in 1953 began the struggle against Batista.

46801.q: To which country did Fulgencio Batista flee on New Year's Eve 1958?
46801.e: Batista first fled to the dictator Trujillo in the Dominican Republic. Later he lived in Portugal and Spain.
46801.m: Batista fled to the dictator Trujillo.

46802.q: Which US mobster greatly expanded the casino and hotel business in Havana under Batista?
46802.e: Meyer Lansky worked closely with Batista and controlled large parts of the gambling in Havana. The links between the regime and the Mafia encouraged corruption.
46802.m: Under Batista Havana was closely tied to the US Mafia.

46803.q: What measure did the USA take against the Batista government in March 1958?
46803.e: Because of the brutal repression, the USA stopped arms deliveries to Batista in 1958. This weakened his army in the fight against the rebels.
46803.m: The US arms embargo of 1958 decisively weakened Batista.

46804.q: In which country did Fulgencio Batista die in 1973?
46804.e: After spells in the Dominican Republic and Portugal, Batista finally lived in Spain. He died near Marbella in 1973.
46804.m: Batista died in exile in Spain in 1973.

46805.q: Against which candidate did Alberto Fujimori win Peru's presidential election in 1990?
46805.e: The little-known agricultural engineer Fujimori defeated the famous writer Mario Vargas Llosa in the run-off. He benefited from distrust of established politics.
46805.m: In 1990 Fujimori surprisingly beat Mario Vargas Llosa.

46806.q: What is Fujimori's step of 5 April 1992, when he dissolved Congress and suspended the constitution, called?
46806.e: In a self-coup (Spanish ‘autogolpe’), a sitting head of state sidelines parliament and the judiciary with the help of the military. Fujimori then governed by decree for a time.
46806.m: With the self-coup of 1992 Fujimori made himself an authoritarian ruler.

46807.q: Who was Fujimori's influential intelligence adviser?
46807.e: Vladimiro Montesinos effectively ran the SIN intelligence service and built up a network of bribery and blackmail. He was later given long prison sentences.
46807.m: Montesinos was the puppet master behind Fujimori's power.

46808.q: What triggered the collapse of the Fujimori government in 2000?
a: A video showing the bribery of a member of Congress
A military coup by the navy
46808.e: In September 2000 a video was published showing Montesinos handing money to an opposition member of Congress. The so-called ‘Vladivideos’ revealed a huge system of corruption.
46808.m: The Vladivideos brought down the Fujimori system.

46809.q: How did Alberto Fujimori resign as president in November 2000?
a: In a television address from Lima
In a letter to the UN
46809.e: Fujimori travelled to a summit and fled to Japan, from where he sent his resignation by fax. Congress did not accept it and removed him for ‘moral incapacity’.

46810.q: For what was Alberto Fujimori sentenced to 25 years in prison in Peru in 2009?
a: For massacres by a secret military unit
For treason in favour of Japan
46810.e: A secret military unit, the Grupo Colina, carried out massacres of civilians under Fujimori. For this, in 2009, Fujimori became the first elected former president to be convicted of human rights crimes in his own country.
46810.m: Fujimori was convicted of human rights crimes in 2009.

46811.q: Why did Alberto Fujimori's pardon in December 2017 trigger large protests?
a: He had been convicted of human rights crimes
He had only been in prison for a few weeks
He had refused the pardon himself
46811.e: Fujimori had been in prison since 2007 and had been convicted of massacres, among other things. President Kuczynski pardoned him on humanitarian grounds, which outraged many victims' families. The pardon was later overturned.
46811.m: Fujimori's 2017 pardon remained legally and politically controversial.

46812.q: Which daughter of Alberto Fujimori won the run-off for the presidency of Peru in June 2026 at her fourth attempt?
46812.e: Keiko Fujimori had lost the run-offs of 2011, 2016 and 2021. In 2026 she narrowly beat Roberto Sánchez. Her brother Kenji was a member of Congress.
46812.m: Keiko Fujimori carries on her father's political movement.

46813.q: Which leader of the ‘Shining Path’ was captured under Fujimori in 1992?
46813.e: Abimael Guzmán was arrested in Lima by a police unit in September 1992. His arrest decisively weakened the terrorist organisation and boosted Fujimori's reputation.
46813.m: Guzmán's arrest in 1992 was a turning point in the fight against the Shining Path.

46814.q: How did the military dictatorship in Brazil shape the party system from 1965?
a: It allowed only one government party and a tame opposition
It made the military itself the only party
46814.e: The regime banned the existing parties and allowed only the pro-government ARENA and the moderate opposition MDB. This created a controlled two-party system.
46814.m: The military in Brazil only allowed a sham opposition.

46815.q: What is the period of strong economic growth in Brazil from about 1968 to 1973 called?
46815.e: In these years the economy sometimes grew by over ten per cent a year, financed partly by foreign debt. At the same time social inequality and repression increased.
46815.m: Brazil's economic miracle came during the harshest phase of the dictatorship.

46816.q: What did the Brazilian law of 1979, which is still controversial today, provide for?
a: The abolition of the death penalty
46816.e: The Amnesty Law allowed exiles to return but also protected torturers from prosecution. The Supreme Court upheld it in 2010.
46816.m: Brazil's Amnesty Law still prevents trials of torturers today.

46817.q: How did the military dictatorship in Brazil end in 1985?
a: Through a gradual handover to a civilian president
46817.e: In January 1985 an electoral college chose a civilian, Tancredo Neves, for the first time in years. Neves died before taking office, and Vice-President José Sarney took over.
46817.m: In 1985 the military in Brazil gradually handed power to civilians.

46818.q: From when to when was there a military dictatorship in Brazil?
46818.e: After a coup in March 1964, generals ruled the country. In 1985 a civilian president took over again; the last military president was João Figueiredo.
46818.m: Brazil was a military dictatorship from 1964 to 1985.

46819.q: Why did the death of the journalist Vladimir Herzog in Brazil in 1975 become a turning point?
a: His death under torture triggered broad protests against the dictatorship
He was the last military president
He had negotiated the Amnesty Law
46819.e: The military claimed that Vladimir Herzog had taken his own life, but he had died under torture. An ecumenical service for him turned into a large protest rally.
46819.m: Vladimir Herzog's death became a symbol against torture.

46820.q: How did some opponents of the Brazilian military dictatorship fight back around 1970?
a: With armed guerrilla groups in the cities and the Amazon region
With a government in exile in Moscow
With a general strike that immediately toppled the regime
46820.e: Left-wing groups robbed banks and kidnapped diplomats, and a Communist Party guerrilla force fought on the Araguaia River. The military crushed them completely; many are still considered disappeared today.
46820.m: The military crushed the armed opposition in Brazil.

46821.q: What was the slow political opening of Brazil towards the end of the military dictatorship called?
46821.e: From 1974 President Ernesto Geisel announced a ‘slow, gradual and safe’ easing. Under his successor it continued as the ‘Abertura’, Portuguese for opening.
46821.m: With the Abertura Brazil gradually opened up.

46822.q: What legally completed Brazil's transition from military dictatorship to democracy in 1988?
46822.e: The military dictatorship lasted from 1964 to 1985. The 1988 constitution strengthened fundamental and social rights and is often called the ‘Citizens' Constitution’.
46822.m: With the 1988 constitution Brazil became a democracy again.

46823.q: Which position did Manuel Noriega use from 1983 as Panama's de facto ruler?
46823.e: Noriega headed the Panama Defence Forces and from there controlled the civilian presidents. He was never formally elected president.
46823.m: Noriega ruled Panama from within the army.

46824.q: For which foreign intelligence service did Manuel Noriega work as an informant for years?
46824.e: For years Noriega received payments from the CIA and was seen as a useful US ally in the Cold War. At the same time he was involved in drug trafficking.
46824.m: Noriega was a US ally for a long time before he became its enemy.

46825.q: What was the US military invasion of Panama in December 1989 called?
46825.e: On 20 December 1989 US troops invaded Panama to overthrow and arrest Noriega. Many civilians also died.
46825.m: With Operation Just Cause the USA overthrew Noriega.

46826.q: Where did Manuel Noriega take refuge during the US invasion?
a: In the Vatican embassy in Panama City
In a barracks in the jungle
On a ship in the Panama Canal
46826.e: Noriega fled to the Apostolic Nunciature. US troops blasted the building with loud rock music for days until he surrendered on 3 January 1990.
46826.m: After days in the nunciature Noriega surrendered to US troops.

46827.q: For which offences was Manuel Noriega convicted in the USA in 1992?
a: Electoral fraud and abuse of office
46827.e: A court in Miami sentenced Noriega to 40 years in prison, later reduced. He was then extradited to France and, in 2011, to Panama.
46827.m: Noriega was convicted in the USA as a drug trafficker.

46828.q: Why did the USA turn against its former ally Noriega in the 1980s?
a: Because of drug trafficking and repression of the opposition
Because he wanted to join Panama to the Soviet Union
Because he closed the Panama Canal to US ships
Because he declared war on Cuba
46828.e: Noriega worked with Colombian drug cartels and dealt brutally with critics. For example, he was blamed for the murder of the regime critic Hugo Spadafora in 1985.
46828.m: Drug trafficking and violence against critics made Noriega unacceptable to the USA.

46829.q: What happened to the presidential election in Panama in May 1989?
a: Noriega had it annulled because the opposition won
Noriega won it by a large majority
It was run by the UN
It was cancelled because of an earthquake
46829.e: The opposition candidate Guillermo Endara had clearly won, but Noriega declared the election invalid. Endara was sworn in as president on the night of the US invasion in December 1989.
46829.m: In 1989 Noriega ignored the opposition's election victory.

46830.q: Which ruler of Panama was Noriega's patron before he died in a plane crash in 1981?
46830.e: General Omar Torrijos dominated Panama from 1968 and negotiated the Panama Canal treaties of 1977. Under him Noriega was head of intelligence.
46830.m: Noriega rose in the shadow of Omar Torrijos.

46831.q: What were the white headscarves of the Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo originally made from?
46831.e: Originally the women tied cloth nappies around their heads so that they could recognise each other on a pilgrimage. This became the world-famous white headscarf.
46831.m: The headscarves recall the childhood of the disappeared.

46832.q: What did the Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo demand at their weekly marches in Buenos Aires?
a: The return of the Falkland Islands
The return of former President Perón
46832.e: During the military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983, tens of thousands of people disappeared without trace. Every Thursday the mothers walked around the square in front of the seat of government and demanded answers.
46832.m: The Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo searched for their disappeared children.

46833.q: How did the Argentine military manage to abduct several Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo in 1977?
a: An officer infiltrated the group posing as a relative
The mothers were arrested at an election
They were arrested at the border
46833.e: Navy officer Alfredo Astiz posed as the brother of a disappeared person and betrayed the group's meetings. In December 1977 several members were then abducted. He was later sentenced to life imprisonment.
46833.m: An informer betrayed the mothers to the military.

46834.q: Who was abducted and murdered together with Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo in December 1977?
46834.e: The nuns Alice Domon and Léonie Duquet supported the mothers and were abducted and murdered with them. The case strained relations between France and Argentina.
46834.m: Foreign supporters of the mothers were also murdered.

46835.q: What did Estela de Carlotto, president of the Grandmothers of the Plaza de Mayo, achieve in 2014?
a: She received the Nobel Peace Prize
She had the junta generals jailed
46835.e: Estela de Carlotto's daughter was killed in custody and her baby was stolen. After 36 years of searching, her grandson was identified in 2014 thanks to a DNA test.
46835.m: Estela de Carlotto found her grandson after decades of searching.

46836.q: Which scientific method do the Grandmothers of the Plaza de Mayo use to identify stolen grandchildren?
a: Genetic matching in a DNA database
46836.e: In 1987 Argentina set up a national genetic database in which relatives' samples are stored. Suspected cases can then be matched beyond doubt.
46836.m: Genetic matching gives stolen children back their identity.

46837.q: Which human rights prize of the European Parliament did the Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo receive in 1992?
46837.e: In 1992 the European Parliament awarded the mothers the Sakharov Prize for Freedom of Thought. The prize honours commitment to human rights and freedom of expression.
46837.m: The Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo received the Sakharov Prize in 1992.

46838.q: At which major event in 1978 did foreign media become aware of the Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo?
a: At the football World Cup in Argentina
At the Olympic Games in Moscow
At the Pope's visit to Buenos Aires
At a UN conference in Geneva
46838.e: During the 1978 football World Cup, foreign television teams, for example from the Netherlands, reported on the women in the square. The junta had actually wanted to use the tournament for propaganda.
46838.m: The 1978 World Cup made the mothers' protest known worldwide.

46839.q: What is the main task of a truth commission such as the one in Peru (2001 to 2003)?
a: To investigate crimes and document the victims' suffering
46839.e: Truth commissions hear victims and witnesses and publish a report. In Peru the commission under Salomón Lerner Febres investigated the violence of the years 1980 to 2000.
46839.m: Truth commissions make past injustice public.

46840.q: According to the Peruvian truth commission, which group was responsible for most deaths?
46840.e: The commission attributed about 54 per cent of the reported deaths to the Shining Path. But it also documented serious crimes by state forces.
46840.m: In Peru the Shining Path killed the most people.

46841.q: What did the truth commission in Guatemala find in 1999 regarding the Maya?
a: The state committed acts of genocide
46841.e: The commission attributed about 93 per cent of the human rights violations to state forces. For certain regions it spoke of acts of genocide against Maya communities.
46841.m: In Guatemala state genocide against the Maya was established.

46842.q: Why was Bishop Juan Gerardi murdered in Guatemala in 1998?
a: He had presented a report on crimes in the civil war
He had supplied the guerrillas with weapons
He was involved in a land dispute
46842.e: In April 1998 Bishop Juan Gerardi presented the report ‘Guatemala: Never Again’. Two days later he was beaten to death; members of the military were later convicted.
46842.m: Bishop Juan Gerardi paid for the search for truth with his life.

46843.q: Which trial followed the truth commission's report in Argentina in 1985?
a: The trial of the military juntas
46843.e: In the ‘Juicio a las Juntas’, leading members of the military governments were convicted, including Videla and Massera, who were sentenced to life imprisonment. The commission's report served as an important basis of evidence.
46843.m: In 1985 Argentina put the junta leaders on trial.

46844.q: What did two Argentine laws of 1986 and 1987 do for many members of the military from the dictatorship?
a: They protected them from further trials
They sentenced them to life imprisonment
They stripped them of the right to vote
46844.e: The Full Stop Law set a deadline for charges, and the Due Obedience Law cleared lower ranks. After they were repealed in 2005, numerous trials took place again from 2006.
46844.m: In 2005 Argentina repealed the impunity laws.

46845.q: Which dictator ruled Paraguay from 1954 to 1989 and was later implicated by a truth commission?
46845.e: Alfredo Stroessner ruled Paraguay for 35 years. From 2004 to 2008 the Truth and Justice Commission documented torture, enforced disappearances and land theft under his rule.
46845.m: Paraguay examined the Stroessner dictatorship with a truth commission.

46846.q: What is special about impunity for members of the military from the dictatorship in Uruguay?
a: The people confirmed it in referendums
It only applied to foreign officers
46846.e: The so-called ‘Ley de Caducidad’ of 1986 waived the prosecution of soldiers and police officers. It was not repealed in referendums in 1989 and again in 2009.
46846.m: Uruguay confirmed impunity twice at the ballot box.

46847.q: What did the Colombian truth commission, which presented its final report in 2022, come out of?
a: The 2016 peace agreement with the FARC
A trade agreement with the USA
46847.e: The commission arose from the 2016 peace agreement between the government and the FARC. Under the Jesuit priest Francisco de Roux it investigated decades of armed conflict.
46847.m: Colombia's truth commission was part of the peace process with the FARC.

46848.q: How did Hugo Chávez first come to national attention in February 1992?
a: With an election victory in Caracas
With a speech at the UN
46848.e: On 4 February 1992 the paratrooper officer Chávez led a coup attempt against President Carlos Andrés Pérez. It failed, but a short television address made him popular.
46848.m: Chávez became known through a failed coup.

46849.q: Which new official name did Venezuela receive with the 1999 constitution?
46849.e: The constitution drawn up under Chávez named the country after the independence hero Simón Bolívar. Chávez called his political project the ‘Bolivarian Revolution’.
46849.m: With his revolution Chávez appealed to Simón Bolívar.

46850.q: How did the coup against Hugo Chávez in April 2002 end?
a: Chávez returned to office after about two days
Chávez fled to Cuba for good
Chávez resigned and never stood again
46850.e: The head of the business federation, Pedro Carmona, became interim president and immediately dissolved parliament and the courts. After mass protests and parts of the military changing sides, Chávez returned.
46850.m: The 2002 coup against Chávez failed after two days.

46851.q: What was the long television programme in which Hugo Chávez regularly spoke directly to the people called?
46851.e: In ‘Aló Presidente’ Chávez often spoke for hours, announced decisions and took phone calls. The programme was a central means of displaying his power.
46851.m: Chávez used television as a direct line to the people.

46852.q: What was decided in Venezuela in the referendum of February 2009?
a: Removing the limit on terms of office
46852.e: Voters allowed unlimited re-election of the president and other officials. This allowed Chávez to stand again in 2012.
46852.m: With the 2009 referendum the limit on terms of office was removed.

46853.q: Which election did the opposition in Venezuela win clearly in December 2015?
a: The election to the Supreme Court
46853.e: The opposition alliance won a two-thirds majority in the National Assembly. The Maduro government then gradually stripped parliament of its power with the help of the courts.
46853.m: In 2015 the opposition won parliament but lost its power.

46854.q: Which body did Maduro have elected in 2017 to get round the opposition-controlled National Assembly?
a: A People's Council of the Communes
46854.e: The 2017 Constituent Assembly was elected without the opposition taking part and effectively took over law-making. Many states did not recognise it.
46854.m: With the Constituent Assembly Maduro stripped parliament of its power.

46855.q: Which international court opened a formal investigation into crimes against humanity in Venezuela in 2021?
a: The Inter-American Court of Human Rights
The European Court of Human Rights
46855.e: The prosecutor of the International Criminal Court in The Hague announced the investigation in November 2021. It was the first such proceeding concerning a Latin American country.
46855.m: The International Criminal Court is investigating crimes in Venezuela.

46856.q: To which country did the opposition candidate Edmundo González go into exile after the disputed 2024 election?
46856.e: An arrest warrant was issued against Edmundo González in Venezuela. In September 2024 he left for Spain, where he was granted asylum.
46856.m: The opposition candidate Edmundo González had to go into exile in 2024.

46857.q: Which Congolese politician and first prime minister was murdered in January 1961 with the involvement of Mobutu's people?
46857.e: After his removal, Lumumba was arrested and handed over to the breakaway province of Katanga, where he was shot. Mobutu had previously arranged his arrest.
46857.m: Lumumba's murder in 1961 paved the way for Mobutu's later rise.

46858.q: What was Mobutu's campaign called, with which he had Western first names and clothing replaced by African ones from 1971?
46858.e: Under ‘Authenticité’, Christian first names had to give way to African ones, and the suit was replaced by the ‘abacost’. Mobutu himself also dropped the name Joseph-Désiré.
46858.m: Authenticité was meant to impose an African identity from above.

46859.q: What did Mobutu want to show when he banned suits and ties in Zaire?
a: A turning away from Western influence
46859.e: Instead of the suit, people wore the ‘abacost’, a collarless jacket. The name comes from ‘à bas le costume’, meaning ‘down with the suit’.
46859.m: Mobutu banned suits and ties as a sign against the West.

46860.q: Which political system prevailed under Mobutu in Zaire?
a: A council republic with workers' councils
46860.e: In 1967 Mobutu founded the Mouvement Populaire de la Révolution (MPR). It was the only permitted party, and every citizen was automatically considered a member.
46860.m: Mobutu's Zaire was a one-party state.

46861.q: What was Mobutu's lavish palace complex in his home town of Gbadolite often called?
46861.e: In Gbadolite Mobutu had palaces built, as well as an airport for supersonic aircraft. The complex earned the nickname ‘Versailles of the jungle’.
46861.m: Gbadolite shows how Mobutu wasted state money on luxury.

46862.q: What name did Zaire receive after Mobutu was overthrown in 1997?
46862.e: Rebel leader Laurent-Désiré Kabila took power in May 1997 and renamed the country. Mobutu died a few months later in exile in Morocco.
46862.m: Since 1997 Zaire has once again been called the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

46863.q: Which conflict in eastern Zaire contributed decisively to the collapse of Mobutu's rule in 1996?
a: The aftermath of the genocide in Rwanda
46863.e: After the genocide in Rwanda in 1994, perpetrators and refugees fled to Zaire. Rwanda and Uganda then supported the uprising that overthrew Mobutu.
46863.m: The genocide in Rwanda set off the war that brought Mobutu down.

46864.q: Why did Mobutu drop his Christian first name Joseph-Désiré in 1972?
a: As part of his Africanisation policy
Because of a dispute with the Pope
46864.e: Under the ‘Authenticité’ campaign, Christian first names had to give way to African ones. From then on Mobutu called himself Mobutu Sese Seko Kuku Ngbendu Wa Za Banga.
46864.m: In 1972 Mobutu dropped his Christian first name.

46865.q: Which party introduced apartheid as state policy in South Africa after its election victory in 1948?
46865.e: The National Party under Daniel François Malan won the election among the white population in 1948. It then governed until 1994.
46865.m: From 1948 the National Party made apartheid law.

46866.q: Which law of 1950 assigned every person in South Africa to a ‘race’?
46866.e: The Population Registration Act of 1950 created a register that assigned every person to a population group. This classification determined where people lived, which school they went to and what rights they had.
46866.m: The racial registration of 1950 was the foundation of apartheid.

46867.q: Which law of 1950 assigned separate residential areas in the cities to the population groups?
46867.e: The Group Areas Act laid down where each group was allowed to live. Many people were forcibly resettled, for example from District Six in Cape Town.
46867.m: The Group Areas Act divided the cities by skin colour.

46868.q: Which document did Black South Africans have to carry at all times under the pass laws?
46868.e: The passbook, called the ‘dompas’ in Afrikaans, controlled where Black people were allowed to stay and work. Anyone who could not show it was arrested.
46868.m: The pass laws controlled Black people's freedom of movement.

46869.q: Which leader of the Black Consciousness Movement died in police custody in 1977?
46869.e: Steve Biko was injured by severe abuse in custody and died in September 1977. His death caused outrage around the world.
46869.m: Steve Biko's death in 1977 became a symbol of the regime's brutality.

46870.q: Which law of 1953 created a deliberately worse-equipped school system for Black children?
46870.e: The law was meant to train Black young people only for simple work. The schools received much less money per child than those for white children.
46870.m: Bantu Education deliberately kept Black children away from a good education.

46871.q: Which means did many states use in the 1980s to put pressure on the apartheid regime?
46871.e: Countries such as the USA imposed sanctions in 1986, and many companies withdrew. Sports boycotts also isolated South Africa.
46871.m: Sanctions and boycotts increased the pressure on the apartheid government.

46872.q: What was the country called that became Zimbabwe in 1980?
46872.e: The white minority government under Ian Smith had unilaterally declared Rhodesia's independence in 1965. After a guerrilla war, Zimbabwe was created in 1980.

46873.q: Which agreement ended the war in Rhodesia in 1979 and prepared the 1980 elections?
46873.e: The negotiations took place at Lancaster House in London. They led to elections, which Mugabe's ZANU won.
46873.m: The Lancaster House Agreement paved Zimbabwe's way to independence.

46874.q: Against which population group were the massacres by Mugabe's Fifth Brigade in Matabeleland in the 1980s directed?
46874.e: The massacres are called ‘Gukurahundi’. From 1983 to 1987 the Fifth Brigade killed thousands of civilians, most of them Ndebele. Mugabe himself belonged to the Shona majority.
46874.m: Under Mugabe thousands of Ndebele were murdered.

46875.q: Which opposition party under Morgan Tsvangirai challenged Mugabe in elections from 1999?
46875.e: The MDC grew out of the trade union movement in 1999. Its supporters were often intimidated and persecuted at elections.
46875.m: The Movement for Democratic Change was the main opposition to Mugabe.

46876.q: Which office did Mugabe take over in 1987, having previously been prime minister?
46876.e: A constitutional amendment abolished the office of prime minister in 1987. As executive president, Mugabe combined power in his hands.
46876.m: From 1987 Mugabe ruled as a powerful president.

46877.q: Whom did Mugabe apparently want to build up as his successor in 2017, which triggered resistance from the army?
46877.e: Mugabe dismissed Vice-President Mnangagwa to clear the way for Grace Mugabe. The army then intervened in November 2017.
46877.m: The power struggle over Grace Mugabe sped up her husband's fall in 2017.

46878.q: Roughly how old was Robert Mugabe when he had to resign in 2017?
46878.e: Mugabe was born in February 1924 and resigned in November 2017. At the time he was the oldest serving head of state in the world.
46878.m: Mugabe ruled until the great age of 93.

46879.q: What did Gaddafi call the political system he officially proclaimed from 1977?
46879.e: The Arabic term Jamahiriya roughly means ‘state of the masses’. Officially the people ruled directly through people's committees; in reality power lay with Gaddafi.
46879.m: The Jamahiriya disguised Gaddafi's sole rule as rule by the people.

46880.q: Which title did Gaddafi hold, although he officially had no state office?
46880.e: In 1979 Gaddafi gave up all formal offices and called himself ‘Brotherly Leader of the Revolution’. His power nevertheless remained unlimited.
46880.m: Gaddafi ruled as Leader of the Revolution without a formal state office.

46881.q: Which country did the USA bomb in 1986 in retaliation for an attack on a Berlin nightclub?
46881.e: The attack on the ‘La Belle’ nightclub killed three people, including two US soldiers. The USA held Gaddafi responsible and bombed Tripoli and Benghazi.
46881.m: The attack on ‘La Belle’ in 1986 led to US strikes on Libya.

46882.q: What did Gaddafi give up in December 2003 in order to improve relations with the West?
46882.e: Libya announced that it would give up its programmes for nuclear and chemical weapons. After that many sanctions were lifted.
46882.m: By giving up weapons of mass destruction in 2003 Gaddafi returned to world politics.

46883.q: What did the UN Security Council decide in March 2011 to protect the civilian population in Libya?
46883.e: With Resolution 1973, the Security Council authorised measures to protect civilians. NATO states then intervened from the air against Gaddafi's troops.
46883.m: In 2011 the UN authorised a no-fly zone over Libya.

46884.q: Near which city was Gaddafi captured and killed in October 2011?
46884.e: Sirte was Gaddafi's home region and one of his last strongholds. He was captured by rebels while fleeing the city.
46884.m: Gaddafi died near his home town of Sirte in October 2011.

46885.q: Which two Swiss men were held in Libya from 2008 to 2010?
46885.e: After Hannibal Gaddafi was arrested in Geneva, Libya prevented the two businessmen from leaving the country. Hamdani was freed at the beginning of 2010, Göldi only in June 2010.
46885.m: The Libya crisis hit Switzerland through two of its citizens being held hostage.

46886.q: In which year did Saddam Hussein officially become president of Iraq?
46886.e: After the Baath coup of 1968, Saddam was already the strongman behind the then president. In July 1979 he took over the presidency himself.
46886.m: Saddam Hussein became president of Iraq in 1979.

46887.q: What happened at a filmed meeting of the party leadership shortly after Saddam took office in 1979?
46887.e: At the meeting the names of alleged conspirators were read out, and they had to leave the room. Many of them were later executed.
46887.m: In 1979 Saddam secured his power with a public purge of the party.

46888.q: What was the military operation of the US-led coalition that liberated Kuwait in 1991 called?
46888.e: After Kuwait was occupied in August 1990, the air war began in January 1991. By the end of February 1991 Kuwait had been liberated.
46888.m: Kuwait was liberated in 1991 with Operation Desert Storm.

46889.q: What was the military campaign against the Kurds in northern Iraq from 1986 to 1989, in which tens of thousands died, called?
46889.e: The Anfal campaign included poison gas attacks, deportations and the destruction of thousands of villages. It is regarded as genocide against the Kurds.
46889.m: The Anfal campaign was a genocide against the Iraqi Kurds.

46890.q: How did the trial of Saddam Hussein in Iraq end in 2006?
a: With a death sentence that was carried out
With life imprisonment in The Hague
46890.e: An Iraqi special tribunal sentenced Saddam to death for the execution of 148 men from Dujail. He was hanged on 30 December 2006.
46890.m: Saddam Hussein was sentenced to death and executed in 2006.

46891.q: Which uprising broke out in the south and north of Iraq in spring 1991 after the Gulf War?
a: An uprising of Shiites and Kurds
An uprising of students in Baghdad
An uprising of the Baath youth
46891.e: Shiites in the south and Kurds in the north rose up against Saddam. The uprising was bloodily crushed by his troops.
46891.m: In 1991 Saddam brutally crushed the uprisings of the Shiites and Kurds.

46892.q: What was the main justification the USA and Great Britain gave for going to war against Iraq in 2003?
46892.e: The US government claimed that Iraq possessed weapons of mass destruction. After the war no such stockpiles were found.
46892.m: The justification for the 2003 Iraq War with weapons of mass destruction turned out to be false.

46893.q: From which city in the region of his birthplace did many of Saddam's close confidants come?
46893.e: Saddam was born in 1937 in the village of al-Awja near Tikrit. He filled important posts with relatives and clan members from this area.
46893.m: Saddam's network of power relied heavily on his clan from Tikrit.

46894.q: What does the Arabic word ‘Baath’ mean?
46894.e: Baath means rebirth or renewal. It refers to the rebirth of a united Arab nation.
46894.m: The name Baath stands for the rebirth of the Arab nation.

46895.q: In which city was the Baath Party officially founded in 1947?
46895.e: The founding congress took place in the Syrian capital in April 1947. Later, branches were set up in several Arab countries.
46895.m: The Baath Party was founded in Damascus in 1947.

46896.q: Which two men are considered the main founders of the Baath Party?
a: Michel Aflaq and Salah al-Din al-Bitar
Gamal Abdel Nasser and Anwar Sadat
46896.e: The two Syrian teachers had studied in Paris. Aflaq came from a Christian background, al-Bitar from a Muslim one.
46896.m: Michel Aflaq and Salah al-Din al-Bitar founded the Baath movement.

46897.q: What is the motto of the Baath Party?
46897.e: Unity means the union of all Arabs, freedom means liberation from foreign rule. Socialism stands for a state-directed economy.
46897.m: The Baath Party combined Arab nationalism with socialism.

46898.q: Which ideology does the Baath Party combine with socialism?
46898.e: Pan-Arabism aims for a common state of all Arabs. Baath ideology was explicitly secular rather than religious.
46898.m: The Baath Party stood for a secular pan-Arabism.

46899.q: What happened to the Baath Party in 1966?
a: It split into a Syrian and an Iraqi wing
46899.e: After a coup in Syria in 1966, the party broke up into two rival branches. Damascus and Baghdad remained enemies after that.
46899.m: From 1966 the Syrian and Iraqi Baath parties fought each other.

46900.q: What is the US occupation's policy from 2003 of removing Baath members from state offices in Iraq called?
46900.e: The administration under Paul Bremer banned senior party members from public office. Critics say this left many experts unemployed and fuelled the insurgency.
46900.m: After 2003 de-Baathification removed Baath members from the Iraqi state.

46901.q: Through which coup in July 1968 did the Baath Party come to power permanently in Iraq?
a: The coup under Ahmad Hasan al-Bakr
The coup under Abd al-Karim Qasim
The coup under King Faisal II
46901.e: Al-Bakr became president and Saddam Hussein his deputy. The party then ruled Iraq until 2003.
46901.m: After the 1968 coup the Baath Party ruled Iraq for 35 years.

46902.q: In which year did Hafez al-Assad take power in Syria through a coup?
46902.e: The then defence minister called his coup in November 1970 the ‘Corrective Movement’. In 1971 he became president.
46902.m: Hafez al-Assad seized power in Syria in 1970.

46903.q: Which religious community does the Assad family belong to?
46903.e: The Alawites are a minority in Syria. Many key posts in the army and intelligence services were filled with Alawites.
46903.m: The Assads relied heavily on the Alawite minority for their power.

46904.q: In which city did Hafez al-Assad have an uprising of the Muslim Brotherhood bloodily crushed in 1982?
46904.e: The army besieged and shelled the city for weeks. Estimates range from 10,000 to over 20,000 dead.
46904.m: The Hama massacre of 1982 was one of the bloodiest crimes of the Assad regime.

46905.q: Which profession had Bashar al-Assad trained in before he became his father's successor?
46905.e: Bashar studied medicine and specialised in ophthalmology in London. After his brother Basil died in an accident in 1994, he was built up as successor.
46905.m: Bashar al-Assad was originally an eye doctor in London.

46906.q: Which poison gas attack by the Assad regime in August 2013 killed hundreds of people near Damascus?
a: The mustard gas attack on Idlib
The sarin attack on Khan Shaykhun
46906.e: According to estimates, over 1,000 people died in the sarin attack on the Ghouta region. Afterwards Syria had to disclose its chemical weapons arsenal.
46906.m: The poison gas attack on Ghouta in 2013 was a serious war crime.

46907.q: Which rebel group led the offensive that led to Assad's fall in December 2024?
46907.e: The group launched an offensive from Idlib province at the end of November 2024. Within about two weeks Aleppo, Hama, Homs and Damascus fell.
46907.m: In December 2024 the HTS militia ended the rule of the Assad family.

46908.q: To which country did Bashar al-Assad flee after the fall of Damascus in December 2024?
46908.e: Along with Iran, Russia was the regime's most important ally. Moscow granted Assad and his family asylum.
46908.m: In 2024 Bashar al-Assad fled to his ally Russia.

46909.q: Which prison north of Damascus is seen as a symbol of torture and mass executions under Assad?
46909.e: After the regime fell in 2024, the prisoners of Sednaya were freed. Human rights organisations called it a ‘human slaughterhouse’.
46909.m: Sednaya stands for the systematic torture under the Assad regime.

46910.q: Which monarch was overthrown by the Islamic Revolution in Iran in 1979?
46910.e: The Shah left Iran on 16 January 1979. He died in exile in Egypt in 1980.
46910.m: The 1979 revolution ended the rule of Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi.

46911.q: What was the Shah's feared secret police called?
46911.e: SAVAK watched, arrested and tortured opposition figures. Its brutality contributed to the hatred of the Shah's regime.
46911.m: SAVAK was the Shah's instrument of repression.

46912.q: What happened in Tehran on 8 September 1978, the so-called ‘Black Friday’?
46912.e: On Jaleh Square the military opened fire on a rally. After that, reconciliation between the Shah and the opposition was hardly possible any more.
46912.m: ‘Black Friday’ in 1978 intensified the revolution against the Shah.

46913.q: How was Iran officially proclaimed after a referendum at the end of March 1979?
46913.e: On 1 April 1979 Khomeini proclaimed the Islamic Republic of Iran. An overwhelming majority had approved it in the referendum.
46913.m: Since April 1979 Iran has been an Islamic Republic.

46914.q: How long did the hostage-taking at the US embassy in Tehran last from November 1979?
46914.e: Students occupied the embassy on 4 November 1979 and held 52 Americans. The hostages were released in January 1981.
46914.m: The Tehran hostage crisis lasted 444 days.

46915.q: Which role has Switzerland taken on for the USA in Iran since 1980?
46915.e: Since diplomatic relations were broken off, the Swiss embassy in Tehran has represented the interests of the USA. It also passes on messages between the two states.
46915.m: Since 1980 Switzerland has been the protecting power for the USA in Iran.

46916.q: Who returned from exile in France in February 1979 and became leader of the revolution in Iran?
46916.e: Ayatollah Khomeini had last lived in exile near Paris. On 1 February 1979 millions welcomed him in Tehran; the Shah's last government collapsed shortly afterwards.
46916.m: Khomeini returned from exile in 1979 and led the revolution.

46917.q: Which war began in September 1980, shortly after the revolution, and lasted eight years?
46917.e: Iraq attacked the weakened Iran. The war ended in 1988 with a ceasefire and hundreds of thousands dead.
46917.m: The First Gulf War between Iran and Iraq lasted from 1980 to 1988.

46918.q: How is the Iranian Guardian Council made up?
a: Of six clerics and six jurists
Of officers of the Revolutionary Guards
46918.e: The six clerics are appointed by the Supreme Leader. The six jurists are proposed by the head of the judiciary and elected by parliament.
46918.m: The Guardian Council has six clerics and six jurists.

46919.q: Which body decides in Iran when parliament and the Guardian Council cannot agree on a law?
a: The Expediency Discernment Council of the System
46919.e: This council, often called the Expediency Council, was created in 1988. It decides in disputes between parliament and the Guardian Council.
46919.m: The Expediency Council mediates between parliament and the Guardian Council.

46920.q: What happens to a law passed in Iran if the Guardian Council rejects it?
a: It is put to the people
46920.e: The Guardian Council can send laws back to parliament to be revised. If parliament insists on them, the Expediency Council decides.
46920.m: If the Guardian Council rejects a law, parliament has to revise it.

46921.q: For which body, which chooses the Supreme Leader, does the Guardian Council also vet the candidates?
46921.e: The Guardian Council also vets the candidates for the Assembly of Experts. In this way it indirectly influences who chooses the Supreme Leader.
46921.m: By vetting candidates, the Guardian Council even influences the choice of the Supreme Leader.

46922.q: Who appoints the six Islamic jurists on Iran's Guardian Council?
a: The people in a direct vote
46922.e: The Guardian Council has twelve members. The Supreme Leader appoints six Islamic jurists, and parliament elects six lawyers proposed by the judiciary.
46922.m: The Supreme Leader directly chooses half of the Guardian Council.

46923.q: Besides reviewing laws, what task does the Guardian Council also have regarding the constitution?
a: It gives the binding interpretation of the constitution
46923.e: Under the Iranian constitution, the Guardian Council has the right to give binding interpretations of the constitution. This requires a three-quarters majority.
46923.m: The Guardian Council is also the highest interpreter of Iran's constitution.

46924.q: What effect did the Guardian Council's vetting of candidates have on Iran's 2021 presidential election?
a: Women were allowed to stand for the first time
46924.e: Of around 600 applicants, the Guardian Council approved only seven, with no prominent reformers among them. Ebrahim Raisi won on a very low turnout.
46924.m: In 2021 the Guardian Council's choice of candidates decided the result in advance.

46925.q: Because he opposed which reforms of the Shah was Khomeini sent into exile in 1964?
46925.e: The White Revolution of 1963 included land reform and votes for women. Khomeini sharply criticised it and the influence of the USA.
46925.m: Khomeini was exiled for criticising the White Revolution.

46926.q: In which Iraqi city did Khomeini live in exile from 1965 to 1978?
46926.e: Najaf is an important centre of Shia scholarship. There Khomeini gave the lectures in which he developed his theory of the state.
46926.m: Khomeini developed his ideas in Najaf in Iraq.

46927.q: From which country did Khomeini lead the revolution in autumn 1978?
46927.e: He lived in Neauphle-le-Château near Paris and gave many interviews there. On 1 February 1979 he returned to Tehran.
46927.m: Khomeini steered the revolution in 1978 from exile in France.

46928.q: Which medium helped most to spread Khomeini's speeches in Iran before the revolution?
46928.e: His sermons were recorded on cassettes and copied in secret. In this way they reached millions of people despite censorship.
46928.m: Cassettes carried Khomeini's message past the censors.

46929.q: Against which writer did Khomeini issue a death sentence (fatwa) in 1989?
46929.e: The reason was the novel “The Satanic Verses”. Rushdie had to live under police protection for years and was seriously injured in an attack in 2022.
46929.m: Khomeini's fatwa against Salman Rushdie shocked the world in 1989.

46930.q: Who became Iran's new Supreme Leader after Khomeini's death in 1989?
46930.e: The Assembly of Experts chose Khamenei in June 1989. Montazeri, the originally intended successor, had fallen from favour earlier.
46930.m: Ali Khamenei succeeded Khomeini as Supreme Leader in 1989.

46931.q: What religious rank did Khomeini hold in Shia Islam?
46931.e: The title Ayatollah means “sign of God”. A Grand Ayatollah is regarded as the highest religious authority whom believers follow.
46931.m: As a Grand Ayatollah, Khomeini belonged to the highest rank of Shia clerics.

46932.q: Which mass crime against political prisoners took place in Iran in 1988 under Khomeini's leadership?
a: The mass executions in the prisons
The poison gas attack on Halabja
46932.e: In the summer of 1988 thousands of prisoners were executed after brief questioning. The number of victims is estimated at several thousand.
46932.m: The prison massacres of 1988 are among the worst crimes of the Islamic Republic.

46933.q: Whose self-immolation on 17 December 2010 sparked the protests in Tunisia?
46933.e: The vegetable seller from Sidi Bouzid was protesting against harassment by the authorities. He died of his injuries in early January 2011.
46933.m: Mohamed Bouazizi's act of despair set off the Arab Spring.

46934.q: Whose troops helped to crush the protests in the Kingdom of Bahrain in March 2011?
a: Troops of the Gulf Cooperation Council
46934.e: Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates in particular sent soldiers and police. After that, the protests at Pearl Roundabout in Manama were broken up.
46934.m: In Bahrain the 2011 uprising was crushed with help from neighbouring states.

46935.q: What is the 2011 revolution in Tunisia also called, after a flower?
46935.e: Jasmine is regarded as a symbol of Tunisia. The Carnation Revolution, by contrast, took place in Portugal in 1974.
46935.m: The revolution in Tunisia went down in history as the Jasmine Revolution.

46936.q: In which Syrian city did protests begin in March 2011 after young people were arrested for graffiti criticising the regime?
46936.e: The young people were mistreated in custody, which enraged the population. From Daraa the protests spread across all of Syria.
46936.m: The Syrian uprising began in the city of Daraa in 2011.

46937.q: Who was elected in 2012 as Egypt's first freely elected president?
46937.e: Morsi came from the Muslim Brotherhood. In July 2013 he was removed by the military after mass protests.
46937.m: Mohamed Morsi was Egypt's first freely elected president but was overthrown in 2013.

46938.q: Which general took power in Egypt after the 2013 military coup and became president in 2014?
46938.e: As defence minister he removed the elected president in July 2013. Since then he has ruled Egypt with a firm hand.
46938.m: With el-Sisi, Egypt returned to military rule in 2013.

46939.q: Which long-serving ruler of Yemen gave up his office in 2012 as a result of the protests?
46939.e: Saleh ruled North Yemen from 1978 and united Yemen from 1990. Under an agreement he handed power to his deputy Hadi.
46939.m: In Yemen, President Saleh stepped down in 2012 after the protests.

46940.q: What is the development called in which civil wars or new dictatorships followed the Arab Spring in several countries?
46940.e: The term describes setbacks such as the wars in Syria, Libya and Yemen. In Egypt, too, military rule returned.
46940.m: In many places the Arab Spring was followed by an “Arab Winter”.

46941.q: How did Jean-Bédel Bokassa come to power in the Central African Republic in 1966?
46941.e: As head of the army, Bokassa overthrew his relative, President David Dacko, on New Year's Eve 1965/66. The coup is named after New Year's Eve, in French Saint-Sylvestre.
46941.m: Bokassa came to power through a military coup.

46942.q: Which country overthrew Bokassa with a military operation in 1979?
46942.e: In Operation Barracuda, French troops landed in Bangui and reinstated the former president David Dacko. France had supported Bokassa for a long time before.
46942.m: In 1979 France overthrew its former ally Bokassa.

46943.q: What was the official name of the state under Bokassa from 1976 to 1979?
46943.e: In 1976 Bokassa turned the republic into an empire and called himself Bokassa I. After his fall the republic was proclaimed again.
46943.m: Under Bokassa the country was briefly an empire.

46944.q: Which affair about gifts from Bokassa damaged the French president Valéry Giscard d'Estaing?
46944.e: In 1979 the newspaper “Le Canard enchaîné” reported that Giscard had received diamonds from Bokassa. The affair hurt him in the 1981 election.
46944.m: The diamonds affair showed the close ties between Bokassa and Paris.

46945.q: What caused the 1979 school pupils' protests that Bokassa had brutally crushed?
a: Having to buy expensive school uniforms
The closure of all secondary schools
A ban on the national language Sango
46945.e: The uniforms had to be bought from a company owned by Bokassa's family. Around 100 children and teenagers were killed.
46945.m: The dispute over school uniforms ended in 1979 with a massacre of schoolchildren.

46946.q: Which country was Bokassa in when he was overthrown in September 1979?
46946.e: Bokassa was visiting Gaddafi when French troops landed in Bangui. Afterwards he went into exile, first in the Ivory Coast.
46946.m: Bokassa was overthrown in 1979 while visiting Libya.

46947.q: What happened to the death sentence passed on Bokassa in 1987?
a: It was confirmed by the people
46947.e: The sentence was changed to life imprisonment and later to a shorter term. In 1993 Bokassa was released under an amnesty, and he died in 1996.
46947.m: Bokassa escaped execution and was released in 1993.

46948.q: Who was the founder and first leader of the Taliban?
46948.e: Mullah Omar founded the movement in 1994 in the Kandahar region. He hardly ever appeared in public and died in 2013, which only became known in 2015.
46948.m: Mullah Omar founded the Taliban in 1994.

46949.q: What does the word “Taliban” literally mean?
46949.e: Taliban is the plural of talib, which means pupil or seeker. Many founding members came from Koran schools in Pakistan.
46949.m: The name Taliban refers to the Koran students from whom the movement arose.

46950.q: Which three states recognised the Taliban regime diplomatically from 1996 to 2001?
a: Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and the UAE
46950.e: The United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan established relations. Most states continued to recognise the government that had been overthrown.
46950.m: Only three states recognised the first Taliban regime.

46951.q: Which event led to the fall of the first Taliban government in 2001?
46951.e: The Taliban refused to hand over the al-Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden. A US-led coalition and the Northern Alliance drove them out by the end of 2001.
46951.m: After 11 September 2001, Taliban rule was ended by military force.

46952.q: Which agreement did the USA and the Taliban conclude in February 2020?
46952.e: In the agreement signed in Doha, Qatar, the USA promised to withdraw its troops. The Afghan government did not take part in the negotiations.
46952.m: The Doha Agreement paved the way for the US withdrawal from Afghanistan.

46953.q: From which city does the supreme Taliban leader run the movement, even though the government is based in Kabul (as of 2026)?
46953.e: Hibatullah Akhundzada has led the Taliban since 2016 and lives in seclusion in Kandahar, where the movement began in 1994. Important decisions are therefore often made there and not in Kabul.
46953.m: The Taliban are led from Kandahar.

46954.q: Which country was the first to officially recognise the Taliban government, in July 2025?
46954.e: Russia had removed the Taliban from its list of terrorist groups in spring 2025 and accepted their ambassador in July 2025. As of 2026, no other state has formally recognised the Taliban government.
46954.m: Russia was the first state to recognise the Taliban government, in 2025.

46955.q: What were women in Afghanistan additionally banned from by the Taliban in December 2022?
46955.e: After girls were excluded from secondary schools, the university ban followed. Later, training in medical professions was also forbidden.
46955.m: Since the end of 2022, women in Afghanistan have not been allowed to study at university.

46956.q: In which year was the Democratic People's Republic of Korea founded under Kim Il-sung?
46956.e: On 9 September 1948 the Democratic People's Republic was proclaimed in the north of Korea, with Kim Il-sung at its head. Shortly before, the Republic of Korea had been created in the south.
46956.m: North Korea was founded in 1948 under Kim Il-sung.

46957.q: Which title was Kim Il-sung given after his death in North Korea's 1998 constitution?
46957.e: The 1998 constitution declared Kim Il-sung, who had died in 1994, the “Eternal President of the Republic”. The office of head of state was thus effectively reserved for him.
46957.m: In North Korea, Kim Il-sung is regarded as the Eternal President.

46958.q: Who took over the leadership of North Korea after Kim Il-sung died in 1994?
46958.e: His son Kim Jong-il led North Korea from 1994 until his death in December 2011. This is regarded as the first hereditary handover of power in a communist-style state.
46958.m: Kim Jong-il succeeded his father Kim Il-sung in 1994.

46959.q: What was the policy under Kim Jong-il that gave the military priority over all other areas called?
46959.e: “Songun” means “military first” and placed the armed forces at the centre of state and economy. It shaped Kim Jong-il's rule from the mid-1990s.
46959.m: Under Kim Jong-il, the Songun policy of putting the military first applied.

46960.q: In which Swiss region is Kim Jong-un said by media reports to have gone to school in the 1990s?
46960.e: According to reports, he attended schools in Gümligen and Liebefeld near Bern under a false name. This is not completely certain, but the authorities confirmed a North Korean pupil in Köniz.
46960.m: Kim Jong-un is said to have gone to school near Bern as a teenager.

46961.q: Which half-brother of Kim Jong-un was killed with a nerve agent at Kuala Lumpur airport in 2017?
46961.e: Kim Jong-nam was attacked with the nerve agent VX in February 2017 and died shortly afterwards. He was Kim Jong-il's eldest son and lived in exile.
46961.m: Kim Jong-nam was murdered with VX in Malaysia in 2017.

46962.q: Which party has governed North Korea since the state was founded?
46962.e: The Workers' Party of Korea is the leading state party; other permitted parties are subordinate to it. Kim Jong-un has been at its head since 2012.
46962.m: North Korea is dominated by the Workers' Party of Korea.

46963.q: According to current research, where was Kim Jong-il actually born?
46963.e: Official propaganda names a secret camp on the sacred Mount Paektu. Historians, however, believe he was born in 1941 in a Soviet military camp near Khabarovsk.
46963.m: Kim Jong-il's birth on Mount Paektu is a propaganda legend.

46964.q: What is the central idea of North Korea's Juche ideology?
46964.e: Juche is usually translated as “self-reliance” or “independence”. The country should not depend on others politically, economically or militarily.
46964.m: Juche stands for the idea of national self-reliance.

46965.q: With which year does North Korea's Juche calendar begin?
46965.e: Juche year 1 is 1912, the year Kim Il-sung was born. The calendar was introduced in 1997.
46965.m: The Juche calendar begins with Kim Il-sung's birth year, 1912.

46966.q: What does the Juche Tower in Pyongyang stand for?
a: The state ideology and Kim Il-sung
46966.e: The 170-metre tower was opened in 1982 for Kim Il-sung's 70th birthday. It is said to consist of 25,550 granite blocks, one for each day of Kim Il-sung's life up to then.
46966.m: The Juche Tower honours the state ideology and Kim Il-sung.

46967.q: According to official teaching, which three principles form the core of Juche?
46967.e: The principles are called chaju (political independence), charip (economic self-sufficiency) and chawi (military self-defence). They are meant to make the country independent of foreign powers.
46967.m: Juche demands political, economic and military independence.

46968.q: Who is officially regarded in North Korea as the founder of the Juche ideology?
46968.e: North Korean propaganda credits Juche to Kim Il-sung. The doctrine was largely worked out by the philosopher Hwang Jang-yop, who fled to South Korea in 1997.
46968.m: In North Korea, Juche is regarded as Kim Il-sung's teaching.

46969.q: Which ideology was gradually pushed out of the North Korean constitution by Juche?
46969.e: Juche was written into the constitution as the guiding ideology in 1972 and gradually displaced Marxism-Leninism. In 2009 the word “communism” disappeared from the constitution.
46969.m: In North Korea, Juche replaced Marxism-Leninism as the state ideology.

46970.q: What is North Korea's official state ideology, which extends Juche with the teachings of the leaders, often called today as a whole?
46970.e: Since 2012 the party has spoken of Kimilsungism-Kimjongilism. This declares the teachings of the two dead leaders to be the binding foundation.
46970.m: North Korea's state ideology is called Kimilsungism-Kimjongilism.

46971.q: What consequence of the goal of economic self-sufficiency became especially clear after the collapse of the Soviet Union?
46971.e: Without Soviet aid and because of failed harvests, a famine known as the “Arduous March” struck in the mid-1990s. Estimates suggest hundreds of thousands died.
46971.m: Isolation contributed to a famine in North Korea in the 1990s.

46972.q: What reason did the army give for the 2021 coup in Myanmar?
46972.e: The military claimed fraud in the November 2020 election, which the NLD had clearly won. The election commission and observers found no evidence of it.
46972.m: The army justified the coup with alleged electoral fraud.

46973.q: Which sign did demonstrators in Myanmar use in 2021 as a symbol of resistance?
46973.e: The three-finger salute comes from “The Hunger Games” films. It had already been used at protests in Thailand.
46973.m: The three-finger salute became the sign of protest in Myanmar.

46974.q: What is the opposition government formed by removed members of parliament in Myanmar called?
46974.e: The National Unity Government (NUG) was formed in April 2021. It sees itself as the legitimate government and works underground and in exile.
46974.m: The National Unity Government is the opposition government to Myanmar's junta.

46975.q: Who took over the leadership of Myanmar after the coup of 1 February 2021?
a: An administrator appointed by the UN
46975.e: Commander-in-chief Min Aung Hlaing put himself at the head of the junta, which ruled through a so-called State Administration Council. The elected head of government, Aung San Suu Kyi, was arrested.
46975.m: After the 2021 coup, army chief Min Aung Hlaing ruled.

46976.q: What was the movement called in which doctors, teachers and civil servants stopped work after the coup?
46976.e: In the Civil Disobedience Movement many state employees refused to work for the junta. Medical staff led the way.
46976.m: After the coup many state employees stopped work in civil disobedience.

46977.q: Roughly how long did the military rule Myanmar (Burma) after the first coup in 1962, until the country partly opened up from 2011?
46977.e: General Ne Win staged a coup on 2 March 1962. After that the military ruled in various forms for almost five decades.
46977.m: In Myanmar the military ruled long before the 2021 coup.

46978.q: Why was Aung San Suu Kyi not allowed to become president of Myanmar under the 2008 constitution?
a: She was too old for the office.
She had never been a member of parliament.
Women were excluded from the office.
46978.e: The constitution excludes people whose spouse or children are citizens of another country. Her sons are British, so in 2016 the office of State Counsellor was created for her.
46978.m: Because of her British sons, Aung San Suu Kyi could not become president.

46979.q: Before which court did Aung San Suu Kyi defend Myanmar in 2019 against the accusation of genocide against the Rohingya?
46979.e: The Gambia had brought a case against Myanmar at the International Court of Justice in The Hague. Her appearance there badly damaged her international reputation.
46979.m: In 2019 Aung San Suu Kyi defended Myanmar in The Hague against the genocide accusation.

46980.q: What did the military in Myanmar do with Aung San Suu Kyi after the coup in February 2021?
a: It had her arrested and convicted several times
It sent her into exile in Britain
It used her as a mediator
46980.e: Aung San Suu Kyi was arrested during the coup. In a series of trials before military courts her sentences added up to 33 years; observers consider the proceedings politically motivated.
