47204.q: What was the anarchist-minded association of watchmakers in the Swiss Jura that sided with Bakunin called?
47204.e: The watchmakers often worked in small workshops and valued self-management. The federation became a centre of anarchism in Europe.
47204.m: The Jura Federation made the Swiss Jura a centre of anarchism.

47205.q: In which town in the Bernese Jura was the anti-authoritarian International founded in 1872?
47205.e: After Bakunin's expulsion, his followers met in Saint-Imier in September 1872. The congress is regarded as the birth of the anarchist movement.
47205.m: The anti-authoritarian International was founded in Saint-Imier in 1872.

47206.q: To which city did the Hague Congress of 1872 move the General Council of the International?
47206.e: Marx wanted to remove the General Council from the influence of Bakunin's followers. After that the organisation quickly lost importance.
47206.m: With the move of the General Council to New York, the First International came to an end.

47207.q: Roughly how long did the Paris Commune of 1871 last?
47207.e: It began on 18 March 1871 and ended on 28 May 1871. Government troops recaptured Paris.
47207.m: The Paris Commune lasted only about two and a half months.

47208.q: What did the government want to do on Montmartre on 18 March 1871, when the Commune uprising began?
47208.e: The people of Paris had paid for the guns with their own money and wanted to keep them. Soldiers joined the crowd, and the government withdrew to Versailles.
47208.m: The dispute over the cannons on Montmartre set off the Paris Commune.

47209.q: Who led the French government in Versailles that moved against the Commune?
47209.e: Thiers was head of the executive of the new republic. He had Paris recaptured by government troops.
47209.m: Adolphe Thiers had the Paris Commune crushed by military force.

47210.q: How did the Paris Commune end in May 1871?
a: Government troops recaptured Paris in a bloody week
The Commune dissolved peacefully after elections
The Communards took over all of France
47210.e: During the “Bloody Week” at the end of May 1871, government troops fought street by street. Thousands of Communards were killed, many of them shot.
47210.m: The Paris Commune was bloodily crushed in 1871.

47211.q: Which measure did the Commune decide on for bakeries?
a: A ban on bread on Sundays
47211.e: The decree of April 1871 was meant to improve the harsh working conditions of journeyman bakers.
47211.m: The Paris Commune banned night work in bakeries.

47212.q: Which painter was blamed for pulling down the Vendôme Column and then fled to Switzerland?
47212.e: Courbet was supposed to pay for rebuilding the column. He lived in La Tour-de-Peilz on Lake Geneva until his death in 1877.
47212.m: After the Commune, Gustave Courbet spent his last years on Lake Geneva.

47213.q: Which teacher and fighter of the Commune was banished to New Caledonia?
47213.e: Louise Michel fought on the barricades and defended herself openly in court. After returning in 1880 she remained a well-known anarchist.
47213.m: Louise Michel became the best-known woman of the Paris Commune.

47214.q: In which work of 1902 did Lenin call for a party of professional revolutionaries?
47214.e: Lenin wanted a tightly organised, disciplined cadre party. As a vanguard it was to lead the working class to revolution.
47214.m: In “What Is to Be Done?” Lenin set out the idea of the vanguard party.

47215.q: According to Lenin, what kind of consciousness do workers develop on their own, without a party?
47215.e: Lenin believed that workers by themselves only fight over wages and working hours. Socialist consciousness had to be brought in from outside by the party.
47215.m: According to Lenin, the party brings revolutionary consciousness into the working class from outside.

47216.q: What does the Russian name “Bolsheviks” mean when translated?
47216.e: At the congress of the Russian Social Democrats in 1903, Lenin's wing won an important vote. Its opponents were then called Mensheviks, meaning those of the minority.
47216.m: The Bolsheviks named themselves after a majority at the 1903 party congress.

47217.q: What is Lenin's organisational principle called, under which the leadership's decisions are binding on all members?
47217.e: Discussion was to be allowed before a decision, but after it strict discipline applied. In practice this led to rule by the party leadership.
47217.m: Democratic centralism binds all party members to the leadership's decisions.

47218.q: In which work of 1920 did Lenin criticise left communists who wanted to boycott parliaments and trade unions?
47218.e: Lenin advised the young communist parties in the West to work in parliaments and trade unions too. He considered pure refusal immature.
47218.m: Lenin rejected boycotting parliaments and trade unions as an infantile disorder.

47219.q: Which slogan was at the centre of Lenin's April Theses of 1917?
47219.e: After returning to Petrograd, Lenin demanded that the Provisional Government should not be supported. Power was to go to the councils.
47219.m: In the April Theses Lenin demanded power for the councils.

47220.q: Which organisation did the Bolsheviks found in Moscow in 1919 to push forward world revolution?
47220.e: It is called the Comintern for short. Its member parties had to submit to strict instructions from Moscow.
47220.m: With the Comintern, Lenin wanted to direct communist parties around the world.

47221.q: Under which ruler did “Marxism-Leninism” become the official state ideology of the Soviet Union?
47221.e: After Lenin's death in 1924, Stalin systematised his teachings. The term became the basis of the ideology of all Eastern Bloc parties.
47221.m: Stalin made Marxism-Leninism the compulsory state doctrine.

47222.q: What does Trotsky's theory of permanent revolution say?
a: The revolution must go beyond the bourgeois stage and continue internationally
Revolutions repeat themselves every hundred years
Every government must be overthrown each year
The revolution should only happen peacefully and slowly
47222.e: Even in backward countries the working class must take power. But socialism is only possible if the revolution spreads to other countries.
47222.m: According to Trotsky, a revolution must not stay limited to one country.

47223.q: Which doctrine of Stalin opposed Trotsky's permanent revolution?
47223.e: From 1924 Stalin argued that the Soviet Union could build socialism on its own. Trotsky saw this as a break with internationalism.
47223.m: Stalin relied on socialism in one country, Trotsky on world revolution.

47224.q: Which army did Trotsky build up from 1918 as People's Commissar for War?
47224.e: During the civil war Trotsky formed the Red Army from volunteers and conscripts. The Whites were its opponents; the other armies belonged to China and East Germany.
47224.m: Trotsky was the founder of the Red Army.

47225.q: In which year did Trotsky found the Fourth International?
47225.e: The founding conference took place near Paris in September 1938. It was meant to be an alternative to the Stalinist Comintern.
47225.m: The Fourth International was founded in 1938.

47226.q: Who murdered Trotsky in Mexico in 1940 on Stalin's orders?
47226.e: The Spanish agent struck Trotsky with an ice axe in Coyoacán. Trotsky died the next day.
47226.m: Trotsky was murdered by a Soviet agent in exile in Mexico in 1940.

47227.q: How did Trotsky describe the Soviet Union under Stalin in “The Revolution Betrayed”?
47227.e: Trotsky thought the property relations were still socialist, but a bureaucracy had seized power. Other left-wingers, by contrast, spoke of state capitalism.
47227.m: Trotsky saw Stalin's Soviet Union as a workers' state degenerated by bureaucracy.

47228.q: What was Leon Trotsky's real name?
47228.e: Trotsky was born in 1879 as Lev Davidovich Bronstein in what is now Ukraine. He took the name Trotsky after escaping from exile.
47228.m: Leon Trotsky's real name was Lev Bronstein.

47229.q: What is the tactic called in which Trotskyists join larger socialist parties as a group?
47229.e: In 1934 Trotsky advised his French followers to join the socialist party. There they were to win members for their ideas.
47229.m: In entryism, Trotskyists deliberately join larger parties.

47230.q: At which university did Rosa Luxemburg receive her doctorate in 1897?
47230.e: Women could already study in Zurich at that time. Her dissertation dealt with Poland's industrial development.
47230.m: Rosa Luxemburg completed her studies with a doctorate in Zurich.

47231.q: In which present-day country was Rosa Luxemburg born in 1871?
47231.e: She was born in Zamość, which then belonged to the Russian-ruled part of Poland. Later she gained German citizenship through a marriage of convenience.
47231.m: Rosa Luxemburg came from the then Russian part of Poland.

47232.q: What is Rosa Luxemburg's famous sentence about freedom?
a: “Freedom is always the freedom of those who think differently”
47232.e: The sentence appears as a note in the margin of her 1918 work “The Russian Revolution”. In it she criticised the Bolsheviks' suppression of the opposition.
47232.m: Rosa Luxemburg demanded freedom also for people with different opinions.

47233.q: With which work of 1899 did Rosa Luxemburg reply to Eduard Bernstein?
a: “The Mass Strike, the Political Party and the Trade Unions”
47233.e: Luxemburg held on to revolution and accused Bernstein of giving up socialism. Reforms alone, she said, could not overcome capitalism.
47233.m: Rosa Luxemburg defended the goal of revolution against Bernstein.

47234.q: What was the group around Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht that opposed the First World War called?
47234.e: The Spartacus League was named after the leader of a Roman slave revolt. It fought against the SPD's support for the war and became the seed of the KPD.
47234.m: Rosa Luxemburg led the Spartacus League with Karl Liebknecht.

47235.q: Why did Rosa Luxemburg oppose the First World War?
a: Because workers had to fight each other for the interests of the rulers
Because Germany had too few soldiers
Because she wanted to support Russia
Because she was against every form of politics
47235.e: For Rosa Luxemburg the war was an imperialist war. Workers of all countries should stick together instead of shooting at each other.
47235.m: Rosa Luxemburg saw the World War as a war against the workers.

47236.q: Which party did Rosa Luxemburg help to found around the turn of the year 1918/1919?
47236.e: The KPD grew out of the Spartacus League, which she led with Karl Liebknecht. The founding congress took place in Berlin.
47236.m: Rosa Luxemburg was a co-founder of the KPD.

47237.q: Who murdered Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht in Berlin in January 1919?
47237.e: After the Spartacist uprising, the two were abducted and murdered by officers of a Freikorps unit on 15 January 1919. The killers were hardly punished.
47237.m: Rosa Luxemburg was murdered by Freikorps soldiers in 1919.

47238.q: Which term is central for Antonio Gramsci to describe rule by consent rather than only by force?
47238.e: According to Gramsci, the ruling class secures its power mainly by having its values regarded as natural. Schools, churches and the press contribute to this.
47238.m: Gramsci explained rule through cultural hegemony.

47239.q: What are the notebooks that Gramsci wrote while held prisoner by the fascists called?
47239.e: In Italian they are called “Quaderni del carcere”. There are around 30 notebooks with notes on politics, culture and history.
47239.m: Gramsci's most important work is the Prison Notebooks.

47240.q: Which party did Antonio Gramsci help to found in 1921?
47240.e: At the Socialists' congress in Livorno in 1921, the left wing split off and founded the Communist Party of Italy. Gramsci later became its general secretary.
47240.m: In 1921 Gramsci was a co-founder of the Communist Party of Italy.

47241.q: What is the prosecutor in Gramsci's 1928 trial said to have demanded?
a: To stop this brain from working for twenty years
To deport Gramsci to the Soviet Union immediately
To read Gramsci's books out in public
47241.e: Gramsci was sentenced to more than 20 years in prison. Even so, he wrote down his most important ideas in prison.
47241.m: The fascists wanted to silence Gramsci through imprisonment.

47242.q: On which Italian island was Antonio Gramsci born in 1891?
47242.e: Gramsci was born in Ales and grew up in poor conditions. Later he studied in Turin with a scholarship.

47243.q: In which year did Antonio Gramsci die?
47243.e: He died in Rome in April 1937 as a result of his long imprisonment. His sentence had ended shortly before.
47243.m: Antonio Gramsci died in 1937 after years in prison.

47244.q: According to Gramsci, what role do intellectuals play for a social class?
a: They put its interests and world view into words
47244.e: Gramsci called such thinkers “organic intellectuals”. Every class produces its own thinkers, who give it awareness and cohesion.
47244.m: According to Gramsci, every class needs its own thinkers to express its view.

47245.q: Which military metaphor did Gramsci use for the long struggle for hegemony in Western societies?
47245.e: In Russia, a quick war of movement had been possible because civil society was weak. In the West, civil society had to be won step by step.
47245.m: Gramsci compared the struggle for hegemony in the West to a war of position.

47246.q: What did Eduard Bernstein demand of the SPD in the revisionism dispute?
a: The abolition of the trade unions
47246.e: Bernstein wanted to adapt Marxist theory to how things had actually developed. The SPD should openly see itself as a democratic reform party.
47246.m: Bernstein relied on reforms instead of revolution.

47247.q: How does Bernstein's famous sentence “The final goal, whatever it may be, is nothing to me, ...” end?
47247.e: For Bernstein, what counted were concrete improvements for the workers. He considered a distant final goal such as revolution to be secondary.
47247.m: For Bernstein, step-by-step progress mattered more than a distant final goal.

47248.q: In which Swiss city did Bernstein edit the newspaper “Der Sozialdemokrat” during Germany's Anti-Socialist Laws?
47248.e: The newspaper was printed in Switzerland and smuggled into Germany. In 1888 Bernstein was expelled and went to London.
47248.m: From Zurich, Bernstein produced a newspaper for the banned German Social Democrats.

47249.q: Which Marxist expectation did Bernstein reject?
47249.e: Bernstein observed that the middle class was not disappearing and crises were becoming milder. So he did not expect a collapse soon but relied on reforms.
47249.m: Bernstein did not believe capitalism would soon collapse.

47250.q: Which theorist, also called the “Pope of Marxism”, defended orthodox Marxism against Bernstein?
47250.e: Kautsky was editor of the journal “Die Neue Zeit”. He had also helped shape the SPD's Erfurt Programme.
47250.m: Karl Kautsky was regarded as the guardian of orthodox Marxism in the SPD.

47251.q: Which British reform movement influenced Bernstein during his time in London?
47251.e: The Fabians relied on gradual reforms instead of revolution. Bernstein lived in London until 1901 and came into contact with their ideas there.
47251.m: Bernstein's reformism was influenced by the British Fabians.

47252.q: With which programme did the SPD finally abandon Marxism as its foundation in 1959?
47252.e: After that the SPD saw itself as a people's party and accepted the market economy. In this way the reformist line won out in the long term.
47252.m: With the Godesberg Programme the SPD became a people's party.

47253.q: Who governed Russia immediately after the Tsar was overthrown in March 1917?
a: The Tsar's brother as the new Tsar
47253.e: The Provisional Government under Prince Georgy Lvov was to lead the country until a constituent assembly met. The Bolsheviks only took power in October 1917.
47253.m: After the Tsar's fall, a Provisional Government ruled first.

47254.q: What effect did “Order No. 1” of the Petrograd Soviet in March 1917 have on the Russian army?
a: The officers lost much of their authority over the soldiers
The army was placed under the Tsar again
47254.e: Order No. 1 allowed elected soldiers' committees and made government orders subject to the Soviet's approval. It badly undermined the officers' discipline.
47254.m: Order No. 1 weakened the officers' power over the soldiers.

47255.q: Which two centres of power faced each other in Russia after the February Revolution of 1917?
a: The Provisional Government and the Petrograd Soviet
47255.e: This is called dual power: the Provisional Government came from a committee of the Duma, while the Soviet represented workers and soldiers.
47255.m: After the February Revolution there was dual power in Russia.

47256.q: Why were there mass protests against the Provisional Government in April 1917?
a: It wanted to continue the war until victory
It wanted to bring back the Tsar
It had closed all the factories
47256.e: Foreign Minister Pavel Milyukov assured the Allies that Russia would fight on until victory. The April Crisis forced him to resign at the beginning of May 1917.
47256.m: Continuing the war cost the Provisional Government a lot of support.

47257.q: Which liberal party was most strongly represented in the first Provisional Government?
47257.e: The Constitutional Democrats, Kadets for short, provided several ministers in the first Provisional Government. They stood for a liberal, middle-class programme.
47257.m: The liberal Kadets shaped the first Provisional Government.

47258.q: Why did Tsar Nicholas II have to abdicate in March 1917?
a: The army leadership withdrew its support
The Bolsheviks had taken him prisoner
He had lost an election against the Duma
He wanted to retire to England
47258.e: As the unrest in Petrograd spread, his generals advised him to step down. Nicholas II signed the abdication in his train at Pskov.
47258.m: Without the support of his generals, Nicholas II had to abdicate in 1917.

47259.q: Which large industrial works in Petrograd locked out tens of thousands of workers in February 1917, fuelling the unrest?
47259.e: The Putilov Works were the largest arms factory in Petrograd. Locking out the workforce shortly before Women's Day drove many workers onto the streets.
47259.m: The lockout at the Putilov Works helped trigger the February Revolution.

47260.q: Which punishment did the Provisional Government abolish in March 1917 but reintroduce at the front in July 1917?
47260.e: The Provisional Government abolished the death penalty in March 1917. Because discipline was collapsing, it was reintroduced for soldiers at the front in July 1917.
47260.m: In 1917 the death penalty was first abolished and then reintroduced at the front.

47261.q: In which city on the Volga was Lenin born?
47261.e: Lenin was born in Simbirsk. Since 1924 the city has been called Ulyanovsk in his honour.
47261.m: Lenin's birthplace Simbirsk is now called Ulyanovsk.

47262.q: Which event of 1887 shaped the young Lenin and drove him towards revolution?
a: The execution of his elder brother
The assassination of Tsar Alexander II
The start of the First World War
47262.e: His brother Alexander Ulyanov was hanged in 1887 for a planned attempt on the Tsar's life. Tsar Alexander II had already been assassinated in 1881.
47262.m: The execution of his brother in 1887 radicalised Lenin.

47263.q: Which work by Lenin from 1902 called for a tightly organised party of professional revolutionaries?
47263.e: In “What Is to Be Done?” Lenin demanded a small, disciplined cadre party. “Das Kapital” and the “Manifesto” are by Marx and Engels, “The Revolution Betrayed” by Trotsky.
47263.m: Lenin's “What Is to Be Done?” set out the idea of the cadre party.

47264.q: Which woman was blamed for the assassination attempt in which Lenin was seriously injured in Moscow in August 1918?
47264.e: Lenin was shot on 30 August 1918 after a speech outside a Moscow factory. The Socialist Revolutionary Fanny Kaplan was arrested and shot a few days later.
47264.m: Fanny Kaplan was executed for the 1918 attempt on Lenin's life.

47265.q: In which country house near Moscow did Lenin die in January 1924?
47265.e: After several strokes, Lenin spent his last period in Gorki, south of Moscow. He died there on 21 January 1924.
47265.m: Lenin spent the last years of his life in Gorki near Moscow.

47266.q: Which decree did Lenin have the Congress of Soviets pass in November 1917 together with the Decree on Peace?
a: The Decree on the Gold Standard
The Decree on the Ban on Factions
47266.e: The Decree on Land took the large estates without compensation and gave the land to the peasants to use. It largely adopted the Socialist Revolutionaries' agricultural programme.
47266.m: Right after the October Revolution, Lenin's government shared out land to the peasants by decree.

47267.q: In which country did Lenin live in exile during the First World War until 1917?
47267.e: From 1914 Lenin lived in Bern and Zurich. In April 1917 he travelled to Russia in the sealed train with German permission.
47267.m: Lenin waited for the revolution in Zurich.

47268.q: Which ban did Lenin push through at the 10th Party Congress in March 1921?
a: The ban on factions within the party
47268.e: The resolution “On Party Unity” prohibited organised groups with their own platform. Later Stalin used this ban against his opponents.
47268.m: The 1921 ban on factions stifled open debate in the party.

47269.q: In which village in the Bernese Oberland did socialist opponents of the war meet for a second conference with Lenin in April 1916?
47269.e: After Zimmerwald in 1915, the Kiental Conference took place in April 1916. There Lenin tried to bring the opponents of the war onto a revolutionary course.
47269.m: The Kiental Conference of 1916 continued the meetings of war opponents in Switzerland.

47270.q: Why did the German government allow Lenin to travel through Germany to Russia in 1917?
a: It hoped Russia would be weakened and end the war
It wanted to arrest Lenin in Germany
It wanted Russia as an ally against Switzerland
It had been forced to do so by Switzerland
47270.e: Germany was fighting a war on two fronts. Lenin demanded an immediate end to the war, so the German leadership hoped he would take Russia out of the war.
47270.m: Germany helped Lenin in order to weaken Russia in the war.

47271.q: In which Swiss city did Lenin begin his journey in the sealed train in April 1917?
47271.e: Lenin's last home was on Spiegelgasse in Zurich. On 9 April 1917 he left Zurich main station with about 30 emigrants towards the German border.
47271.m: Lenin's journey to Russia began in Zurich in 1917.

47272.q: In which city did Lenin arrive at the end of his journey in April 1917 and give his first speech?
47272.e: On 16 April 1917 Lenin arrived at the Finland Station in Petrograd, today's St Petersburg. Shortly afterwards he presented his April Theses.
47272.m: In 1917 Lenin arrived at the Finland Station in Petrograd.

47273.q: Which Federal Councillor had to resign in June 1917 because he wanted to encourage a separate peace between Germany and Russia through a sounding-out attempt?
47273.e: In the Grimm-Hoffmann affair, a telegram from Federal Councillor Arthur Hoffmann to National Councillor Robert Grimm in Petrograd became public. The affair violated neutrality, and Hoffmann resigned.
47273.m: The Grimm-Hoffmann affair of 1917 led to a Federal Councillor's resignation.

47274.q: What did it mean that Lenin's carriage through Germany was “sealed”?
a: Nobody was allowed to get on or off on the way
The carriage was armoured against gunfire
The carriage ran without a locomotive
47274.e: The carriage counted as extraterritorial, like foreign territory. There were no checks, but also no contact with Germans during the journey.
47274.m: The sealed carriage was cut off from its surroundings.

47275.q: Through which neutral country did Lenin's group travel on to Russia after the journey through Germany?
47275.e: From the German Baltic coast they took the ferry to Sweden. Via Stockholm the group travelled north and then through Finland to Petrograd.
47275.m: In 1917 Lenin travelled to Russia via Sweden.

47276.q: What did the travellers promise in return for being allowed through?
a: To campaign for the release of Germans interned in Russia
To take Russia out of the Entente
47276.e: The emigrants promised to campaign in Russia for an exchange for Germans and Austrians interned there. In this way the journey looked like a prisoner exchange.
47276.m: In return, the travellers promised to support a prisoner exchange.

47277.q: Which force set off major fighting along the Trans-Siberian Railway with its revolt in May 1918?
47277.e: The legion of former prisoners of war was to be taken to France via Vladivostok. When the Bolsheviks tried to disarm it, it occupied large parts of the railway line.
47277.m: The revolt of the Czechoslovak Legion widened the civil war in 1918.

47278.q: Which White general advanced from the south as far as Oryol in 1919 and threatened Moscow?
47278.e: Denikin's Armed Forces of South Russia reached Oryol, about 350 kilometres south-west of Moscow, in October 1919. Then they were pushed back by the Red Army.
47278.m: Denikin's advance on Moscow failed at Oryol in 1919.

47279.q: To which city did the Bolsheviks move Russia's capital in March 1918?
47279.e: Petrograd was close to the front and in danger. So the government moved to Moscow, which has been the capital ever since.
47279.m: Since 1918 Moscow has again been Russia's capital.

47280.q: From which peninsula did General Wrangel evacuate his troops in November 1920?
47280.e: Wrangel held out in Crimea as the last White commander in the south. In November 1920 he took about 150,000 people by ship to Constantinople.
47280.m: The evacuation of Crimea in 1920 ended the Whites' fight in the south.

47281.q: Which anarchist led his own peasant army in Ukraine during the civil war?
47281.e: With his Revolutionary Insurgent Army, Nestor Makhno fought sometimes against the Whites, sometimes against the Reds. In 1921 he fled abroad.
47281.m: Nestor Makhno led an anarchist peasant movement in Ukraine.

47282.q: Which large peasant uprising of 1920 to 1921 was put down using poison gas, among other things?
47282.e: In Tambov province, peasants under Alexander Antonov rose up against the grain requisitions. The Red Army also used chemical weapons to crush them.
47282.m: The Tambov Rebellion showed the peasants' resistance to the Bolsheviks.

47283.q: What were the Bolsheviks' opponents in the Russian Civil War called?
47283.e: The Bolshevik “Reds” were opposed by the “Whites”. These included monarchists, officers and liberals, who often disagreed among themselves.
47283.m: In the Russian Civil War, Reds fought against Whites.

47284.q: Which city in the Far East did the Reds take in October 1922 as the last major stronghold of their opponents?
47284.e: Japanese troops withdrew from the Far East in 1922. On 25 October 1922 the Reds marched into Vladivostok.
47284.m: The capture of Vladivostok in 1922 ended the civil war in the Far East.

47285.q: What did peasants have to do under War Communism?
a: Hand over their grain to the state by force
Give their land back to the big landowners
Move to the factories in the cities
47285.e: Under this forced requisition, called prodrazvyorstka in Russian, the state decided how much grain each region had to hand over. Often even the seed grain was taken.
47285.m: Under War Communism, peasants had to hand over their grain to the state.

47286.q: What were the armed squads of workers who seized grain in the countryside called?
47286.e: The food detachments, prodotryady in Russian, went into the villages and took grain by force. This led to many peasant revolts.
47286.m: Under War Communism, armed food detachments took grain from the villages.

47287.q: Which committees were meant to mobilise poor peasants against better-off peasants in the village from June 1918?
a: The Committees of the Village Poor
The peasant councils of the collective farms
47287.e: The Committees of the Village Poor, kombedy for short, helped to seize grain. They were dissolved again at the end of 1918 because they divided the villages.
47287.m: The Committees of the Village Poor were meant to bring class struggle into the village.

47288.q: What did a decree of June 1918 order for large-scale industry?
47288.e: With the decree of 28 June 1918, the large industrial enterprises were nationalised. By 1920 many small businesses had also come under state control.
47288.m: War Communism brought the nationalisation of almost all industry.

47289.q: How were workers increasingly paid under War Communism because of the severe loss of money's value?
a: In kind, such as food rations
47289.e: Inflation made paper money lose almost all its value. Wages were therefore largely paid in the form of rations and goods.
47289.m: Under War Communism, rations largely replaced money wages.

47290.q: What did Leon Trotsky propose in 1920 to deal with the shortage of workers?
47290.e: Trotsky wanted to use army units that were no longer needed as labour armies. Work was to be organised according to military rules.
47290.m: In 1920 Trotsky wanted to organise labour like an army.

47291.q: How did many city dwellers get food under War Communism, despite the ban?
a: Through the black market with peasants from the countryside
Through fields in the middle of the city
47291.e: Private trade was banned, but black marketeers carried food in sacks from the countryside into the cities. Despite harsh punishments they kept many city dwellers alive.
47291.m: The banned black market helped many city dwellers survive under War Communism.

47292.q: With the New Economic Policy, what replaced the forced handover of grain?
47292.e: The peasants only had to hand over a fixed share of their harvest as tax. They were allowed to keep the rest.
47292.m: A fixed tax in kind gave the peasants a reason to grow more.

47293.q: Which problem was a new, partly gold-backed currency meant to solve in the NEP period?
a: The severe inflation after the civil war
47293.e: After war and civil war, the rouble was almost worthless. From 1922 the State Bank issued the gold-backed chervonets and so stabilised the money.
47293.m: After the inflation, the NEP brought back a stable currency.

47294.q: What were small traders and craftsmen allowed to do again during the New Economic Policy?
a: Run private businesses and make a profit
Own factories with thousands of workers
47294.e: Under the NEP, small shops, crafts and private trade were allowed again. Large industry, banks and foreign trade stayed in state hands.
47294.m: In the NEP period, small private trade was allowed again.

47295.q: What was the 1923 crisis called, in which prices for industrial goods rose and those for farm products fell?
47295.e: Trotsky compared the price curves moving apart to an open pair of scissors. The peasants could hardly afford industrial goods.
47295.m: The scissors crisis showed the imbalance between town and country.

47296.q: Which crisis of 1927 and 1928 did Stalin use as a reason to take harsh measures against the peasants?
47296.e: The peasants delivered too little grain at the low state prices. Stalin then had grain seized again, which marked the beginning of the end of the NEP.
47296.m: The grain procurement crisis began the end of the NEP.

47297.q: Which party theorist called out to the peasants in 1925: “Enrich yourselves!”?
47297.e: Nikolai Bukharin wanted to win the peasants over to socialism through prosperity. He was regarded as the most important defender of the NEP.
47297.m: Bukharin defended the NEP with the call “Enrich yourselves!”.

47298.q: What did Lenin call the mixed economic system of the NEP under state control?
47298.e: Lenin saw the NEP as a temporary retreat. Private business was to be allowed under the supervision of the proletarian state.
47298.m: Lenin called the NEP a form of state capitalism.

47299.q: Who ended the NEP at the end of the 1920s and relied on forced collectivisation and five-year plans?
47299.e: Stalin broke with the NEP from 1928. The peasants were forced into collective farms, and industry was to grow rapidly through five-year plans.
47299.m: Stalin replaced the NEP with collectivisation and five-year plans.

47300.q: Who was the first head of the Cheka?
47300.e: Felix Dzerzhinsky came from a Polish noble family. He led the Cheka and its successors until his death in 1926.
47300.m: Felix Dzerzhinsky built up the Soviet secret police.

47301.q: What does the abbreviation Cheka literally mean?
47301.e: Cheka is made up of the Russian initial letters of Chrezvychainaya Komissiya. That means Extraordinary Commission.
47301.m: The name Cheka stands for an Extraordinary Commission.

47302.q: Which authority replaced the Cheka in February 1922?
47302.e: In 1922 the Cheka was turned into the State Political Directorate, GPU for short. Formally, it had narrower powers.
47302.m: In 1922 the Cheka became part of the GPU.

47303.q: Which campaign did the Soviet government announce in September 1918 after the attempt on Lenin's life?
47303.e: A decree of 5 September 1918 officially declared the Red Terror. Thousands of hostages and supposed opponents were shot.
47303.m: The Red Terror began in 1918 as persecution ordered by the state.

47304.q: In which Moscow building did the secret police have its headquarters from 1918?
a: In the House on the Embankment
In the Peter and Paul Fortress
47304.e: In 1918 the Cheka moved into the former building of an insurance company on Lubyanka Square. Later the NKVD and KGB also used the building.
47304.m: The Lubyanka became the symbol of the Soviet secret police.

47305.q: According to its own leaders, what should the Cheka mainly judge suspects by?
47305.e: In 1918 the Chekist Martin Latsis wrote that one should not look for evidence but ask about origin and education. This shows the class character of the Red Terror.
47305.m: For the Cheka, social origin often counted for more than any act.

47306.q: Which power did the Cheka have that a normal police force does not?
a: To pass and carry out sentences without a trial
47306.e: The Cheka could arrest, sentence and shoot suspects without any court being involved. It was police, prosecutor and judge all at once.
47306.m: The Cheka combined investigation, sentencing and execution in one hand.

47307.q: Which camp on a group of islands in the White Sea is regarded as the forerunner of the Gulag system?
47307.e: From 1923 the Cheka's successor set up a camp in the monastery on the Solovetsky Islands. Methods of forced labour were tested there that later shaped the whole country.
47307.m: The Solovki camp was an early model for the Soviet prison camps.

47308.q: Which founding republic of the Soviet Union united Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan?
47308.e: The Transcaucasian Socialist Federative Soviet Republic existed from 1922 to 1936. After that, Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan became separate Union republics.
47308.m: Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan first joined the Soviet Union together.

47309.q: With whom did Lenin quarrel in 1922 about how the Soviet republics should be joined together?
47309.e: Stalin wanted to place the other republics under the Russian Soviet Republic and acted harshly against Georgian communists. Lenin criticised him sharply and pushed through a union of formally equal republics.
47309.m: The founding of the Soviet Union led to a break between Lenin and Stalin in 1922.

47310.q: What was Stalin's plan to incorporate the other Soviet republics into the Russian Soviet Republic as autonomous regions called?
47310.e: Stalin wanted to place the republics under the RSFSR. Lenin instead pushed through a union of formally equal republics.
47310.m: Lenin rejected Stalin's plan of autonomisation.

47311.q: Which right did the Union republics formally have under the constitution?
a: The right to leave the Union
The right to their own army
The right to their own currency
The right to their own embassies abroad
47311.e: The constitution guaranteed every Union republic the right to leave the Union freely. In practice this was not possible until 1990.
47311.m: For a long time the Soviet republics' right to leave existed only on paper.

47312.q: Which two chambers did the Central Executive Committee of the Soviet Union have under the 1924 constitution?
a: Soviet of the Union and Soviet of Nationalities
People's Chamber and Chamber of States
47312.e: The Soviet of the Union represented the population as a whole, the Soviet of Nationalities the republics and peoples. This two-chamber system remained in the later Supreme Soviet.
47312.m: The Soviet parliament had one chamber for the population and one for the nationalities.

47313.q: In 1946 a city was renamed after Mikhail Kalinin, the Soviet Union's long-serving formal head of state. What was it called before?
47313.e: Königsberg in East Prussia went to the Soviet Union after the Second World War and has been called Kaliningrad ever since. Kalinin was formal head of state from 1919 to 1946, but power lay with the party leadership.
47313.m: Since 1946 Königsberg has been called Kaliningrad, after Mikhail Kalinin.

47314.q: How did the young Soviet Union deal with the languages of the non-Russian peoples in the 1920s?
a: It promoted schools and newspapers in these languages
It banned all languages except Russian
It left teaching entirely to the church
It introduced German as a second official language
47314.e: With the policy of korenizatsiya, roughly “taking root”, schools, newspapers and administration in local languages were meant to anchor Soviet power among the peoples. Later Stalin relied more on Russian again.
47314.m: In the 1920s the Soviet Union promoted the non-Russian languages.

47315.q: Which economic policy did Lenin introduce in March 1921, shortly after the Kronstadt uprising?
47315.e: The uprising showed Lenin how great the discontent was. With the New Economic Policy (NEP) he allowed small trade again, and peasants were allowed to sell their surpluses.
47315.m: After the Kronstadt uprising, Lenin gave way with the NEP.

47316.q: What did the Kronstadt sailors demand in their resolution, among other things?
a: New elections to the soviets by secret ballot
47316.e: The sailors demanded free and secret elections to the soviets, as well as freedom of speech and of the press for left-wing parties. They wanted to free the councils from party rule.
47316.m: The Kronstadt sailors demanded councils free from party control.

47317.q: Who rose up against the Bolsheviks in Kronstadt in March 1921?
47317.e: The sailors and soldiers of the Kronstadt fortress demanded free councils and more freedoms. A revolutionary committee under the clerk Stepan Petrichenko led the uprising.
47317.m: In 1921 sailors in Kronstadt rose up against the Bolsheviks.

47318.q: How did the Kronstadt uprising end in March 1921?
a: The Red Army crushed it bloodily
The sailors surrendered without a fight
47318.e: Troops under Mikhail Tukhachevsky stormed the fortress after heavy losses. On 18 March 1921 Kronstadt fell, and many rebels were shot or sent to camps.
47318.m: The Kronstadt uprising was bloodily crushed in 1921.

47319.q: How did the Red Army troops attack the Kronstadt fortress?
a: Across the ice of the Gulf of Finland
Through a tunnel under the sea
47319.e: In March the sea around Kronstadt was still frozen. The soldiers charged across the open ice in white camouflage capes.
47319.m: The Red Army stormed Kronstadt across the frozen sea.

47320.q: Which city does the Kronstadt fortress protect from the sea?
47320.e: Kronstadt lies on Kotlin Island in the Gulf of Finland off St Petersburg, which was called Petrograd in 1921. Peter the Great had it fortified as a naval base.
47320.m: Kronstadt protects the sea route to St Petersburg.

47321.q: Why did the uprising of the Kronstadt sailors hit the Bolsheviks particularly hard in 1921?
a: The sailors had strongly supported the revolution in 1917
The sailors were Lenin's personal bodyguard
The sailors all came from abroad
The sailors had freed the Tsar
47321.e: In 1917 Trotsky had praised the Kronstadt sailors as the “beauty and pride of the revolution”. The fact that they of all people rose up showed how great the discontent had become.
47321.m: The once celebrated Kronstadt sailors became opponents of the Bolsheviks in 1921.

47322.q: What was the main aim of forced collectivisation in the Soviet Union from 1929?
a: To merge farms into state-controlled collective farms
To give the big landowners' land to the peasants
47322.e: The peasants had to bring their land, livestock and tools into collective farms. In this way the state wanted to secure grain for the cities and for export and to finance industrialisation.
47322.m: Forced collectivisation pushed peasants into state-controlled collective farms.

47323.q: Under which slogan did Stalin call for action against the better-off peasants in December 1929?
a: “Liquidation of the kulaks as a class”
47323.e: This slogan marked the start of dekulakisation. Hundreds of thousands of families had their property taken and were arrested or deported.
47323.m: The 1929 slogan made the kulaks enemies who were to disappear.

47324.q: How did many peasants react when they had to hand over their livestock to the collective farms?
a: They preferred to slaughter their animals themselves
They sold them to the West
They took them to the cities
47324.e: Out of protest and need, many peasants slaughtered their animals instead of handing them over. As a result the Soviet Union's livestock numbers fell sharply in the early 1930s.
47324.m: Many peasants slaughtered their livestock before they had to hand it over to the collective farm.

47325.q: What is the 1932 to 1933 famine in Ukraine called, which many states today recognise as genocide?
47325.e: Holodomor means roughly “killing by hunger”. Millions of people died because the state forced high grain deliveries despite failed harvests.
47325.m: The Holodomor was the famine in Ukraine caused by Stalin's policies.

47326.q: Which people lost a particularly large share of their population through forced settlement and the famine of 1930 to 1933?
47326.e: The nomadic Kazakhs had to give up their herds and settle in one place. More than a million people died, and many fled to China.
47326.m: The famine in Kazakhstan devastated the nomadic population.

47327.q: What did collective farm workers at first not receive under the passport system introduced at the end of 1932?
47327.e: Without an internal passport, peasants were not allowed to move freely to the cities. In practice they were tied to their collective farm.
47327.m: Without an internal passport, collective farm workers stayed tied to their village.

47328.q: Under the model statute of 1935, what were collective farm workers allowed to farm privately?
47328.e: The household plot was usually smaller than half a hectare. Even so, it supplied a large share of the country's vegetables, milk and meat.
47328.m: The small household plot was vital for feeding collective farm workers.

47329.q: Which economic policy with small private trade did Stalin end at the end of the 1920s in favour of collectivisation?
47329.e: From 1921 the New Economic Policy (NEP) had allowed peasants to sell surpluses on the market. Stalin replaced it with a planned economy and forced collectivisation.
47329.m: With collectivisation, Stalin ended the New Economic Policy.

47330.q: Which two former companions of Lenin were at the centre of the first Moscow Trial in August 1936?
47330.e: Grigory Zinoviev and Lev Kamenev were sentenced to death along with 14 other defendants. They were shot immediately after the verdict.
47330.m: The first Moscow Trial was directed against Zinoviev and Kamenev.

47331.q: What are trials like the Moscow Trials called, in which the verdict is decided in advance and the public is meant to be impressed?
47331.e: Show trials are not about the truth but about propaganda. The defendants were to confess in public, and the verdict had already been decided by the party leadership.
47331.m: The Moscow Trials were show trials with verdicts decided in advance.

47332.q: What did the prosecution accuse most of the defendants in the Moscow Trials of?
a: A conspiracy with the exiled Trotsky
47332.e: The defendants were said to have planned attacks and sabotage with Trotsky and foreign intelligence services. The accusations were invented.
47332.m: In the Moscow Trials, people were charged with invented conspiracies with Trotsky.

47333.q: Which murder in December 1934 served Stalin as a pretext for the persecutions?
47333.e: Sergei Kirov, the party chief of Leningrad, was shot on 1 December 1934. The crime was later blamed on opposition members.
47333.m: The murder of Kirov in 1934 gave Stalin a pretext for persecuting opponents.

47334.q: What were the verdicts in the Moscow Trials mainly based on?
47334.e: Under pressure, threats against relatives and torture, the defendants confessed to invented crimes. There was hardly any other evidence.
47334.m: The Moscow Trials were based almost entirely on forced confessions.

47335.q: In which country was Trotsky living in exile when he was murdered on Stalin's orders in 1940?
47335.e: Trotsky was accused in the Moscow Trials as the chief conspirator, even though he lived abroad. After stays in Turkey, France and Norway he came to Mexico, where a Soviet agent killed him in 1940.
47335.m: Trotsky was murdered in Mexico in 1940 on Stalin's orders.

47336.q: What is the wave of persecution in the Soviet Union from 1936 to 1938, which included the Moscow Trials, called?
47336.e: In the Great Terror, Stalin had hundreds of thousands of people shot and many more sent to camps. The Moscow Trials were the publicly visible part of it.
47336.m: The Moscow Trials were part of the Great Terror under Stalin.

47337.q: Which 1940 novel by Arthur Koestler deals with the Moscow Trials?
47337.e: In “Darkness at Noon” the old revolutionary Rubashov confesses to crimes he did not commit. The novel made the logic of the trials known in the West.
47337.m: Koestler's “Darkness at Noon” shows how revolutionaries were brought to make false confessions.

47338.q: By which other name is the Communist International also known?
47338.e: The Comintern saw itself as the successor to the First International and as the counterpart to the social democratic Second International. That is why it is also called the Third International.
47338.m: The Comintern is also called the Third International.

47339.q: How many conditions did parties have to meet from 1920 to be admitted to the Comintern?
47339.e: The second World Congress in 1920 decided on 21 conditions for admission. Among other things, they demanded strict discipline and a break with moderate socialists.
47339.m: With 21 conditions, the Comintern sharply separated itself from social democracy.

47340.q: In which year was the Comintern dissolved?
47340.e: Stalin dissolved the Comintern in May 1943. He wanted to reassure his Western allies during the Second World War.
47340.m: The Comintern was dissolved in the middle of the Second World War.

47341.q: Which new strategy did the seventh World Congress of the Comintern adopt in 1935?
a: A break with the Soviet Union
47341.e: After Hitler took power, communists were to work with social democrats and middle-class parties against fascism. Popular Front governments were formed in France and Spain.
47341.m: From 1935 the Comintern relied on alliances against fascism.

47342.q: Which Bulgarian communist was general secretary of the Comintern from 1935 to 1943?
47342.e: Georgi Dimitrov became famous in 1933 at the Reichstag fire trial in Leipzig, because he defended himself skilfully and was acquitted. Afterwards he went to Moscow.
47342.m: Georgi Dimitrov led the Comintern in its last years.

47343.q: With which slogan did the Comintern attack the social democrats around 1929?
47343.e: The Comintern declared social democrats to be the twins of the fascists. This attitude made joint resistance against Nazism in Germany more difficult.
47343.m: The theory of social fascism split the labour movement before 1933.

47344.q: What was the leading body of the Comintern between the World Congresses called?
47344.e: The Executive Committee of the Communist International, ECCI for short, was based in Moscow. It gave binding instructions to the national parties.
47344.m: The Executive Committee in Moscow directed the communist parties of many countries.

47345.q: Which states did the Soviet Union absorb in 1940 as a result of the Hitler-Stalin Pact?
a: Austria, the Czech lands and Slovakia
47345.e: Under the secret agreements, the Baltic states fell into the Soviet sphere of interest. In summer 1940 they were occupied and incorporated as Soviet republics.
47345.m: The Baltic states became part of the Soviet Union in 1940.

47346.q: Which Soviet foreign minister signed the pact with Hitler's Germany in 1939?
47346.e: Molotov signed the pact on 23 August 1939 with the German foreign minister Joachim von Ribbentrop. That is why it is also called the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact. His predecessor Litvinov had been removed in May 1939.
47346.m: After its signatories, the Hitler-Stalin Pact is also called the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact.

47347.q: Which country did Germany and the Soviet Union divide between them in autumn 1939 under the secret additional protocol?
47347.e: On 1 September 1939 Germany attacked Poland, and on 17 September the Red Army invaded from the east. The country was divided along the line agreed beforehand.
47347.m: In 1939 Poland was divided between Germany and the Soviet Union.

47348.q: Which negotiations in Moscow failed in August 1939, shortly before the pact?
a: Military talks with Britain and France
Talks about joining the League of Nations
47348.e: The British and French delegation had few powers, and Poland refused to let the Red Army march through. Stalin then turned to Germany.
47348.m: The failure of the talks with the Western powers came directly before the pact.

47349.q: In which year did the Soviet Union's Congress of People's Deputies officially condemn the secret additional protocol?
47349.e: For a long time the Soviet Union denied that the secret protocol existed. In December 1989 the Congress declared it invalid from the start.
47349.m: Only in 1989 did the Soviet Union officially admit the secret protocol.

47350.q: In which city did the Wehrmacht and the Red Army hold a joint parade in September 1939?
47350.e: On 22 September 1939 the Wehrmacht handed Brest-Litovsk over to the Red Army in a joint ceremony. The city lay in the Soviet sphere.
47350.m: The joint parade in Brest-Litovsk showed the cooperation between the two dictatorships.

47351.q: How long did the Hitler-Stalin Pact last before Germany attacked the Soviet Union?
47351.e: The pact was concluded in August 1939 and was actually meant to last ten years. On 22 June 1941 Germany invaded the Soviet Union.
47351.m: The pact was meant to last ten years but did not even last two.

47352.q: Which European day of remembrance is held on the anniversary of the Hitler-Stalin Pact?
a: The day of remembrance for the victims of Stalinism and Nazism
47352.e: In 2008 the European Parliament declared 23 August a day of remembrance for the victims of totalitarian regimes. It recalls the consequences of the pact.
47352.m: In Europe, 23 August remembers the victims of Stalinism and Nazism.

47353.q: Which document by Lenin did Khrushchev quote in the Secret Speech to incriminate Stalin?
a: Lenin's work “What Is to Be Done?”
47353.e: In his so-called Testament of 1922/23, Lenin had called Stalin too rude and suggested removing him as general secretary. Khrushchev read out this text, which had long been kept quiet.
47353.m: Khrushchev used Lenin's Testament as a weapon against Stalin's memory.

47354.q: To which audience did Khrushchev give his speech against the personality cult in February 1956?
a: Only to Soviet party congress delegates
To the UN General Assembly in New York
To the whole country in a radio broadcast
47354.e: The speech took place in a closed session after the official end of the party congress. Even the delegations of foreign communist parties were excluded.
47354.m: The Secret Speech was meant only for Soviet delegates.

47355.q: How was the content of the Secret Speech first spread in the Soviet Union after the party congress?
a: By reading it aloud at party meetings
47355.e: The text was read aloud at meetings of party members and the Komsomol, but not printed. In this way millions learned about it without an official text being available.
47355.m: In the Soviet Union the Secret Speech was read aloud but for a long time not printed.

47356.q: According to the Secret Speech, what happened to most of the members and candidates of the Central Committee elected in 1934?
47356.e: Khrushchev named 98 of 139 members and candidates who had been arrested and shot in the years of terror. He stressed above all the victims within the party.
47356.m: Stalin's terror also hit his own party leadership hard.

47357.q: What was the group around Molotov, Malenkov and Kaganovich, which tried in vain to overthrow Khrushchev in 1957, called?
47357.e: The old Stalinists had a majority in the Presidium, but the Central Committee backed Khrushchev. His opponents lost their posts but were not executed.
47357.m: In 1957 Khrushchev defeated the Anti-Party Group.

47358.q: What happened to Nikita Khrushchev after he was removed in October 1964?
a: He lived as a pensioner near Moscow.
He was sent to a labour camp.
47358.e: Unlike under Stalin, the fallen party leader was not persecuted. Khrushchev lived as a pensioner until his death in 1971 and secretly dictated his memoirs.
47358.m: Khrushchev survived his fall as a pensioner.

47359.q: From 1956, what did Khrushchev call his foreign policy, according to which a war between East and West was not inevitable?
47359.e: At the 20th Party Congress Khrushchev declared that socialism and capitalism could exist side by side and compete. The conflict between the systems was to be fought out without a major war.
47359.m: Khrushchev relied on peaceful coexistence instead of an inevitable war.

47360.q: Which communist state rejected de-Stalinisation and later accused Moscow of “revisionism”?
47360.e: Mao Zedong saw the reckoning with Stalin as a betrayal of Marxism-Leninism. Out of this the Sino-Soviet split developed around 1960.
47360.m: De-Stalinisation contributed to the split between China and the Soviet Union.

47361.q: Which novel by Boris Pasternak first appeared in Italy in 1957 because it was banned in the Soviet Union?
47361.e: The Milan publisher Feltrinelli brought out the book in 1957. Pasternak received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1958 but had to turn it down under political pressure.
47361.m: Pasternak's “Doctor Zhivago” first appeared in the West.

47362.q: In which literary magazine did Solzhenitsyn's story about a day in a camp appear in 1962?
47362.e: Editor-in-chief Alexander Tvardovsky received Khrushchev's personal approval to print it. Novy Mir was regarded as the most important publication of the Thaw.
47362.m: The magazine Novy Mir was the voice of the Thaw.

47363.q: Which international event brought tens of thousands of young guests from all over the world to Moscow in 1957?
a: World Festival of Youth and Students
47363.e: The 1957 World Festival opened the city to many foreigners for the first time. For young Soviet citizens it was a rare contact with Western fashion and music.
47363.m: In 1957 Moscow welcomed the youth of the world.

47364.q: What did Khrushchev criticise in 1962 during his notorious visit to an art exhibition at the Moscow Manege?
a: Ticket prices that were too high
47364.e: Khrushchev fiercely insulted the young abstract artists. The incident showed that the Thaw had clear limits.
47364.m: The Thaw did not allow free abstract art.

47365.q: With which political event is the end of the Thaw often linked?
a: The founding of the UN in 1945
47365.e: When Brezhnev came to power in 1964, culture was again more tightly controlled. The show trial of the writers Sinyavsky and Daniel in 1966 confirmed the change.
47365.m: With Khrushchev's fall the Thaw came to an end.

47366.q: Which poet of the Thaw denounced the silence about the mass murder of the Jews of Kyiv in his 1961 poem “Babi Yar”?
47366.e: In the Babi Yar ravine, German units had murdered more than 33,000 Jews in 1941. Yevtushenko criticised the fact that there was no memorial there to the Jewish victims.
47366.m: Yevtushenko's “Babi Yar” broke a taboo of the Thaw.

47367.q: Which Soviet film won the Palme d'Or in Cannes in 1958?
47367.e: Mikhail Kalatozov's film tells a love story in the Second World War with human doubts instead of heroic pathos. It is regarded as a masterpiece of Thaw cinema.
47367.m: “The Cranes Are Flying” showed the new, more human cinema of the Thaw.

47368.q: With which type of rocket did the Soviet Union put Sputnik 1 into orbit?
47368.e: The R-7 was the world's first intercontinental missile. That is exactly why the launch frightened the West: the rocket could also have carried nuclear warheads.
47368.m: Sputnik flew on the R-7, the first intercontinental missile.

47369.q: Which designer led the Soviet rocket programme that put Sputnik into space?
47369.e: Sergei Korolev was chief designer; his name was kept secret during his lifetime. He was also behind Gagarin's flight in 1961.
47369.m: Sergei Korolev was the secret father of Sputnik.

47370.q: In which area did the USA invest heavily after the Sputnik shock with the National Defense Education Act of 1958?
47370.e: People believed that the Soviet Union was training more and better engineers. That is why more than a billion dollars went into schools, scholarships and universities.
47370.m: The Sputnik shock led to an education drive in the West.

47371.q: Which fear in the West was behind the catchphrase “missile gap”?
a: The Soviet Union had more nuclear missiles than the USA.
The USA had built too many missiles.
Missiles were too expensive for Europe.
47371.e: After Sputnik, many suspected that the Soviet Union was far ahead in intercontinental missiles. Later it turned out that the USA actually had more missiles.
47371.m: The missile gap was an exaggerated fear of the West.

47372.q: How did the press mock the failed American satellite launch of December 1957?
47372.e: The Vanguard rocket exploded in front of the cameras shortly after lift-off. The pun made the USA's humiliation after Sputnik even worse.
47372.m: The failed launch of 1957 was mocked as “Flopnik”.

47373.q: From which cosmodrome was Sputnik 1 launched?
47373.e: Baikonur lies in the steppe of present-day Kazakhstan. Yuri Gagarin also took off from there in 1961.

47374.q: Which US president came under pressure during the Sputnik shock?
47374.e: Eisenhower was president from 1953 to 1961. Critics accused his government of having neglected space travel.
47374.m: The Sputnik shock hit the Eisenhower government.

47375.q: After which event was the Brezhnev Doctrine formulated in 1968?
a: The crushing of the Prague Spring
The building of the Berlin Wall
47375.e: Warsaw Pact troops invaded Czechoslovakia in the night of 20 to 21 August 1968. The doctrine provided the justification afterwards.
47375.m: The Brezhnev Doctrine justified the end of the Prague Spring.

47376.q: What was the key statement of the Brezhnev Doctrine?
a: The sovereignty of socialist states is limited.
Every state may freely choose its system.
47376.e: If socialism was threatened in a fraternal country, the other socialist states were allowed to intervene. That is why it is called the doctrine of limited sovereignty.
47376.m: The Brezhnev Doctrine allowed intervention in fraternal socialist states.

47377.q: Which Warsaw Pact state did not take part in the invasion of Czechoslovakia in 1968?
47377.e: The Romanian leader Nicolae Ceaușescu publicly condemned the invasion. East Germany did provide troops, but they did not cross the border.
47377.m: Romania stayed out of the 1968 invasion of Prague.

47378.q: What did a Soviet government spokesman jokingly call the policy that replaced the Brezhnev Doctrine in 1989?
47378.e: Gennadi Gerasimov was referring to Frank Sinatra's song “My Way”. Every country in the Eastern Bloc should be allowed to go its own way.
47378.m: With the Sinatra Doctrine, Moscow let the Eastern Bloc go in 1989.

47379.q: Which Czechoslovak party leader stood for “socialism with a human face”?
47379.e: Dubček became party leader in January 1968 and introduced reforms. After the invasion he was removed and replaced by Gustáv Husák.
47379.m: Alexander Dubček was the face of the Prague Spring.

47380.q: What was the policy of returning to strict control in Czechoslovakia after 1968 called?
47380.e: Under Husák, reformers were removed from the party and from their jobs. About half a million party members were expelled or struck off.
47380.m: After 1968 Prague had the so-called normalisation.

47381.q: How many people fled from Czechoslovakia to Switzerland after the 1968 invasion?
47381.e: Switzerland took in about 12,000 refugees from Czechoslovakia. They were received without red tape, and the welcome was considered especially warm.
47381.m: About 12,000 Czechs and Slovaks found refuge in Switzerland in 1968.

47382.q: Which Soviet politician coined the term “stagnation” for the Brezhnev years?
47382.e: From 1986 Gorbachev spoke of “zastoi”, standstill. He used this to justify the need for his reforms.
47382.m: Gorbachev called the Brezhnev years a time of standstill.

47383.q: Which income kept the Soviet economy afloat in the 1970s despite the stagnation?
a: Exports of oil and natural gas
47383.e: The 1973 oil crisis made prices rise sharply, and Siberia provided new reserves. When the oil price fell in the mid-1980s, the crisis got worse.
47383.m: Oil and gas financed the late Soviet Union.

47384.q: What is a regime called that, like the Soviet leadership around 1980, is led by very old men?
47384.e: Andropov and Chernenko were 68 and 72 when they took office, and Brezhnev died in office in 1982 at the age of 75. Between 1982 and 1985 three party leaders died one after another.
47384.m: At the end of the stagnation, a gerontocracy ruled in the Kremlin.

47385.q: Who succeeded Leonid Brezhnev as General Secretary of the CPSU in 1982?
47385.e: Andropov had previously been head of the KGB for 15 years. He died as early as February 1984.
47385.m: The former KGB chief Andropov succeeded Brezhnev in 1982.

47386.q: Which goods did the Soviet Union have to import in large quantities from the West during the stagnation?
47386.e: Collective farming was not very productive. From the 1970s the Soviet Union regularly bought grain from the USA and Canada.
47386.m: The land of collective farms had to import grain.

47387.q: What is the unofficial economy of barter, black market and connections that grew strongly during the stagnation called?
47387.e: Because many things were missing in the shops, people got goods through connections (“blat”) and black markets. This shadow economy undermined the planned economy.
47387.m: The shadow economy flourished in the economy of shortages.

47388.q: What did the Brezhnev Doctrine, announced after the invasion of Czechoslovakia in 1968, say?
a: The sovereignty of socialist states is limited
Every state may freely choose its political system
The Soviet Union gives up nuclear weapons
All collective farms will be dissolved
47388.e: Moscow claimed the right to intervene if socialism seemed to be in danger in an Eastern Bloc state. This was used to justify crushing the Prague Spring.
47388.m: The Brezhnev Doctrine justified interventions in other socialist states.

47389.q: How did many Western states react to the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in 1979?
a: They boycotted the 1980 Olympic Games in Moscow
They declared war on the Soviet Union
They sent their own troops to Kabul
47389.e: At the initiative of the USA, about 60 states stayed away from the Summer Games in Moscow. In return, the Soviet Union and its allies boycotted the 1984 Games in Los Angeles.
47389.m: The Afghanistan war led to the Olympic boycott of 1980.

47390.q: When did the last Soviet soldiers leave Afghanistan?
47390.e: The basis was the Geneva Accords of 1988. On 15 February 1989 General Boris Gromov was the last to cross the bridge over the Amu Darya.
47390.m: In February 1989 the Soviet army withdrew from Afghanistan.

47391.q: According to official figures, roughly how many Soviet soldiers died in the Afghanistan war?
47391.e: Officially, almost 15,000 Soviet soldiers died. On the Afghan side, an estimated 600,000 to 1.5 million people died, and millions fled.
47391.m: The Afghanistan war cost the lives of about 15,000 Soviet soldiers.

47392.q: Which Afghan party had taken power in 1978 and later called on the Soviet Union for help?
47392.e: The communist party came to power in April 1978 through the so-called Saur Revolution. Its radical reforms triggered uprisings across the country.
47392.m: Afghanistan's communist People's Party called the Soviets into the country.

47393.q: With which expression did Gorbachev describe the war in Afghanistan in 1986?
47393.e: At the 27th Party Congress Gorbachev spoke openly of a bleeding wound. In this way he prepared the withdrawal of the troops.
47393.m: Gorbachev called Afghanistan a bleeding wound.

47394.q: Which weapon from the USA helped the mujahideen shoot down Soviet helicopters from 1986?
47394.e: The portable Stinger missiles were delivered via Pakistan. They threatened Soviet control of the air and helped lead Moscow to decide to withdraw.
47394.m: Stinger missiles made the Afghanistan war even more costly for the Soviet Union.

47395.q: Which Afghan president stayed in power until 1992 after the Soviet troops withdrew?
47395.e: Najibullah went on ruling with Soviet economic and military aid. When this stopped after the end of the Soviet Union, his regime collapsed in 1992.
47395.m: Najibullah held on until 1992, as long as Moscow helped.

47396.q: Which disaster of 1986 showed the weaknesses of the information policy and gave glasnost new momentum?
a: The shooting down of flight KAL 007
47396.e: At first the authorities kept the accident quiet for days. Gorbachev concluded from this that more openness was needed.
47396.m: Chernobyl sped up the policy of openness.

47397.q: What did the Communist Party of the Soviet Union lose in 1990 through a change to the constitution?
a: Its monopoly on power as the leading party
47397.e: In March 1990 Article 6 of the constitution, which laid down the party's leading role, was changed. This made other parties possible.
47397.m: In 1990 the CPSU lost its constitutional monopoly on power.

47398.q: Which body was elected in the Soviet Union's first partly free elections in 1989, with its debates broadcast live on television?
47398.e: Millions followed the open debates on television. For the first time, deputies such as Andrei Sakharov criticised the leadership in public.
47398.m: In 1989 the Congress of People's Deputies brought open debates onto television.

47399.q: Which historical crime did the Soviet Union officially admit in 1990 as part of glasnost?
a: The murder of Trotsky in Mexico
47399.e: In 1940 the NKVD had shot thousands of Polish officers; for decades Moscow had blamed the Germans for the crime. In April 1990 the Soviet Union admitted responsibility.
47399.m: In 1990 glasnost brought the truth about Katyn to light.

47400.q: What effect did glasnost have on the nationalities of the Soviet Union?
a: The republics were merged into a single state.
The borders were closed to everyone.
47400.e: Popular fronts were formed in the Baltic states, the Caucasus and Ukraine. The Baltic Way of 1989 was a human chain more than 600 kilometres long.
47400.m: The new openness strengthened the independence movements.

47401.q: What changed for newspapers in the Soviet Union because of glasnost?
a: They were allowed to report more openly on problems
They were only allowed to write about other countries
They had to appear in English
47401.e: From 1986 newspapers and magazines reported on Stalin's crimes, corruption and the Afghanistan war. Some reached print runs of millions.
47401.m: Glasnost brought more openness to the newspapers.

47402.q: Which previously hushed-up topic could be dealt with openly in films and books from 1987 thanks to glasnost?
a: The victories in the Second World War
47402.e: Works about arrests, camps and executions under Stalin had long been banned. With glasnost they reached cinemas and bookshops, for example the Georgian film “Repentance”.
47402.m: Glasnost made it possible to come to terms with Stalinist terror.

47403.q: In which present-day country is the Chernobyl nuclear power plant?
47403.e: Chernobyl lies in the north of Ukraine, close to the border with Belarus. In 1986 Ukraine still belonged to the Soviet Union. Belarus was hit particularly hard by the radioactive fallout.

47404.q: What does the half-life of a radioactive substance such as caesium-137 from Chernobyl mean?
a: The time until half of the substance has decayed
The time until the substance has disappeared completely
The time until the radiation is twice as strong
The time until the substance weighs half as much as lead
47404.e: After one half-life, half of the atoms have decayed; after two, a quarter is left. Caesium-137 has a half-life of about 30 years and therefore contaminates soil for a long time.
47404.m: After one half-life, half of a radioactive substance has decayed.

47405.q: What was actually supposed to be tested in Unit 4 at Chernobyl on the night of the accident?
a: Whether the turbine could still power the cooling pumps during a power cut
Whether the reactor could produce more electricity
Whether Kyiv's emergency power grid worked
Whether the fire brigade arrived quickly enough
47405.e: The aim was to check whether the slowing turbine would supply enough electricity until the emergency diesel generators started. Operating errors and design flaws led to the explosion.
47405.m: At Chernobyl a safety test turned into a disaster.

47406.q: What was the concrete shell built over the destroyed reactor by November 1986 called?
47406.e: The shell was built in a few months at great risk. However, it leaked and was only meant to last a few decades.
47406.m: The sarcophagus was meant to contain the radiation of the destroyed reactor.

47407.q: Why was a new protective shell slid over the destroyed reactor at Chernobyl in 2016?
a: The old sarcophagus was leaking and in danger of collapsing
The reactor was to produce electricity again
Tourists were to be protected from the rain
The old shell was too small for visitors
47407.e: The 1986 sarcophagus had been built in great haste and was only meant to last a few decades. The new steel shell is meant to contain the radiation for about 100 years.
47407.m: In 2016 a new steel shell replaced the leaking sarcophagus.

47408.q: Roughly what radius does the exclusion zone around the Chernobyl power plant have?
47408.e: The 30-kilometre zone was set up in 1986 and is still largely uninhabited today. Only a few elderly people returned illegally.
47408.m: There is an exclusion zone of about 30 kilometres around Chernobyl.

47409.q: Which radioactive substance from Chernobyl led to many cases of thyroid cancer in children in Ukraine and Belarus?
47409.e: Iodine-131 builds up in the thyroid, mainly through contaminated milk. Iodine tablets taken in time could have prevented many cases.
47409.m: Radioactive iodine was especially dangerous for children's thyroid glands.

47410.q: Which treaty, due to be signed on 20 August 1991, did the coup plotters want to prevent?
47410.e: The New Union Treaty would have given the republics much more independence. The hardliners saw it as the end of the Soviet Union.
47410.m: The coup was meant to stop the New Union Treaty.

47411.q: In front of which building, the seat of the Russian parliament, did tens of thousands gather in August 1991 to protect it from the coup plotters?
47411.e: Boris Yeltsin led the resistance from the White House. People built barricades, and many soldiers refused to act against them.
47411.m: The White House in Moscow was the centre of resistance in 1991.

47412.q: How many people died during the August coup in Moscow?
47412.e: In the night of 20 to 21 August, three young men were killed in a confrontation with armoured vehicles. They were later honoured as Heroes of the Soviet Union.
47412.m: Three young men died resisting the coup.

47413.q: Which monument did the crowd pull down outside the KGB headquarters on Lubyanka Square on 22 August 1991?
a: The monument to Peter the Great
47413.e: Dzerzhinsky had founded the Cheka, the forerunner of the KGB, in 1917. Its toppling became an image of the end of Soviet power.
47413.m: With Dzerzhinsky's monument, a symbol of the secret police fell in 1991.

47414.q: Which republic declared independence on 24 August 1991, immediately after the coup?
47414.e: The Ukrainian parliament proclaimed independence. In the referendum of 1 December 1991, more than 90 per cent voted in favour.
47414.m: Ukraine declared independence after the coup.

47415.q: Where was Gorbachev when hardliners staged a coup against him in August 1991?
a: On a state visit to Washington
47415.e: Gorbachev was held at his holiday residence in Foros in Crimea. The coup plotters declared him ill and unable to carry out his duties.
47415.m: During the coup, Gorbachev was stuck in Crimea.

47416.q: Which party did Yeltsin first suspend in Russia after the failed coup and then ban in November 1991?
47416.e: Because leading communists had supported the coup, Yeltsin suspended the party's activities in Russia. Gorbachev resigned as general secretary.
47416.m: After the coup the Communist Party lost its power.

47417.q: Which flag became Russia's state symbol after the victory over the coup plotters in August 1991?
a: The white, blue and red tricolour
The red flag with hammer and sickle
The black, yellow and white tsarist flag
The red flag with a blue stripe
47417.e: The defenders of the White House waved the old Russian tricolour. Since 22 August 1991 it has been the official flag, and the day is celebrated as Flag Day.
47417.m: The white, blue and red flag became the symbol of the new Russia in 1991.

47418.q: Where were the Belovezha Accords signed?
a: In a hunting lodge in a forest area in Belarus
On a ship in the Black Sea
47418.e: The signing took place at the government dacha of Viskuli in the Białowieża Forest. This primeval forest lies on the border with Poland.
47418.m: The end of the Soviet Union was sealed in the Białowieża Forest.

47419.q: Which Ukrainian president signed the Belovezha Accords?
47419.e: Kravchuk had been Ukraine's first elected president since December 1991. Stanislav Shushkevich signed for Belarus and Boris Yeltsin for Russia.

47420.q: When did Mikhail Gorbachev resign as president of the Soviet Union?
47420.e: Gorbachev announced his resignation on television. That same evening the Soviet flag was lowered over the Kremlin.

47421.q: Which head of state did Yeltsin phone after signing the Belovezha Accords, even before Gorbachev?
47421.e: Yeltsin informed the US president first; Gorbachev learned of it through a call from Shushkevich. Gorbachev felt this was a humiliation.
47421.m: Washington learned of the end of the Soviet Union before Gorbachev.

47422.q: Which state took over the Soviet Union's permanent seat on the UN Security Council in 1991?
47422.e: The CIS states supported Russia as the continuing state of the Soviet Union. In this way Russia also took over embassies and nuclear weapons.
47422.m: Russia inherited the Soviet Union's seat on the Security Council.

47423.q: Which state never ratified the CIS Charter and was therefore only a participant, not a full member?
47423.e: Ukraine did not want to limit its sovereignty with firm ties. In 2018 it ended its participation in the CIS bodies.
47423.m: Ukraine was never a full member of the CIS.

47424.q: Which treaty concluded in Tashkent in 1992 became the basis of a military alliance around Russia?
47424.e: In 2002 the treaty gave rise to the Collective Security Treaty Organization. Only some CIS states belong to it.
47424.m: The Tashkent treaty tied several CIS states militarily to Russia.

47425.q: Which state downgraded its CIS membership to associate membership in 2005?
47425.e: Turkmenistan sees itself as a permanently neutral state. This neutrality has been recognised by the UN since 1995.
47425.m: Neutral Turkmenistan is only an associate member of the CIS.

47426.q: Which office did Boris Yeltsin hold from 1985, before he was removed in 1987 after sharply criticising the party leadership?
a: Foreign minister of the Soviet Union
47426.e: Gorbachev brought Yeltsin in as a reformer to lead the Moscow party organisation. After criticising the pace of reform, he lost the post in 1987.
47426.m: Yeltsin was removed as Moscow party chief in 1987.

47427.q: In which region of the Soviet Union did Boris Yeltsin begin his party career?
47427.e: From 1976 to 1985 Yeltsin led the party in Sverdlovsk region in the Urals, around today's Yekaterinburg. There he was regarded as an energetic construction engineer.
47427.m: Yeltsin's career began in the Urals.

47428.q: Which economic policy did Russia pursue under Yeltsin from 1992?
a: Rapid freeing of prices and privatisation
A return to the planned economy
47428.e: The so-called shock therapy under Yegor Gaidar led to high inflation. In the privatisation a few so-called oligarchs became very rich.
47428.m: Under Yeltsin, Russia went through economic shock therapy.

47429.q: Which office did Boris Yeltsin take on in May 1990?
a: Chairman of the Supreme Soviet of Russia
Prime minister of the Soviet Union
47429.e: The parliament of the Russian Soviet Republic narrowly elected Yeltsin as its chairman. Shortly afterwards Russia declared its sovereignty within the Soviet Union.
47429.m: From 1990 Yeltsin had his own power base in the Russian parliament.

47430.q: Which war did Russia begin under President Yeltsin in December 1994?
47430.e: The republic of Chechnya had declared itself independent. The war ended in 1996 with a ceasefire after heavy losses.
47430.m: The First Chechen War began under Yeltsin in 1994.

47431.q: Against which Communist candidate did Yeltsin win the 1996 presidential run-off?
47431.e: At the start of the campaign Yeltsin was far behind in the polls. With strong support from the media and business people, he won the run-off.
47431.m: In 1996 Yeltsin beat the Communist Zyuganov.

47432.q: Which crisis hit Russia in August 1998 under President Yeltsin?
a: A financial crisis with a devaluation of the rouble
47432.e: The state could no longer pay its debts, and the rouble lost much of its value. Many people lost their savings.
47432.m: The rouble crisis of 1998 shook Russia.

47433.q: How did Sakharov learn in December 1986 that he was allowed to return from exile?
a: Through a phone call from Gorbachev
Through a visit from the KGB chief
47433.e: A telephone was specially installed in his flat, and Gorbachev called him on it. His release was seen as a sign of glasnost.
